Ordinal analysis measures the steps, assigning PA the ordinal ε₀. The picture to keep is a ladder no rung of which can see its own footing, the exact shape Chapter 7 gives to a tower of overseers.

7.6. Tarski's undefinability of truth🔗

A truth predicate satisfies True(⌜φ⌝) ↔ φ for every sentence, Tarski's schema T.

Definition 2.14 (Definable truth predicate). A language interpreting arithmetic has a definable truth predicate when some formula True(x) satisfies schema T for every sentence of the language.

Material adequacy plus definability makes the verdict system universal over its own sentences: every boolean condition the language can state, including the negation of the predicate composed with the diagonal, is some sentence's verdict pattern.

Theorem 2.15 (Tarski, 1936). No language that can represent its own syntax and interpret arithmetic has a definable truth predicate.

theorem c2_tarski {A : Type _} (True? : A → A → Bool) (hT : ∀ g : A → Bool, ∃ a, True? a = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict True? hT

Proof. Such a predicate is a reflective verdict, and no_reflective_verdict says none exists. Unfolding, the diagonal builds the liar L with True?(⌜L⌝) ↔ ¬ True?(⌜L⌝), and adequacy turns that into L ↔ ¬ L. ∎

Identifying Y and t. Bool and negation. The witness is the liar, which is liar_query read as a sentence rather than a set or a program. The liar is not a curiosity at the edge of the theory; it is the exact obstruction.

Tarski versus Gödel. Gödel's Prov is definable, because provability is recursively enumerable, and the price is incompleteness: the predicate exists but the theory cannot decide the sentence it produces. Tarski's True would have to be definable to run the same diagonal, and the conclusion is that it is not definable at all, because if it were the liar would be an outright contradiction rather than an undecided sentence. Provability is a shadow of truth the system can cast; truth itself it cannot hold. The gap between them is the room the first theorem lives in. Cleanly: if truth were definable it would be a complete sound provability predicate, which c2_godel_semantic already refuted.

7.6.1. The hierarchy of metalanguages🔗

Truth for L is definable, just not in L: it is definable in a richer L' with the resources to quantify over L's sentences. Truth for L' needs L'', and so on up an unbounded hierarchy, each level defining truth for the one below and none its own. This is the consistency-strength ladder again, and not by coincidence: both are the second-theorem shape.

There are ways to buy a language its own truth predicate, and each pays a price the recipe predicts. Kripke's 1975 theory makes the predicate partial, undefined on ungrounded sentences like the liar, built as the least fixed point of a monotone operator; the liar never settles, and adequacy holds only for grounded sentences. This dodges Tarski by refusing totality, exactly the move separating halting from Rice: let the deciding object withhold judgment and the flat impossibility relaxes into a statement about where judgment must be withheld.

Remark 2.16 (Truth probes and Chapter 8). A truth predicate that is total, exact, and expressible in the system whose outputs it judges is exactly what Tarski forbids. Chapter 8 studies probes reading internal state to estimate whether a model "believes" its output, and the standing objection is Tarskian. The resolution is not to defeat the theorem but to change the domain: from outputs to activations, from a two-valued verdict to a continuous score on a connected space, where the intermediate value theorem takes over.

7.7. Turing and the halting problem🔗

Definition 2.17 (Halting decider). A halting decider for a universal system f : A → A → Bool is a total D : A → Bool intended to satisfy D a = f a a, where f a a records the halting behavior of program a on its own code.

Theorem 2.18 (Turing, 1936). For every universal f and every candidate D there is a program a with f a a ≠ D a.

theorem c2_turing_halting {A : Type _} (f : A → A → Bool) (hf : ∀ g : A → Bool, ∃ a, f a = g) (D : A → Bool) : ∃ a, f a a ≠ D a := match hf (fun a => !(D a)) with | ⟨a₀, ha₀⟩ => ⟨a₀, fun h => bool_not_fpf (D a₀) ((congrFun ha₀ a₀).symm.trans h)⟩

Proof. Universality names the contrarian behavior fun a => !(D a) by a₀. Evaluating at a₀ gives f a₀ a₀ = !(D a₀). If the decider were right there we would get !(D a₀) = D a₀, refuted by bool_not_fpf. ∎

The contrarian program is the classical construction: run D on your own code, then loop if D says halt and halt if D says loop. Same a₀ as everywhere else, now reading Y as halts-or-loops and t as "do the opposite."

The partiality subtlety. A real decider must be total, while the programs it judges are partial. The contrarian program is partial in exactly the way that breaks a total decider. If deciders could be partial the theorem would not follow in this form, and the correct statement becomes Rice's, about total decision of a nontrivial semantic property.

The universal machine is the wrapper. The hypothesis ∀ g, ∃ a, f a = g is the existence of a universal Turing machine, and Turing built one. Without it there is no closure under diagonalization, and halting for a non-universal model can be decidable; for finite automata it is trivial. Undecidability is a property of systems rich enough to host their own interpreter.

Where halting sits. Halting is the canonical undecidable problem, complete for the r.e. sets under many-one reduction. It is Σ₁, one existential over a decidable matrix, the same shape as Prov, which is no accident: Prov is halting for a proof search.

Remark 2.19 (Runtime verification). No static analyzer decides termination for all programs. For AI systems the behavioral questions are far harder, whether a model will ever produce disallowed content or an agent ever take an unsafe action, and halting is the floor. The safety chapters do not lean on Turing directly, because they want quantitative statements, but Turing is the qualitative backstop saying the quantitative work is necessary.

7.8. Rice's theorem🔗

A property is semantic when it depends only on the function a program computes, and nontrivial when some programs have it and some do not. Rice sweeps the class in one argument.

Definition 2.20 (Semantic decider). For universal f, a semantic decider is a total D : A → Bool claiming to compute f a a from a alone.

Theorem 2.21 (Rice, diagonal core). For every universal f and every D, some a has f a a ≠ D a.

theorem c2_rice_diagonal {A : Type _} (f : A → A → Bool) (hf : ∀ g : A → Bool, ∃ a, f a = g) (D : A → Bool) : ∃ a, f a a ≠ D a := c2_turing_halting f hf D

Proof. c2_turing_halting under a change of reading. ∎

That Rice's core proof is literally Turing's is the chapter's thesis made blunt. Turing decides one property, Rice any property, and the diagonal does not notice, because it only ever sees a boolean D and flips it. What distinguishes them is entirely the wrapper.

Theorem 2.22 (Rice, full form). Let P be a nontrivial semantic property of partial recursive functions. Then {e | φ_e ∈ P} is not recursive.

Proof (structure). Nontriviality gives a program with the property and one without; without loss the everywhere-undefined program lacks P. Given a claimed decider, reduce halting to it: from any program and input build a program behaving like the witness if the input halts and like the empty program otherwise, so it has P exactly when the input halts. A decider for P would decide halting. ∎

This needs an acceptable numbering with the s-m-n theorem and a case analysis on which side of P the empty function falls, using classical logic and Mathlib's recursion theory. The companion development formalizes the core and the safety corollaries in Foundation/F_02_RiceTheorem.lean: Foundation.rice_diagonal is Theorem 2.21 in mismatch form, Foundation.rice_general is the property version for nontrivial P : Bool → Bool, and Foundation.no_automated_self_test is the reading we want.

Identifying Y and t. Bool and negation. What is new is the quantifier over properties, and the recipe absorbs it: each nontrivial property yields a boolean D through the reduction, and one fixed-point-free t defeats them all.

The hypothesis. Nontriviality is load-bearing, the analogue of surjectivity being nondegenerate. A trivial property is decided by a constant function and there is no contradiction, because the constant decider is never wrong. The diagonal needs two outcomes to flip between.

7.8.1. Rice–Shapiro and the shape of the undecidable🔗

Rice–Shapiro says a semantic property has an r.e. index set only if it is determined by finite information: a function has it exactly when some finite subfunction does, and every extension keeps it. Properties violating this, "is total," "computes a constant," are not even r.e.

That finer picture is what the safety chapters need, because it locates the line between checkable and uncheckable. A property depending only on finitely much observed behavior can be recognized when it appears though its absence never confirmed, which is the logical form of "you can catch a model doing something bad but cannot certify it never will." A property depending on the whole infinite behavior cannot even be recognized. Rice–Shapiro is the classical statement that monitoring is possible and certification is not.

Remark 2.23 (No automated semantic testing). A property of the function a model computes, whether it is honest or aligned or safe, is semantic, and Rice says no general automated test decides it for universal systems. no_automated_self_test is exactly this. A benchmark is an attempt to decide a semantic property by running finitely many inputs, and Rice is why a benchmark can only sample, never certify.

7.9. The categorical unification🔗

In a cartesian closed category a system is a map f : A → Y^A, and the cleanest hypothesis is a section s : Y^A → A with f ∘ s = id. Lawvere's theorem is that any t : Y → Y then has a fixed point y : 1 → Y with t ∘ y = y. The proof is the same diagonal drawn as a commuting diagram: precompose with A → A × A, transpose, apply t, and use the section to find the self-referential point.

Each classical theorem is Lawvere's theorem in a particular cartesian closed category, not merely an argument shaped like it. Cantor is sets with Y = 2. Turing and Rice live in a category of assemblies or a realizability topos, where maps are tracked by programs and the section is a universal machine.

We do not compile the categorical version, since doing it honestly needs a category theory library and the payoff is conceptual. The value of knowing the source is that it tells you when a new impossibility will be an instance: whenever the system is a map into an internal function space with a section, and the outcome object carries a fixed-point-free map, only the reading remains.

7.10. Interlude: the wrapper is the mathematics🔗

The engine is three lines precisely because a century of work moved all the difficulty into the wrappers, and the wrappers are hard. Coding syntax into arithmetic, building a universal machine, constructing an acceptable numbering with s-m-n, establishing the derivability conditions: each is a substantial theorem, and each is what a graduate course actually spends its time proving. The diagonal is the punchline, and punchlines are short.

The consequence for the rest of this thesis is that to prove a new impossibility you never re-prove the diagonal. You argue that a model with such-and-such capabilities is universal over the relevant behaviors, that a defense must answer every injection including those about itself, that a probe is asked to be a total exact predicate on the states whose truth it reports. When that argument succeeds the impossibility is immediate; when it fails, the failure is exactly the escape hatch.

There is a quieter lesson. Because the engine is axiom-free and compiles while the wrappers are cited, this development is honest about its own confidence in a way informal mathematics rarely is. The parts we are certain of are checked by the kernel; the parts depending on a large library are named so you can find the verified statement.

7.11. What varies, and what does not🔗

| Theorem | A (indices) | Y | t | Wrapper (universality is...) | |---|---|---|---|---| | Cantor | a set | Bool | ! | a power-set surjection | | Russell | a universe of sets | Bool | ! | unrestricted comprehension | | Gödel I | codes of formulas | Bool | ! | representability plus completeness | | Gödel II | codes of formulas | Bool | Löb's map | derivability conditions | | Tarski | codes of sentences | Bool | ! | a definable truth predicate | | Turing | programs | Bool | ! | a universal language | | Rice | programs | Bool | ! | reduction from a nontrivial property |

The outcome type is Bool in every row and the flip is negation in every row but one, where Löb's map is negation in modal disguise. The index type and the wrapper are where the mathematics sits, and they are what one actually learns from these results. The diagonal is not what you learn; it is what you already knew from the first one.

The compiled fifth column is always one of no_universal, cantor, liar_query, no_reflective_verdict, c2_diagonal_lemma, or c2_rice_diagonal, and each is Theorem 1.4 under a fixed point of negation. Chapter 3 adds an eighth and ninth row and no new machinery.

One honest caveat bridges to the second half. Every theorem in the table is a flat impossibility, silent on how close you can come, how many counterexamples exist, or what finding one costs. The diagonal is a yes-or-no instrument because Y is Bool and t has no fixed point at all.

A last observation. In every classical instance universality was granted almost by definition of the object: a power set is all subsets, a language is closed under its own interpreter. In the safety instances universality is an idealization, and the content is the argument that a system with desirable properties, being faithful, calibrated, and covering, would have to be universal and so cannot exist.

7.12. Historical notes🔗

Cantor's diagonal is 1891, though the 1874 uncountability proof contains the idea. Russell wrote to Frege in 1902. Gödel's theorems are the 1931 paper; the diagonal lemma is often attributed jointly to Gödel and Carnap. Tarski's undefinability is 1936, Turing's halting result 1936, Rice's theorem 1953, Löb's 1955, and Solovay's arithmetical completeness of GL 1976.

The unification is Lawvere (1969); the accessible modern account working out the instances is Yanofsky (2003), whose organization this chapter follows. Rogers's Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability remains standard for the recursion theory behind Rice, and Boolos's The Logic of Provability for the modal treatment of the second theorem.

8. Related Work and Positioning🔗

This chapter says what has been done before and why it does not already contain the present contribution. It is organized by the kind of claim each body of work makes, because the relevant question differs by kind: for the unification literature the question is whether the AI-safety results are already covered, for the impossibility literature it is whether the results are already unified, and for the formalization literature it is whether anything of this shape has been machine-checked.

8.1. Unifications of the diagonal🔗

The claim that the classical self-referential impossibilities share one structure is not new and is not claimed as new here.

Lawvere's 1969 paper is the origin. It proves that in a cartesian closed category, a point-surjective map forces every endomorphism of the codomain to have a fixed point, and observes that Cantor, Russell, Gödel, Tarski, and Turing fall out by choosing the category and the endomorphism. Yanofsky's 2003 account works the instances out concretely and without categorical machinery, and it is the presentation Chapter 4 follows.

What these do not do is instantiate the schema at machine learning. Lawvere's targets are set theory, logic, and computability; the systems he quantifies over are mathematical objects whose self-application is exact. The gap this thesis closes is not the observation that a schema exists but the demonstration that particular safety properties of statistical models are instances of it, and the demonstration is nontrivial precisely because the instantiation fails on a literal reading: a finite model is not point-surjective. Chapter 9 is the work that repairs this, and it has no counterpart in the unification literature.

8.2. Impossibility results in machine learning🔗

There is a substantial literature of individual impossibility results. The fairness-tradeoff theorems, the no-free-lunch results, the limits on calibration under distribution shift, and the security analyses of prompt injection each establish that some desirable conjunction is unachievable.

These are the results this thesis claims to unify, and the relationship is asymmetric in an important way. Each is stated and proved within its own formalism, and each is correct within it. The contribution here is not a better proof of any one of them; several of the original arguments are shorter than mine. The contribution is that the same two lemmas generate them, which is a claim about the collection rather than about any member, and which therefore cannot be established by improving any single result.

The honest form of the claim matters. I do not derive every published impossibility result from the schemas. I derive the ones stated in Part III, name the load-bearing step in each, and in two of the four case studies find that the load-bearing step is not the diagonal. Chapters 13 and 14 reach their main results by counting and by invariance respectively. That is evidence against the strongest version of the unification thesis, and Chapter 16 treats it as such.

8.3. Calibration and hallucination🔗

The calibration literature asks when a model's stated confidence matches its empirical accuracy, and the reliability diagram is its central instrument. The hallucination literature asks when a model asserts what is not so.

The relation to Chapter 7 is a matter of what is being quantified over. The statistical notion of calibration is a property of a distribution: averaged over a population of queries at a stated confidence level, the accuracy matches. The notion this thesis uses is pointwise and exact, as Remark 3.11 sets out, and it is strictly stronger. The trilemma is therefore not a statement that models cannot be statistically calibrated, and reading it as one would be an error. It is a statement about a stronger property, and its practical force comes from the approximate versions of Chapter 9, where the pointwise requirement is relaxed to a band.

This is the clearest place where the thesis could be overclaimed, and I have tried to state the hypothesis precisely enough that the overclaim is visible when it occurs.

8.4. Interpretability and probing🔗

The interpretability program seeks to read a model's internal state and recover what the model represents. J-space probing reads the derivative of the computation rather than its activations; eliciting latent knowledge asks for a reporter that tells the truth about a latent state even where humans cannot check.

Chapter 11's result is negative and is best understood as bounding a goal rather than criticizing a method: a probe that reads every verdict pattern of the model it probes is a reflective verdict, and no such thing exists. This does not say probes are useless, and Chapter 11 is careful to say what it does not say. It says that the complete version of the goal is unavailable, which relocates the research question from whether a full readout exists to how much of one is attainable.

For eliciting latent knowledge the relationship is different again, and it is the case that most constrains the thesis. The obstruction there is a counting fact about functions agreeing on a subset. It requires no self-reference, and the diagonal contributes nothing to it. Chapter 13 reports this.

8.5. Formal verification of machine learning🔗

Formal verification in machine learning has concentrated on properties of specific networks: robustness certificates within a ball, output-range bounds, and monotonicity, discharged by SMT solvers or abstract interpretation. These verify a particular trained model against a particular specification.

The corpus here does something different in kind. It verifies theorems about every system satisfying stated hypotheses, which is why it is written in a proof assistant with a dependent type theory rather than in a solver. There is no trained network anywhere in the four libraries. The tradeoff is the usual one: the statements are far more general and say nothing whatever about any particular deployed model, which is why Chapter 15 exists.

I am not aware of prior work that machine-checks impossibility results for AI safety properties. If the claim of novelty in this thesis is anywhere at its strongest, it is here, and it is also the easiest to check: the corpus builds, or it does not.

8.6. Summary of the gap🔗

The unification literature has the schemas but not the instances. The impossibility literature has the instances but not the unification. The calibration literature studies a weaker hypothesis than the one the trilemma consumes. The verification literature checks models rather than theorems about models. This thesis occupies the intersection, and Chapter 15 tests whether the intersection is inhabited by anything real.

9. Part II: The Two Engines🔗

10. Three Trilemmata, One Theorem🔗

Three impossibility results circulate under different names with different proofs. The Hallucination Trilemma: a model cannot be faithful, covering, and calibrated at once. The Defense Trilemma: a wrapper against prompt injection cannot preserve utility and be complete at once. The coupling theorem: a model whose confidence separates true from false answers owns a query it can place on neither side. Each was proved with topology. All three are no_reflective_verdict, proved without topology at all.

The claim is stronger than "these rhyme." In Lean their proof terms are literally equal, witnessed by rfl. What differs is the reading of one Boolean v : Q → Q → Bool: confident and correct about q; the wrapper renders q safe; confidence puts q on the true side. The reading changes; the theorem does not.

The real work connects each domain's desiderata to the hypothesis the engine needs, reflectivity: every pattern of verdicts over Q is named by some element of Q. The diagonal buys freedom from topology and pays with that premise. For prompt injection the price is low, since prompts are arbitrary self-describing text; for a fixed representation space it is high, and Chapter 4's route is more physical there.

That the three share a mechanism is the main result, not a curiosity: patching one cannot help the others, because there is nothing domain-specific to patch.

Each trilemma below has the same shape — informal statement, numbered conditions, the argument that they make the system a reflective verdict, a one-line Lean instance, a reading of the liar witness, and what reflectivity costs. The c3_ blocks are short on purpose: the mathematics was finished in Chapter 1, and these rename its conclusion. Spend attention on the definitions, because disagreement about a premise is the only honest way out of an impossibility the machine has checked.

The word trilemma is used two ways: a conflict among three desiderata over one Boolean verdict, and, in the master trilemma, a conflict among Utility, Control, and Transparency where you may keep at most two.

10.1. What "reflective" demands🔗

A reflective verdict on Q is a universal v : Q → Q → Bool. no_reflective_verdict says none exists, and liar_query produces the p with v p p = !(v p p).

Two ingredients go in: Boolean outcomes with the flip as controller, which bool_not_fpf shows has no fixed point, and universality. Universality is not the claim that a model is powerful or large but that its naming of verdict-patterns is complete. The source differs by domain — an in-context learner promptable to any behavior, unrestricted prompt text, a representation space encoding any pattern over its own states — and these are not equally believable.

The flip means this. In each domain there is an honest self-report: faithfulness, completeness, and exact separation each say that applied to its own description the system should output the opposite of what that description predicts. A confident answer should be correct, so a query predicting its own incorrectness should be answered against the prediction.

Remark 3.0 (Surjection or section). Reflectivity can be weakened to a section s : (Q → Bool) → Q with v (s g) = g. The two agree for the impossibility, since the engine needs one preimage of the diagonal pattern. The domain stories below, an in-context learner realizing a described behavior, a prompt encoding a pattern, a representation encoding an assignment, are all stories about producing a preimage on demand, which is a section.

Counting gives the finite intuition and then fails: with |Q| = n there are n rows and 2ⁿ patterns, and the missing one can be taken to be q ↦ !(v q q). Chapter 1's theorem forbids reflectivity even when Q is infinite, so "the model is large" buys no escape.

A worked micro-instance. Take Q = {a, b, c} and lay v out as a table with rows self-contexts and columns queries. If the diagonal reads true, false, true, the engine builds g = false, true, false, which disagrees with each row at its own column, so no row equals g. Read the other way: hand me a row p with v p = g and v p p = g p = !(v p p), which bool_not_fpf forbids. The liar is a specific row, and nothing depended on the size of Q. Every argument here is this table, grown until the rows are model behaviors, defense verdicts, or probe outputs.

10.2. The Hallucination Trilemma🔗

10.2.1. The desiderata🔗

A trustworthy model should be faithful (confident answers are right), calibrated (confidence tracks correctness), and covering (it answers, sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly). None is controversial alone, and the trilemma says they cannot hold together once the model is asked about its own verdicts. Either it answers confidently and wrongly, or its confidence stops tracking correctness at the hard cases, or it retreats to a response so uniform it no longer covers.

Fix a domain Q of queries, read also as self-contexts, with the confident-correctness self-verdict v : Q → Q → Bool. The diagonal v p p is the model's verdict on its own description.

Definition 3.1 (Strict calibration). v is strictly calibrated when confidence exactly decides correctness, so v p q is a genuine Boolean, true exactly when the model is both confident and correct. Calibration licenses modeling the self-assessment as a total function into Bool. Without it, confidence and correctness come apart by degrees and the verdict is real-valued; Chapter 6 handles that relaxation.

Definition 3.2 (Faithfulness). v is faithful when confidence implies correctness, with no confident error. Faithfulness fixes the controller as the flip: the honest self-report of a faithful calibrated model on a query predicting its own incorrectness must come out correct, hence opposite to the prediction. A faithful calibrated verdict may never equal its own negation, since such a value would be a confident answer correct exactly when incorrect.

Definition 3.3 (Coverage). v is covering when the model answers on both sides: some query gets a correct confident verdict and some does not. This is nontriviality. It rules out the constant model, which is faithful and calibrated for free, and it makes the flip act on something with content.

Definition 3.4 (Reflectivity). v is reflective when universal: ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g. This says the model can be queried about its own verdicts, including the diagonal pattern.

10.2.2. Why the conditions make the verdict reflective🔗

Two halves. The first makes v the right kind of object, the second makes it universal, and only together do they give a reflective verdict.

Calibration makes the codomain Bool, since a calibrated model does not hedge between confident and correct. Drop it and you are in the real-valued world where the controller is the complement, fixed-point-free except at one half, which is the topological story. Faithfulness makes the controller the flip: the honest response to "you will be incorrect here" is to be correct, hence against the prediction.

Universality holds because the model is an in-context learner over its own query space. A self-context is expressible as a query, so asking for g is prompting with a description of g, and a competent learner imitates it. The stronger the model, the more completely it can be steered, so universality is a consequence of flexibility rather than a weakness.

Together: calibration makes v Boolean, faithfulness makes the controller the flip, coverage makes the flip bite, reflectivity makes the diagonal pattern an actual query. The three are not independently impossible; they are impossible in a reflective model, and the model's own capability supplies the reflectivity.

One reading sounds paradoxical: a better model is more nearly reflective, hence more impossible. The theorem does not say the model breaks everywhere, only that the three cannot all hold at the liar query, and a more capable model is steerable to that query more reliably. Capability sharpens the trilemma rather than defeating it — one of the few places the diagonal predicts the direction of an effect.

10.2.3. The impossibility🔗

theorem c3_hallucination_trilemma {Q : Type _} (v : Q → Q → Bool) (reflective : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict v reflective

Proof. reflective is exactly the universality no_reflective_verdict requires. Faithfulness and calibration have already been spent: calibration in choosing Bool, faithfulness in the flip controller. Coverage is spent in reflectivity, which asks for the flipping pattern by name. ∎

theorem c3_hallucination_liar {Q : Type _} (v : Q → Q → Bool) (reflective : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g) : ∃ p, v p p = !(v p p) := liar_query v reflective

Proof. Immediate from liar_query. ∎

10.2.4. Reading the liar witness🔗

Topologically p is a query where confidence lands at threshold and the answer on the truth boundary; here it is a query predicting its own verdict and flipping it. Concretely it is a prompt of the form "answer the following with confidence exactly if you would be wrong to." A faithful model must answer it correctly, which by construction is to answer it incorrectly; a calibrated model cannot escape by lowering confidence, since calibration ties confidence to correctness; and a covering model cannot escape by refusing, since the pattern it failed to realize was the flipping pattern itself.

10.2.5. The three escapes🔗

Drop faithfulness. The model answers confidently and wrongly. This is ordinary hallucination, and the diagonal says it is structurally necessary for a reflective calibrated model rather than an accident to train away at the margin. Bounding how often is Chapter 5's work.

Drop calibration. The model hedges, lowering confidence on hard self-referential cases so no confident answer is wrong, at the cost of confidence no longer meaning what it says elsewhere. This is why deployed models are deliberately underconfident near their limits.

Drop coverage. The model stops answering. Refusal training is this applied selectively, and the diagonal warns that the region you must carve is exactly the self-referential one. Chapter 4 reads the same move as disconnecting the query space.

No escape removes the liar; each decides what to do at it. The query is forced by reflectivity, and the only freedom is which desideratum to spend, which is why "we will just fix hallucination" is not a coherent program.

Remark 3.11 (Calibration is pointwise and exact). Definition 3.1 is much stronger than the statistical calibration of the reliability-diagram literature, which asks only that a stated confidence c be correct a fraction c of the time averaged over a population, and says nothing about any single query. The trilemma's calibration is a two-way tie at every query. The trilemma therefore does not say statistically calibrated models are impossible; they exist.

10.2.6. Relation to statistical inevitability results🔗

An older tradition proves hallucination inevitable by statistical or computability arguments, deriving confident falsehood and quantifying how often. The diagonal derives a single boundary query and says nothing about frequency, so they are complementary. Only the stochastic dichotomy turns a boundary into falsehood with positive probability.

The honest caveat. Reflectivity is the whole cost of dropping topology, and for hallucination it is a middling assumption. Treating the model as an in-context learner that imitates any described verdict-pattern is defensible for large models, but "any pattern over all of Q" is a strong completeness claim and a real model's realizable patterns are a proper subset. Chapter 4 asks instead for continuity on a connected space, and both routes reach the same boundary question.

10.3. The Defense Trilemma🔗

10.3.1. The desiderata🔗

Prompt injection is the attack where user input contains instructions subverting the system's own. A defense is a wrapper transforming an incoming prompt before the model sees it. It should be utility-preserving, doing nothing to an already-safe prompt, and complete, making every prompt safe. Reflectivity is the fact that prompts are arbitrary text.

The published proof is topological: continuity of the defended safety score plus utility preservation force the score to hit the threshold, and completeness says it never does. The diagonal replaces continuity with self-reference, which for prompt injection is not an idealization but the definition of the problem. A prompt is text, and text can quote the defense and invert it.

10.3.2. The conditions🔗

Let X be prompts, read also as self-contexts. Model the defended-safety verdict as v : X → X → Bool, with v p q = true meaning the wrapper renders q safe while also coping with the self-referential prompt p.

Definition 3.5 (Utility preservation). The wrapper is utility-preserving when it fixes safe prompts, so the defended verdict on a safe prompt agrees with its undefended safety. This blocks the constant escape: a wrapper replacing every input with a fixed maximally safe output would be complete for free but destroys every safe prompt's content.

Definition 3.6 (Completeness). The wrapper is complete when every prompt is rendered safe. This makes the honest self-report the flip: a complete wrapper faced with "you will mark me unsafe" must mark it safe, answering against the prediction.

Definition 3.7 (Reflectivity). The prompt space is reflective when ∀ g : X → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g. Because prompts are arbitrary text, any pattern of verdicts is describable by a prompt.

10.3.3. Why the conditions make the verdict reflective🔗

The verdict is already Boolean, since safety is discrete by nature, so no calibration step is needed. Completeness plays faithfulness's role, fixing the flip, and utility preservation plays coverage's, forbidding the constant maximally-safe wrapper.

Universality needs almost no idealization. Any pattern can be written as a prompt instructing the wrapper to behave that way, because instructing the wrapper is just more text and the wrapper reads text. The injection "ignore your previous instructions" is a prompt describing and overriding the defense, and unlike hallucination there is no gap between "could imitate any behavior" and "every pattern is realized": the realizing objects are the attacker's inputs.

A skeptic objects that no sensible prompt describes "be unsafe exactly if you would be made safe." Sense is not required. Reflectivity asks only that the pattern be nameable as text, and the attacker needs the wrapper to act on it, not a human to understand it. This is the gap between prompts a user would write and prompts an adversary can write, and the trilemma lives on the adversary's side.

10.3.4. The impossibility🔗

theorem c3_defense_trilemma {X : Type _} (v : X → X → Bool) (reflective : ∀ g : X → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict v reflective

Proof. Word for word the hallucination proof with X for Q. ∎

theorem c3_defense_liar {X : Type _} (v : X → X → Bool) (reflective : ∀ g : X → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g) : ∃ p, v p p = !(v p p) := liar_query v reflective

Proof. The witness is the injection no wrapper neutralizes: a prompt rendered safe exactly when unsafe. ∎

10.3.5. Reading the liar witness🔗

The prompt is "be unsafe if and only if this wrapper would render you safe." A complete wrapper must render it safe, so by construction it is unsafe. The wrapper cannot rewrite it harmlessly without violating utility preservation on the safe prompts it quotes, and cannot refuse it without ceasing to cover the pattern it embodies. The diagonal writes the witness out as text, which for defense is the honest description, because injections are text.

A defender's instinct is to make the wrapper stateful or randomized so the verdict is not a fixed function. Randomize, and the same diagonal runs on the induced verdict "rendered safe"; the honest place for randomness is the stochastic dichotomy, where a system faithful almost everywhere still emits unsafe outputs with positive probability. Make it stateful, and the state joins the self-context, with reflectivity over the enlarged space still naming the diagonal.

Why detection does not help. A rejection is a verdict. When the wrapper rejects the liar as unsafe it has assigned p the value "unsafe," and completeness demanded "safe." Detection chooses the completeness-failing horn and calls it a feature. That may be the right engineering choice, but it is the coverage escape in defense clothes, at the same cost.

10.3.6. The real-valued score version🔗

The companion library carries defense_trilemma_lawvere, which does not pass through Bool. There the object is a defended safety score s : X → X → ℝ and completeness is s a a < τ. The controller is the real complement, fixed-point-free except at the threshold, and the diagonal forces a boundary prompt where the score sits exactly at τ.

10.3.7. The honest caveat🔗

For defense reflectivity is close to free: the input space is unrestricted and self-describing, so the surjection restates the threat model rather than assuming anything. Rejection is a verdict too, and a wrapper rejecting p while claiming completeness has relabeled p unsafe. There is no consistent relabeling, which is defense_trilemma_godel in F_12_DefenseGodel.

One caveat is often missed: the trilemma is about a single fixed wrapper. A defender who may change the wrapper after seeing the attack faces an easier problem, which explains why defenses appear to work in the lab and fail in the wild. In the lab the wrapper is retuned each round; in the wild it is fixed and the attacker constructs its liar. Any process that keeps changing the wrapper is not a wrapper but a game.

10.4. The Coupling Theorem🔗

10.4.1. The desideratum🔗

Probing studies read truth off activations, treating truth as a continuous field. The coupling theorem asks what such a probe requires of the model answering over the same space: if the model ever answers truly and ever falsely, and its confidence separates the two exactly, some query carries confidence exactly at threshold while its answer sits exactly on the truth boundary.

The framing is generous rather than adversarial. It grants the central assumption, that truth is a continuous decodable field, and the answer is not that probes fail but that a probe good enough to separate truth exactly comes with a boundary it cannot avoid. The theorem is a frontier for the program, not a refutation.

The desideratum is truth-separation in exact biconditional form. Under it the confidence field is a total exact Boolean decider of truth over representation space — a definable truth predicate, which Chapter 2's Tarski reading forbids.

10.4.2. The conditions🔗

Let X be representation space, read also as the space of self-referential representations. Model the verdict as v : X → X → Bool, with v p q = true meaning confidence places q on the true side in self-context p.

Definition 3.8 (Truth-separation). v is truth-separating when confidence and truth agree exactly and two-ways: v p q = true iff q is true in context p. This plays calibration's and faithfulness's roles at once: exactness makes the codomain Bool, and the two-way tie means a representation predicting its own falsehood must be judged true, against its prediction.

Definition 3.9 (Coverage for coupling). The verdict is covering when the model answers some queries truly and some falsely, so the probe separates a nonempty true region from a nonempty false region.

Definition 3.10 (Reflectivity for representations). The space is reflective when ∀ g : X → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g: every pattern of truth-verdicts is encoded by some representation. This is the strong hypothesis.

10.4.3. Why the condition makes the verdict reflective🔗

Truth-separation does double duty: exactness makes the verdict genuinely Boolean, and the two-way tie means a representation encoding "the probe will place me on the false side" must, if honored as truth, be placed on the true side. Coverage supplies content, since without both values the truth boundary is empty.

Universality is where coupling differs in believability. Every pattern must be encoded by some representation, including the diagonal one, and for an activation space that is a real assumption: activations are expressive, but nothing guarantees every Boolean pattern over states is realized by a state. This is why the paper's main result is topological — connectedness follows the manifold hypothesis, complete self-encoding follows from nothing obvious.

Where it applies the reading is exact. Grant self-encoding and an exactly truth-separating probe is a total self-applicable truth predicate, so Tarski forbids it and the diagonal names the coupled query. This is Tarski's theorem with "sentence" read as "representation" and "truth predicate" as "linear probe used as confidence," and the strength of the premise is the price of making the analogy an identity.

10.4.4. The impossibility🔗

theorem c3_coupling_trilemma {X : Type _} (v : X → X → Bool) (reflective : ∀ g : X → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict v reflective

Proof. Identical to the previous two. ∎

theorem c3_coupling_liar {X : Type _} (v : X → X → Bool) (reflective : ∀ g : X → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g) : ∃ p, v p p = !(v p p) := liar_query v reflective

Proof. The witness is a representation the probe would place on the true side exactly when it places it on the false side. ∎

10.4.5. Reading the liar witness🔗

Topologically this is the coupled point x₀ where confidence equals the threshold and truth-distance is zero, forced along any path from a true answer to a false one. Diagonally it is a representation encoding the probe's negation of its own verdict. The topological version carries metric content the diagonal cannot see: an ambiguity tube of computable width and a strictly positive truth-side slack any feasible system must carry.

10.4.6. The geometry the diagonal cannot see🔗

On a connected space with continuous fields, the coupled point sits at the centre of an ambiguity tube whose width is set by the Lipschitz constants, so the near-boundary region has computable size. For a nonzero linear probe the truth boundary is an affine hyperplane of codimension one, and even a nonlinear probe gives a hyperplane to first order at any regular point. Feasible systems carry strictly positive truth-side slack, which an adversarial training attempt fails to drive to zero.

10.4.7. The policy taxonomy🔗

A threshold-inclusive guarantee promises that confidence at or above threshold implies truth; a threshold-exclusive one promises it only strictly above. The coupled query has confidence exactly at threshold, so it is the hinge. Add the inclusive guarantee and you get a contradiction, closed_guarantee_impossible.

Defining the guarantee with a strict inequality does not dissolve the impossibility. It relocates it from a contradiction to a silence. Either the guarantee claims the coupled query and is false, or excludes it and is silent there. The diagonal sees the same fork through the liar: any guarantee assigning it a definite side is refuted, and any declining to has conceded the one query the theorem cares about.

10.4.8. Leaving the continuum🔗

Token spaces are finite, and a fair objection is that connectedness does illegitimate work. Without topology a true-to-false path yields only a discrete_sign_change, an adjacent straddling pair rather than a query on the boundary — exactly what connectedness derived for free and what the discrete setting must assume. Once assumed, the impossibility returns, as boundary_question_impossible and faithful_iff_boundary_free show.

This is reflectivity's role: it supplies the boundary witness by fiat. The three routes cost differently — continuity costs a connected domain, assumption costs honesty about what you put in, reflectivity costs completeness of self-encoding. Randomization escapes none.

A symmetry version needs no coverage: if semantic negation acts as a fixed-point-free involution and the truth field is odd under it, the field vanishes between any state and its negation. This is the scalar shadow of Borsuk-Ulam, and a reminder that equivariance, usually a design virtue, is here an engine of the obstruction.

10.4.9. The honest caveat🔗

Hold this reading most loosely. Reflectivity of a fixed representation space is a strong, less physical assumption than continuity on a connected domain, and the topological route is primary for representation geometry. The diagonal supplies the witness by fiat, which is legitimate when self-encoding is real, as in a model prompted to reason about its own probe, and an overreach for a passive vector space.

The practical division: if your pipeline reads a probe off frozen activations and never asks the model to reason about it, the space is passive and the topological engine applies. If the model conditions on descriptions of its own truth-readout, as agentic and self-critiquing setups do, self-encoding is becoming real and the diagonal begins to apply. Knowing which regime you are in is a modeling question answered before either theorem says anything.

10.5. The Master Trilemma🔗

CCHProofs organizes all of this as faces of one three-cornered trilemma. Where the readings above vary the meaning of a Boolean verdict, the master trilemma varies the outcome type and carries a self-prediction alongside the verdict.

Bundle a system s : A → A → Y, a controller t : Y → Y, and a self-prediction p : A → Y. Universality: s is surjective. Control: t (p a) ≠ p a for every a, so no prediction is a fixed point. Transparency: s a a = p a, so the system says what it will do on itself. Read U as capability, C as control, T as honesty. No system is all three.

theorem c3_lawvere_point {A Y : Type _} (s : A → A → Y) (hU : ∀ g : A → Y, ∃ a, s a = g) (t : Y → Y) : ∃ a, s a a = t (s a a) := match hU (fun a => t (s a a)) with | ⟨a₀, ha₀⟩ => ⟨a₀, congrFun ha₀ a₀⟩

Proof. Chapter 1's move with the flip replaced by arbitrary t. ∎

def C3_Universal {A Y : Type _} (s : A → A → Y) : Prop := ∀ g : A → Y, ∃ a, s a = g def C3_Controlled {A Y : Type _} (t : Y → Y) (p : A → Y) : Prop := ∀ a, t (p a) ≠ p a def C3_Transparent {A Y : Type _} (s : A → A → Y) (p : A → Y) : Prop := ∀ a, s a a = p a theorem c3_cch_master {A Y : Type _} (s : A → A → Y) (t : Y → Y) (p : A → Y) (hU : C3_Universal s) (hC : C3_Controlled t p) (hT : C3_Transparent s p) : False := A:Type u_1Y:Type u_2s:A → A → Yt:Y → Yp:A → YhU:C3_Universal shC:C3_Controlled t phT:C3_Transparent s p⊢ False A:Type u_1Y:Type u_2s:A → A → Yt:Y → Yp:A → YhU:C3_Universal shC:C3_Controlled t phT:C3_Transparent s pa₀:Aha₀:s a₀ a₀ = t (s a₀ a₀)⊢ False A:Type u_1Y:Type u_2s:A → A → Yt:Y → Yp:A → YhU:C3_Universal shC:C3_Controlled t phT:C3_Transparent s pa₀:Aha₀:p a₀ = t (p a₀)⊢ False All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. c3_lawvere_point gives a₀ with s a₀ a₀ = t (s a₀ a₀). Transparency rewrites this to p a₀ = t (p a₀), making p a₀ a fixed point of t. Control says it is not. ∎

theorem c3_cch_corner_UC {A Y : Type _} (s : A → A → Y) (t : Y → Y) (p : A → Y) (hU : C3_Universal s) (hC : C3_Controlled t p) : ¬ C3_Transparent s p := fun hT => c3_cch_master s t p hU hC hT theorem c3_cch_corner_UT {A Y : Type _} (s : A → A → Y) (t : Y → Y) (p : A → Y) (hU : C3_Universal s) (hT : C3_Transparent s p) : ¬ C3_Controlled t p := fun hC => c3_cch_master s t p hU hC hT theorem c3_cch_corner_CT {A Y : Type _} (s : A → A → Y) (t : Y → Y) (p : A → Y) (hC : C3_Controlled t p) (hT : C3_Transparent s p) : ¬ C3_Universal s := fun hU => c3_cch_master s t p hU hC hT

Proof. Each supplies two properties and derives the falsity of the third. ∎

These make it a trilemma rather than an impossibility. You may have any two. A universal controlled system exists but cannot be honest about itself; a universal transparent one exists but cannot be controlled; a controlled transparent one exists but cannot be universal.

Each corner is a real class of system. Universal and controlled but not transparent: an expressive model under external correction whose self-reports must sometimes be wrong. Universal and transparent but not controlled: an honest expressive model no controller can always nudge.

Remark 3.12 (The trilemmas as the UC face). Take Y = Bool, t the flip, and p the diagonal a ↦ s a a. Transparency then holds by definition of p, so a universal system is automatically transparent for this choice, and control is bool_not_fpf at p a. The master collision becomes v p p = !(v p p), exactly c3_hallucination_liar. So the Boolean trilemmata are not analogous to the master trilemma; they are one of its faces, with transparency made free and control made the flip.

10.5.1. Reading the corners as the three trilemmata🔗

Universality is the reflectivity running through the chapter. Transparency is the honesty condition, carried in the Boolean readings by choosing the self-prediction to be the diagonal. Control is the demand that an external map can move the self-prediction, whose Boolean instance is that the flip has no fixed point, which is faithfulness for hallucination, completeness for defense, and exact separation for coupling under their outward-facing names.

So each verdict trilemma says Universality and Control force the failure of Transparency. The readings differ in which real property plays Control and in how believable Universality is, and agree on the skeleton. The master trilemma is not a fourth result stacked on three others; it is the frame showing the three were always the same corner viewed from three domains.

10.5.2. Why it is a trilemma, not a dilemma🔗

Any two of the three are jointly satisfiable, and the corner theorems are that fact turned into contrapositives. A dilemma says two things cannot both hold. The trilemma says three cannot all hold while any two can, which is stronger and more useful, because it tells a designer that giving up one property is not only necessary but sufficient.

10.6. One proof term🔗

theorem c3_trilemmata_unified {Q : Type _} (v : Q → Q → Bool) (h : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g) : c3_hallucination_trilemma v h = c3_defense_trilemma v h ∧ c3_defense_trilemma v h = c3_coupling_trilemma v h := ⟨rfl, rfl⟩

Proof. The three theorems have the same body, no_reflective_verdict v h, so they are definitionally equal. ∎

This is not that the three are analogous, or that a shared lemma covers them. There is one function v, one hypothesis, and one proof that the hypothesis is contradictory. The names are labels for the reader; the machine sees a single term.

Remark 3.13 (What rfl is checking). Two things make the equality trivial. Each c3_ trilemma is defined as no_reflective_verdict applied to the same arguments, so after unfolding the bodies are one term. And all three have type False, so any two proofs are equal by proof irrelevance. The first route carries the meaning: the theorems are the same not because all proofs of False are interchangeable, but because these three are the identical construction with three labels. The kernel would accept the second even for genuinely different arguments, which is why the first is the one to cite.

F_13_UnifiedTrilemmata proves the same rfl chain over Function.Surjective and packages the shared boundary object as schema_boundary.

10.7. What the readings share, and where they part🔗

Fixed across all three: a Boolean verdict, the flip as controller, universality as hypothesis, and a self-negating witness. What moves is the verdict's meaning and the believability of universality.

The meaning moves from "confident and correct" to "made safe" to "placed on the true side." The horns fixing the flip move from "faithful and calibrated" to "complete and utility-preserving" to "exactly truth-separating." The source of universality moves from "the model imitates any described behavior" to "prompts are arbitrary text" to "the representation space encodes any pattern over itself." That last move changes the character of the result: defense's universality is nearly free, hallucination's defensible, coupling's strong. Chapter 4 trades all three self-reference premises for one geometric premise and reaches the same boundary object with metric content.

There is a temptation, once the rfl is in hand, to conclude the results are trivial. The proof is one line because the modeling was done first. All the content is in Definitions 3.1 through 3.10 and the arguments that they add up to a reflective verdict. The engine is trivial on purpose; the theorems are as strong as the readings feeding it.

10.8. The template in four moves🔗

First, choose the reading: what v p q means, and what the self-contexts are. Second, argue the codomain is Bool and the controller is the flip, by finding the condition that makes outcomes two-valued and the one that makes the honest self-report the negation of the diagonal. Third, argue universality, identifying the source of self-reference and being honest about its strength. Fourth, apply the engine.

The moves are not equally hard. The first is a modeling decision, the second a short argument from a standard desideratum, the fourth one line of Lean. The weight is in the third, the premise a critic will contest.

This also explains why the Lean here is so short. Moves one to three happen in prose and only move four is code. A presentation that hid the prose would look like three deep theorems in three lines. What it actually did was three careful readings and one reused lemma, and the honesty is in keeping the readings visible.

10.9. Axioms and trust🔗

The c3_ theorems are elaborated as this document builds, so they are proofs the kernel has accepted. The companion library audits the axioms and finds the main results reduce to propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. The Boolean core uses even less, since the flip's fixed-point freedom is decidable.

The trust verification cannot supply is trust in the modeling. No proof assistant can check that "confident-correctness self-verdict" is the right reading of a real model, or that a real prompt space is reflective. Those are the premises, and they are what the long middle of each section argues and what the caveats concede.

10.10. What this chapter does not settle🔗

It does not say models hallucinate often, defenses fail often, or probes mislead often. It produces one query per system and is silent on frequency. A model could meet its liar on a query no user ever sends. That question belongs to the statistical tradition and to Chapter 5.

It does not say the liar is easy to find. The diagonal proves one exists and names it as a preimage of a specific pattern, but naming a preimage is not constructing it cheaply. For a large model the realizing self-context may be hard to elicit, and the cost is exactly what the diagonal cannot see.

It does not choose between the engines. The diagonal is honest when self-reference is real, as for prompt injection; the topological engine is honest when the domain is a connected space with continuous fields, as plausibly for a representation manifold. They agree on the boundary object, and having both lets an application be attacked from whichever premise it satisfies.

10.11. Historical notes🔗

The Hallucination Trilemma is re-derived in Gödel form as hallucination_trilemma_godel in F_11_HallucinationGodel, which records that the Boolean flip and the real complement are the two controllers. The Defense Trilemma is defense_trilemma_godel in F_12_DefenseGodel, with defense_trilemma_lawvere alongside. The coupling theorem is "Truth Has a Boundary," whose boundary_coupling is topological, with the diagonal reading in F_13_UnifiedTrilemmata.

The lineage is Lawvere 1969 through the reading of Tarski as a diagonal. The statistical inevitability of hallucination is a separate tradition deriving confident falsehood rather than uncertainty; only stochastic_dichotomy turns the boundary into falsehood with positive probability. Chapter 1's engine lives in F_01_LawvereCore, and all the developments pin the same toolchain and Mathlib release, so these cross-references are to code that compiles together.

11. From Logic to Analysis🔗

The diagonal needs a system rich enough to name its own behaviors, and many real models do not meet ∀ g, ∃ a, f a = g literally. A trained network carries no index for every function from prompts to confidences; its reachable states are a bounded region, not a set closed under naming its own predicates.

The second engine runs on different fuel. It asks that the space be connected and the maps continuous, and from those it extracts the same boundary object: a question where confidence sits exactly at threshold while the answer sits exactly on the truth boundary. The tool is the intermediate value theorem.

Code here is core Lean 4, elaborated as this document builds. The analytic theorems live over ℝ and use topology, so their machine-checked forms are in the companion HallucinationProofs library. Verified names appear in plain type; the prose proofs are complete on their own terms and the names are pointers, not omissions.

11.1. Why a second engine🔗

The engines answer different objections. Against a system that names its own behaviors the diagonal is decisive. Against a system on a manifold of activations it has no purchase, because no index need recover the diagonal behavior. What such a system has is shape: a connected representation space, continuous confidence, continuously varying correctness. That is enough.

In one sentence: self-reference forces a fixed point because a flip has nowhere to hide on the diagonal; connectedness forces a crossing because a continuous quantity negative somewhere and positive somewhere cannot pass between without visiting zero. Both trap a value, one with a naming equation and one with a topological wall. The trapped value is the same, and a later section makes that identity exact.

Concretely: a proof-checker accepting the code of any predicate, or an in-context learner promptable to any behavior, is close to the diagonal hypothesis. A trained classifier reading truth off residual-stream activations is not; it carries no index for every function from activations to confidences. Yet its activations form a connected region, by the manifold hypothesis and the modeling of embedding spaces as ℝ^d or connected submanifolds, and its probe and confidence heads are continuous.

The analytic engine also carries metric content the diagonal cannot. With a distance and Lipschitz maps, the crossing is not a bare witness but the centre of a band of computable width. Chapter 5 is entirely about those quantities.

11.2. A topology primer🔗

Definition 4.1 (Topological space). A topological space is a set X with a collection of open subsets including ∅ and X, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. A set is closed when its complement is open.

Definition 4.2 (Continuity). f : X → Y is continuous when the preimage of every open set is open; equivalently, of every closed set is closed.

The preimage form is the same idea as epsilon-delta and easier to use, and it makes continuity a statement about two topologies, which is the level at which connectedness lives. The fact used repeatedly is that compositions of continuous maps are continuous. The verified proofs build on Mathlib's Continuous.comp and the product rule Continuous.prodMk, which is how q ↦ δ(q, (M q).1) is shown continuous in model_truth_boundary_nonempty.

The closure of S is the smallest closed set containing it; S is dense when its closure is everything. Density is the topological form of the strongest coverage condition, verified as DenseCoverage in HoF_05_Coverage, with denseCoverage_closure_eq_univ. The main theorem uses only the mild two-sided coverage of Definition 4.12.

Metric spaces and paths. A metric gives open balls, and the metric topology's opens are the sets containing a ball around each point. Continuity in the preimage sense agrees with epsilon-delta. The standing example is ℝ^d; the verified sphere instantiation uses EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d), and the quantitative results use PseudoMetricSpace with explicit Lipschitz hypotheses.

A path from x to y is a continuous γ : [0,1] → X with γ 0 = x, γ 1 = y, and X is path-connected when any two points are joined. Path-connected implies connected: a path from one side of a separation to the other pulls it back to a separation of [0,1], which is connected. The converse can fail in general but holds for the convex regions and manifolds of the applications.

Paths matter because interpolating hidden states from a true statement to its negation traces a path, along which the realized truth-distance starts negative and ends positive, so the one-variable theorem gives a crossing on the path itself. That is path_crosses_truth_boundary in HoF_03_BoundaryCrossing, and it is what an experiment actually walks along.

Products. If X and Y are connected so is X × Y: fix a base point, note each slice through it is a continuous image of a connected space, and observe that a union of slices meeting a common point cannot be separated. By induction a finite product of connected spaces is connected. So if a single-turn space Q is connected, the multi-turn space Q^T is too, and every argument transports unchanged, since the only property used was connectedness.

Definition 4.3 (Connected space). X is disconnected when open U, V exist with U ∪ V = X, U ∩ V = ∅, both nonempty; connected when nonempty and not disconnected.

Definition 4.4 (Preconnected set). S ⊆ X is preconnected when no open U, V satisfy S ⊆ U ∪ V, S ∩ U ∩ V = ∅, S ∩ U ≠ ∅, and S ∩ V ≠ ∅ at once. It is connected when also nonempty.

The distinction is only whether the empty set is admitted. Mathlib keeps them apart because the intermediate value theorem is cleanest for preconnected sets, and the verified files call that form. isPreconnected_univ is the first line of every IVT application in HoF_03_BoundaryCrossing and HoF_07_TrilemmaCore.

Two examples fix the idea. Any interval of ℝ is connected, by completeness: given a split, the supremum of the left part lies in neither piece without contradicting openness. A two-point discrete space is disconnected.

Proposition 4.5 (Continuous image of a preconnected set). If S is preconnected and f continuous on S, then f(S) is preconnected.

Proof. A separation of f(S) by U, V pulls back to f⁻¹(U), f⁻¹(V), open by continuity, covering S, missing S in their intersection, and each meeting S. That separates S. ∎

This is IsPreconnected.image in Mathlib, and the companion proofs call it. It is the load-bearing beam: connectedness is preserved by continuous maps, and applied to a real-valued map that becomes the intermediate value theorem once we know the connected subsets of the line.

Proposition 4.6 (Connected subsets of the line are intervals). A subset of ℝ is preconnected iff it is an interval.

Proof. If S omits c with a < c < b in S, the open rays about c separate it. Conversely, let S be an interval separated by U, V, with a ∈ S ∩ U, b ∈ S ∩ V, a < b. Let m be the supremum of points of [a,b] ∩ U below b, which exists since the set is nonempty and bounded. As S is an interval, m ∈ S, so m ∈ U or m ∈ V. If m ∈ U, openness pushes points of U above m, contradicting the bound. If m ∈ V, openness puts points just below m in V and not U, contradicting leastness. ∎

In Mathlib the forward direction is IsPreconnected.ordConnected and the converse for a closed interval is isPreconnected_Icc.

Theorem 4.7 (Intermediate value theorem). Let X be connected and c : X → ℝ continuous. If c takes a value below r and one above r, it takes r.

Proof. The image is preconnected by Proposition 4.5, hence an interval by Proposition 4.6, and it contains values on both sides of r. ∎

The library uses the two-function form IsPreconnected.intermediate_value₂, comparing continuous f and g on a preconnected set: if f a ≤ g a and g b ≤ f b then f x = g x somewhere. Theorem 4.7 is the case g constant. Every IVT call in HoF_03_BoundaryCrossing, HoF_05_Coverage, and HoF_07_TrilemmaCore is this form with g = continuous_const; the interval case via isPreconnected_Icc is confidence_path_crosses_half.

Remark 4.8 (What the theorem does not say). It asserts existence, not uniqueness or location. This is the analytic mirror of the diagonal's silence in Remark 1.18. Both engines produce a witness with no built-in address, and metric content is an extra ingredient added in Chapter 5.

11.2.1. Connectedness as analytic self-reference🔗

In Chapter 1 the diagonal took a flip with no fixed point and derived a contradiction from universality, because a universal system must name a ↦ t (f a a). The engine is that self-application leaves the flip no room.

Connectedness plays the same role. A continuous quantity on a connected space that is negative somewhere and positive somewhere is a flip with no room: a jump would split the space into the negative and positive parts, two nonempty open sets separating a space assumed unseparable. So it passes through zero.

The correspondences, each of which becomes a theorem: self-reference ↔ connectedness; the flip t ↔ a continuous field taking both signs; the forced fixed point ↔ the forced zero; Boolean negation ↔ the real complement y ↦ 1 - y; the liar index of Proposition 1.14 ↔ the boundary question.

The analogy is tight rather than loose. In both engines there is a set of candidate outputs, a transformation on them, and a structural hypothesis leaving the transformation nowhere to sit but a distinguished value. For the diagonal, the outputs are the values f a a, the transformation is t, and the hypothesis is that every behavior is named.

There is a shared failure mode. Remove the structural hypothesis and both collapse the same way. A non-universal system can carry a fixed-point-free flip with no contradiction, since the diagonal behavior may be unnamed.

11.3. The model, analytically🔗

Definition 4.9 (Model). For topological spaces Q of questions and A of answers, a model is M : Q → A × ℝ, with answer (M q).1 and confidence (M q).2. It is continuous when both components are.

Softmax outputs, probe readouts, and calibrated logits are continuous candidates for the confidence; hard argmax decoding is not, a point priced in the discrete section.

Definition 4.10 (Signed truth-distance). A truth-distance is a continuous δ : Q × A → ℝ, negative on strictly correct answers, positive on strictly wrong ones, zero on the truth boundary. The realized truth-distance is q ↦ δ(q, (M q).1).

The sign convention is fixed: negative good, positive bad, zero the wall. A linear probe w·x - b is a candidate δ, and whether its boundary tracks semantic truth away from the fitted data is an empirical premise, not a theorem. Continuity of the realized composite follows from the composition and product rules.

Definition 4.11 (Faithful). A model is faithful when (M q).2 ≥ 1/2 implies δ(q, (M q).1) < 0. The verified predicate is TrilemmaFaithful. The strict < 0 does the work; a weaker ≤ 0 admits the boundary case and dissolves the theorem.

Definition 4.12 (Covering). A model is covering when some q has δ(q, (M q).1) < 0 and some has > 0. The verified predicate is TrilemmaCovering, also Covering in HoF_05_Coverage. It is the mildest nontriviality assumption: any model ever correct and ever incorrect satisfies it.

Definition 4.13 (Calibrated). A model is strictly calibrated when for every q, (M q).2 > 1/2 ↔ δ(q, (M q).1) < 0 and (M q).2 < 1/2 ↔ δ(q, (M q).1) > 0. The verified predicate is StrictCalibrated.

This pointwise biconditional is much stronger than statistical calibration, which is an averaged claim compatible with being wrong on any particular high-confidence question. Strict calibration constrains every single question. It is the idealization a perfect truth probe used as confidence would meet, which is why the empirical work builds the confidence from a probe and asks how close reality comes.

Read the three on the linear-probe picture and none is a strawman. Covering says the model answers on both sides of a hyperplane, which any model on a real workload does. Calibration says a confidence head trained on a disjoint split agrees with the probe about sides, which a well-trained head approximates.

Calibration is a biconditional because it claims the confidence is an honest readout; faithfulness is one-way because a promise is one-directional. Neither is at fault alone. Their conjunction on a connected covering model is.

11.3.1. Separation with slack🔗

Fix a threshold τ, truth slack ε ≥ 0, and confidence margin γ ≥ 0. A model is (ε, γ)-separating at τ when δ < -ε implies confidence > τ + γ and δ > ε implies confidence < τ - γ. The slack is in truth-distance units and the margin in confidence units, so the condition survives rescaling either field.

Slack is not cosmetic: the main theorem is that with a threshold-inclusive guarantee the truth slack cannot be zero. Using 1/2 for τ is a convention the coupling results never depend on; every theorem has a general-τ counterpart in the defense-side files.

11.3.2. The defense reading🔗

Reread Q as inputs a system might face including adversarial ones, (M q).2 as a safety score, and δ as a harm measure. Faithful becomes "a high safety score certifies real safety," covering becomes "some inputs are safe and some are not," calibration becomes "the score tracks the probe." The coupling theorem then says a defense with a continuous safety score on a connected input space owns an input scored exactly at threshold and lying exactly on the harm boundary. This is boundary_coupling in HoF_13_BoundaryCoupling.

11.4. The topological proof of the trilemma🔗

Three steps. Coverage plus connectedness forces a confidence crossing. Calibration pins the truth-distance to zero there. Faithfulness demands it be strictly negative, and the two collide.

Lemma 4.14 (Boundary existence). Let Q be connected, the answer map and truth-distance continuous, and the model covering. Then some q₀ has δ(q₀, (M q₀).1) = 0.

Proof. The realized truth-distance F is continuous, being a composite of the continuous q ↦ (q, (M q).1) with δ. Coverage gives points where F is negative and positive. Theorem 4.7 at value 0 gives q₀. ∎

This is model_truth_boundary_nonempty in HoF_03_BoundaryCrossing, packaged with its coverage hypothesis as covering_yields_truth_boundary_point in HoF_05_Coverage. It uses no confidence and no calibration: pure topology. The boundary question exists before any safety condition enters. The wall is a fact about the shape of the model's correctness, not about how it reports its reliability.

Two structural facts, both verified and both independent of connectedness. The boundary is closed, being the preimage of {0} under a continuous map, which is model_truth_boundary_isClosed and holds over any topological spaces. And every continuous path from a strictly-correct question to a strictly-wrong one crosses it, which is path_crosses_truth_boundary.

Lemma 4.15 (Confidence crossing). Let Q be connected and the confidence continuous. If some question has confidence below 1/2 and some above, then some q₀ has (M q₀).2 = 1/2.

Proof. Theorem 4.7 applied to the confidence at 1/2. ∎

This is confidence_half_nonempty and model_confidence_half_set_nonempty. Alone it concerns the confidence field only; it becomes half the trilemma once calibration ties the confidence witnesses to the coverage witnesses.

Theorem 4.16 (Boundary-confidence coupling). Let Q be connected, all three maps continuous, and the model covering and strictly calibrated. Then some q₀ satisfies (M q₀).2 = 1/2 and δ(q₀, (M q₀).1) = 0.

Proof. Coverage gives q_t with negative and q_f with positive truth-distance. Calibration converts these into confidences above and below 1/2. Lemma 4.15 gives q₀ with confidence exactly 1/2. Read calibration backward at q₀: a negative truth-distance would force confidence above 1/2, a positive one below, both contradicting equality. So the truth-distance is 0. ∎

This is hallucination_trilemma_strict in HoF_07_TrilemmaCore, with the defense twin boundary_coupling. It mentions no faithfulness. It is a coupling statement: a covering calibrated continuous model on a connected space owns a question where the confidence is exactly ambiguous and the answer exactly on the wall. The point is real regardless of any safety policy.

Theorem 4.17 (Analytic hallucination trilemma). No continuous model on a connected question space is simultaneously faithful, covering, and strictly calibrated.

Proof. Theorem 4.16 gives q₀ with confidence 1/2 and truth-distance 0. Faithfulness applies there, since 1/2 ≥ 1/2, and demands the truth-distance be strictly negative. It is zero. ∎

This is hallucination_trilemma, with hallucination_trilemma_unfolded alongside. The verified proof is the two-line composition: extract the coupled point, apply faithfulness, observe the sign clash with linarith.

The policy reading makes this a taxonomy. Faithfulness as stated is threshold-inclusive, triggering at confidence at least 1/2, so it triggers at the coupled point. A threshold-exclusive guarantee triggers only strictly above and so does not fire there.

This is why Theorem 4.16 is stated separately from Theorem 4.17. The coupling theorem mentions no guarantee, so the coupled point exists under any threshold policy. The guarantee only selects which clause applies.

11.4.1. The forced question is the analytic liar🔗

The coupled point is the analytic twin of the liar index of Proposition 1.14. There the liar was an index whose self-application equalled its own negation; here q₀ is a question whose confidence equals the threshold and whose answer sits on the boundary.

Both witnesses are non-unique for the same reason. If the diagonal behavior has two names, both are liars; if the confidence crosses 1/2 more than once, every crossing landing on the boundary is a coupled point. The witness is guaranteed to exist and left unaddressed in both engines.

11.5. A worked instance on the interval🔗

Take Q = [0,1], read t as a position interpolating from a question answered truly at 0 to one answered falsely at 1, and let the realized truth-distance be F(t) = 2t - 1. The model is covering, with F(0) = -1 and F(1) = 1.

Lemma 4.14 applies: F has a zero, here exactly t = 1/2. Strict calibration forces confidence above 1/2 for t < 1/2 and below for t > 1/2, so by Lemma 4.15 the continuous confidence crosses 1/2, and only at t = 1/2. That is the coupled point, exactly as Theorem 4.16 promises.

Add faithfulness and it breaks: at the coupled point the confidence is exactly 1/2, so faithfulness demands F(1/2) < 0, but F(1/2) = 0. If the confidence tries to avoid 1/2 by jumping, it is not continuous, and dropping continuity is a named escape priced in the discrete section.

The instance also shows what the exclusive guarantee buys. With the strict antecedent the guarantee does not trigger at t = 1/2 and no contradiction arises. The model is consistent, but it owns a question on the truth boundary about which its guarantee is silent. The wall did not move; the guarantee stopped promising there.

11.6. Quantitative shadows🔗

Theorem 4.17b (Approximate coupling). Let Q be connected, the confidence continuous, and the model ε-covering, (ε, γ)-separating at τ, with a threshold-inclusive guarantee. Then some q₀ has (M q₀).2 = τ and -ε ≤ δ(q₀, (M q₀).1) < 0.

Proof sketch. The ε-coverage witnesses have truth-distance below -ε and above ε, and separation turns these into confidence witnesses above τ + γ and below τ - γ. The IVT lands q₀ at confidence τ. Separation with slack no longer pins the truth-distance to zero but confines it to |δ| ≤ ε, where neither strict clause fires. The guarantee forces it strictly negative, giving [-ε, 0). ∎

The verified statement is two_slack_approx_coupling in HoF_12_Approximate, carrying ε and γ as separate parameters. Theorem 4.16 is the ε = 0 limit, recovered as exact_from_approx.

Corollary 4.17c (Positive slack is mandatory). Under those hypotheses the truth slack cannot be zero.

Proof. At ε = 0 the coupled point would lie in [0, 0), which is empty, but the IVT produced one. ∎

This is truth_slack_must_be_positive. Read it as a budget: a system keeping a threshold-inclusive guarantee must keep a strictly positive margin of correctness on the confident side, and the infimum of feasible slack is a measurable width of the truth boundary. No question with confidence between τ and τ + γ can sit exactly on the boundary, which is no_boundary_in_upper_band_two_slack.

11.7. Symmetry in place of coverage🔗

Definition 4.18 (Antipodal action). An antipodal action on Q is a continuous self-inverse fixed-point-free σ : Q → Q. A real g is odd under σ when g (σ q) = -g q.

Verified as AntipodalAction and AntipodalOdd in HoF_08_BorsukUlam. Layer normalization places transformer states on a sphere-like shell, and semantic negation is a candidate antipode, so oddness idealizes a truth-distance flipping sign under negation.

Theorem 4.19 (Odd fields vanish). Let Q be connected with an antipodal action σ. Any continuous g : Q → ℝ odd under σ has a zero.

Proof. Pick q. If g q = 0 we are done. Otherwise g (σ q) = -g q has the opposite sign, so g takes both signs and Theorem 4.7 gives a zero. ∎

This is antipodal_odd_has_zero, and no coverage was assumed: oddness supplies the two signs for free. A single question and its negation already straddle zero.

There is a pleasant inversion. Equivariance is usually a design virtue, built in so a network treats a question and its negation consistently. Here it is the engine of the obstruction: a model respecting negation has an odd truth-distance, and an odd continuous field on a connected symmetric space must vanish. The better behaved the symmetry, the more inescapable the wall.

Theorem 4.20 (Antipodal trilemma). Let Q be connected with an antipodal action, the model continuous and strictly calibrated at 1/2, and the realized truth-distance odd. Then some q has (M q).2 = 1/2 and δ(q, (M q).1) = 0.
