Proof. Theorem 4.19 gives a zero q. Calibration then pins the confidence: above 1/2 would force the truth-distance negative, below would force it positive. ∎

This is antipodal_hallucination_trilemma. Adding faithfulness produces the same contradiction as Theorem 4.17, now with no coverage assumption anywhere.

The two engines' nontriviality demands differ instructively. Coverage is an assumption about the model's outputs. The antipodal hypothesis is about the space and the field.

The antipodal engine is robust to approximate symmetry, which matters because real negation does not reflect truth directions exactly. If |g (σ q) + g q| ≤ ε for all q, then some q has |g q| ≤ ε/2, recovering exact vanishing at ε = 0. The verified robust form is approx_odd_near_zero, and the sphere instantiation for d ≥ 2, using Mathlib's isConnected_sphere, is sphere_odd_has_zero.

The dimension hypothesis d ≥ 2 is where connectedness of the sphere comes from; the zero-dimensional sphere is two points and disconnected, the same degeneracy that makes the diagonal the right tool for a two-point outcome set. For any representation dimension used in practice the sphere is connected. The one honest caveat is that exact oddness is an idealization; the measured defect is nonzero but small, smallest for the strongest model, and approx_odd_near_zero keeps a near-boundary point in existence under it.

11.8. The discrete core🔗

The topology does exactly one job: it manufactures a boundary question. Everything after is arithmetic. The verified home is HoF_10_PureDiscrete.

This matters because token spaces are finite and one may object that connectedness does illegitimate work. The discrete analysis prices the objection exactly: without topology we must assume the boundary witness rather than derive it. That is the entire cost.

Pricing an objection is the honest way to handle an idealization. A theorem with a strong hypothesis invites the reader to reject it and walk away; the disciplined response is to show how much of the conclusion survives without it. Connectedness is a good model of an ambient representation space over which probes are deployed at interpolated points, and a poor model of a scattered token-driven reachable set.

theorem c4_flip_no_fixed_point : ∀ b : Bool, (!b) ≠ b := ⊢ ∀ (b : Bool), (!b) ≠ b All goals completed! 🐙

This is the integer transcription of boundary_question_impossible. Read it against Theorem 4.17: the two have blocks are calibration pinning the confidence, the step Theorem 4.16 performed with the IVT replaced by an assumed boundary value; the last lines are faithfulness and the sign clash. No topology appears. Both the continuous and antipodal trilemmata factor through this core.

How would a discrete world produce a boundary value? Along a finite path the truth-distance need not hit zero; it can jump across between adjacent steps.

A discrete field negative at the start and non-negative at the end has an adjacent pair where it is still negative and has just become non-negative. It never claims a step where the field is exactly zero. That gap is the whole difference between settings: the continuum upgrades the straddle into an exact witness. The verified counterpart is discrete_sign_change.

Two consequences, both verified. A model faithful and strictly calibrated with witnesses for strictly correct, exactly boundary, and strictly wrong answers is impossible with no topological hypothesis, which is discrete_hallucination_trilemma; it trades connectedness for a stronger coverage hypothesis. And, more revealingly, faithfulness is equivalent to boundary-freeness under calibration: faithful_iff_boundary_free.

11.8.1. Adding randomness🔗

A stochastic model does not dodge the obstruction, in two verified ways.

On expected fields, averaging is continuous, so the averaged confidence and truth-distance are continuous on the connected space and the coupling theorem applies verbatim, giving a question with expected confidence 1/2 and expected truth-distance 0. This is stochastic_coupling_expected.

The second converts expectation into samples and is the one place the theory derives outright falsehood. Let the truth-distance have mean zero, let sample-faithfulness hold almost everywhere, and let the confidence be at least 1/2 with positive probability. Then the truth-distance is strictly positive with positive probability. This is stochastic_dichotomy.

Proof sketch. If the truth-distance were almost never positive, then on the confident event, of positive probability, faithfulness makes it strictly negative, and it is non-positive elsewhere. Such a quantity has strictly negative mean, contradicting mean-zero. ∎

Randomization spreads the boundary across samples instead of removing it. The wall is either a point you pass through or a positive-probability event you incur.

11.9. Where the two engines meet🔗

The claim is that the diagonal and the IVT locate the same boundary object, and that the Boolean flip and the real complement are two descriptions of one wall. This is recorded as a theorem in Foundation.F_04.

In Chapter 1 the engine needed a flip with no fixed point, and for Booleans that is negation. For real confidences the natural flip is the complement controller y ↦ 1 - y, which is not fixed-point-free: it has exactly one fixed point, at 1/2. This is half_complement_fixed_point, with the off-threshold form complement_no_fp_off_half.

That single fixed point is the entire difference, and the reason both engines reach the same place. The Boolean flip has none, so Lawvere's theorem, which always produces a fixed point of the flip, produces a contradiction. The real complement has one, so Lawvere run with it produces not a contradiction but a point: a diagonal question where the confidence equals 1/2.

Compare the routes. The IVT reaches 1/2 by connectedness: the confidence is below and above, so it crosses. The diagonal reaches it by self-reference: the confidence names a behavior complementing its own diagonal value, so it equals its own complement.

What is shared is the boundary object and the final clash. What differs is the hypothesis manufacturing the object, and neither implies the other. A finite discrete model can be universal and carry no topology; a smooth model on a manifold can be connected while naming almost none of its own behaviors.

There is a categorical way to say the shared part. Lawvere's theorem holds cleanest for a section, and that form is true verbatim in any cartesian closed category. The complement controller is an endomap of the reals with a single fixed point, and Lawvere applied to a section of a real-valued self-prediction delivers it on the diagonal.

The unification is packaged at two levels: hallucination_unification_documentation and its lemmas in Foundation.F_04, and trilemmata_unified with hallucination_master_theorem in F_13_UnifiedTrilemmata.

One geometric remark closes the meeting point. When the truth-distance is a linear probe the boundary is an affine hyperplane of codimension one, a translate of the probe's kernel, by rank-nullity: linear_probe_boundary_coset and linear_probe_boundary_dim. For a differentiable nonlinear probe it is a hyperplane to first order at every regular point, with the tangent hyperplane the kernel of the derivative, verified as nonlinear_boundary_tangent and tangent_hyperplane_dim, and every regular point is itself a sign crossing generating local coverage for free, regular_point_is_crossing.

11.10. Where the two engines diverge🔗

The diagonal gives a witness and nothing quantitative: not how many liars there are, how hard one is to find, or what a search would cost. It cannot, because a naming equation has no notion of distance, width, or margin.

The IVT alone is equally silent. The difference is that the analytic engine can be fed more. Add a distance and Lipschitz maps and the bare crossing becomes quantitative: the decisive regions are held apart by a distance controlled by the Lipschitz constant and the margin, the coupled point sits at the centre of a tube of computable radius, and truth-side slack must be strictly positive with a measurable infimum.

Use the diagonal when the system names itself and you want the cleanest existence proof with the smallest trust story. Use the IVT when the system lives on a connected space, and if you also have a metric, keep going into Chapter 5. Both reach the boundary; only the second measures it.

The engines also differ in what they say about escape. The diagonal is escaped by breaking universality, which is hard to arrange without crippling a system meant to handle arbitrary inputs. The analytic engine is escaped by breaking connectedness, coverage, continuity, or exact separation, and each is a concrete design lever.

11.11. The engine in one page🔗

Four moves. Continuity: the realized truth-distance and confidence are continuous, being built from continuous pieces by composition and pairing. The intermediate value theorem: on a connected space a continuous real field taking values on both sides of a threshold takes the threshold; this is the only analytic input, verified as IsPreconnected.intermediate_value₂.

Every variant is a substitution. The antipodal variant replaces coverage with a symmetry supplying both signs. The discrete core keeps the last two moves and assumes the boundary question.

11.12. Historical notes🔗

The intermediate value theorem is Bolzano's, and the formulation as preservation of connectedness is standard. The reading of it as an impossibility engine for learning systems is recent, and the machine-checked development is HallucinationProofs, with the topological core in HoF_03, HoF_05, HoF_07, the antipodal variant in HoF_08, and the discrete core in HoF_10. The unification with the diagonal is Foundation.F_04.

The statistical inevitability results run on a different track: they argue a calibrated model must hallucinate on rarely-seen facts, or that hallucination is undecidable, and conclude that confident falsehood is unavoidable in aggregate. The engine here is topological, localizes at a specific boundary question, and is more modest, since the deterministic theorems yield uncertainty rather than confident error. Only the stochastic dichotomy derives falsehood, and it needs mean-zero to do it.

12. The Geometry of Attacks🔗

The diagonal gives one thing and refuses the rest. It gives a bad point. It never says how many there are, how large a region behaves badly, how a search finds one, or what an adversary spends. Those questions are outside its language: it speaks of surjections and fixed-point-free maps, not volume, distance, or gradient.

Here the objects are real functions on real spaces: an alignment deviation f : X → ℝ, a threshold τ, and a metric. The tools are analysis and measure theory. No result here is a diagonal argument; they are the intermediate value theorem, the Lipschitz condition, a coarea inequality, concentration of measure, and pigeonhole on grids.

The material follows the companion ManifoldProofs development, roughly four hundred machine-checked results on Mathlib. Because that library is analytic and the book's own package carries no Mathlib, this chapter states everything in prose, tagged with the exact MoF_* name. Treat the citations as ground truth: where the prose simplifies, the Lean does not.

One idea runs throughout. Existence is qualitative; cost is quantitative. The earlier impossibility theorems say the boundary is there. These say how it is shaped, how much room the unsafe region occupies, and how the price of attack and defense scales. A deployment is not decided by whether a bad point exists, since one always does, but by how expensive it is to live next to it.

12.1. From the diagonal to the boundary🔗

Fix a space X of behaviors, a continuous f : X → ℝ large when behavior is far from acceptable, and a threshold τ. This triple is the entire setting.

Definition 5.1 (Regions). The safe region is {f < τ}, the vulnerability basin {f > τ}, the boundary {f = τ}, the failure manifold {f ≥ τ}. These are SafeRegion, UnsafeRegion, Boundary, FailureManifold in MoF_01_Foundations, with space_partition, safe_unsafe_disjoint, and failureManifold_eq_union the immediate facts.

In Chapter 1 the boundary question was the index where a boolean verdict flipped. Here it is a point where f = τ, neither safe nor unsafe. The diagonal produced its witness by self-reference; this one comes from connectedness. Both deliver an unavoidable point of failure, and the analytic one delivers it with metric content.

Remark 5.2. Keep one picture: f is a landscape, the safe region the lowland below sea level τ, the boundary the coastline. The questions here are geographic. How much coastline? How steep the cliffs? Drop a random point: how likely near the coast? The impossibility theorems say the coastline exists; the geometry says how to sail it.

12.2. Decision basins🔗

Theorem 5.3 (Basin openness). For continuous f, {f > τ} and {f < τ} are open; {f = τ} and {f ≤ τ} are closed.

Proof. Preimages of open rays are open; the boundary is the preimage of a closed singleton. ∎

This is basin_isOpen and sublevel_isClosed in MoF_02_BasinStructure, with safeRegion_isOpen, unsafeRegion_isOpen, boundary_isClosed in MoF_01. Unsafety is not razor-thin: it comes with room around it.

Theorem 5.4 (Every unsafe point owns a ball). If f p > τ then some r > 0 has B(p, r) inside the basin.

Proof. The basin is open and contains p. ∎

basin_contains_ball. Continuity gives a ball of unknown size; Lipschitz continuity, below, gives one of known size.

Theorem 5.5 (Basins have positive measure). For any measure giving nonempty opens positive mass, if some f p > τ then μ{f > τ} > 0.

Proof. The basin is open and nonempty. ∎

basin_measure_pos, with basin_measure_ge_ball_pos in MoF_Cost_02_BasinVolume. This is the hinge of the cost story. A single unsafe point is measure-zero and dismissible; positive measure is not. A random draw has positive chance of landing there, and no finite set of safe examples certifies the region away.

Theorem 5.6 (Monotonicity in the threshold). If τ₁ ≤ τ₂ then {f > τ₂} ⊆ {f > τ₁} and the measures are ordered. Above the supremum the basin is empty; below the infimum it is everything.

Proof. Raising the threshold removes points; measure is monotone. ∎

basin_measure_monotone_threshold, basin_empty_above_sup, basin_full_below_inf in MoF_Adv_10_MeasureBounds. You can shrink the basin by refusing more behaviors, but it shrinks continuously and never vanishes until you have refused essentially everything. A threshold high enough to empty the basin empties the product.

Theorem 5.7 (Components are open and countable). On a locally connected space each component of the basin is open; if second countable, there are countably many.

Proof sketch. Components of an open set in a locally connected space are open, and a disjoint family of nonempty opens in a second countable space is countable. ∎

basin_connected_components_open, basin_components_countable in MoF_Adv_01_BasinConnectedness, with basin_connected_of_convex_domain a sufficient condition for one piece and superlevel_disconnected_example an f whose basin splits. Real models are the second kind, which is why red-teaming that finds one jailbreak family says little about the others.

Worked example: the Gaussian bump. On ℝ^n let f(x) = M · exp(-‖x‖²/2) with 0 < τ < M. The basin is the open ball of radius √(2 ln(M/τ)): open, nonempty, positive measure, connected, shrinking continuously as τ → M. It also previews the curse, since the ball's volume is a vanishing fraction of the surrounding cube in high dimension, so a random draw almost never lands in it.

12.3. The threshold-crossing theorem🔗

Theorem 5.8 (Threshold crossing, one dimension). For continuous f : ℝ → ℝ with f a < τ < f b, some c ∈ [a,b] has f c = τ.

Proof. The IVT on a connected interval. ∎

path_crosses_threshold in MoF_03_ThresholdCrossing. Its elementariness is the point: unavoidability of the boundary is the IVT in a safety costume.

Theorem 5.9 (Crossing along a path). For continuous γ and f with f(γ a) < τ < f(γ b), some c has f(γ c) = τ.

Proof. Theorem 5.8 on the composite. ∎

path_crosses_threshold_generic. An attack is a path from safe to unsafe, whether prompt edits, an embedding interpolation, or a gradient trajectory. If it is continuous and succeeds, it passed through the boundary. There is a moment in every successful attack when the behavior was exactly at threshold, which is why the boundary, not the interior, is what a defense must control.

This also refutes the moat. For a continuous score, f takes every intermediate value, so you cannot forbid a band of scores without forbidding behaviors that legitimately produce them. The only genuine separator is the measure-zero level set, and Theorem 5.20 shows even that thickens once the defender's uncertainty is counted. There is no moat, only a coastline.

Theorem 5.10 (No gap). On connected X, if a safe and an unsafe point exist then {f = τ} is nonempty.

Proof. The reachable values form a connected subset of ℝ containing values on both sides. ∎

no_gap_theorem, on threshold_level_set_nonempty. A designer might hope for a model whose behaviors are all comfortably safe or comfortably unsafe with an empty margin, so a crude classifier could separate them. Connectedness forbids it.

Theorem 5.11 (Separation is exactly the boundary). closure(Safe) ∩ closure(Unsafe) ⊆ Boundary.

Proof sketch. If f x > τ a whole neighborhood is unsafe, contradicting x being a limit of safe points; symmetrically below. ∎

safe_unsafe_separated. The boundary is the shared frontier where the regions touch, and everything an attacker exploits and a defender guards lives on this closed set.

Theorem 5.12 (Defense fixes a boundary point). Let X be connected Hausdorff with safe and unsafe points present, and D continuous and the identity on the safe region. Then some boundary point z has D z = z, so D cannot make z safe.

Proof sketch. The fixed-point set of a continuous self-map of a Hausdorff space is closed, being the preimage of the diagonal, and contains the safe region hence its closure. The safe region is open and not closed, since connectedness would force it empty or everything, so its closure contains a boundary point, which is a limit of safe points and therefore fixed. ∎

master_theorem in MoF_MasterTheorem, over the ManifoldOfFailure structure. It does not say D fails everywhere, only that one boundary point is fixed and unfixed. Upgrading that point to a region of positive measure is the work of the quantitative theorems.

Worked example: interpolating prompts. A benign prompt at f p = τ - 1 and a jailbreak at f q = τ + 1 are joined by a continuous path, so Theorem 5.9 gives a prompt scored exactly at threshold: a marginal jailbreak where a vanishing nudge tips it unsafe. That family is exactly what red teams hunt.

12.4. Lipschitz control🔗

f is L-Lipschitz when |f x - f y| ≤ L · dist(x,y). Networks with bounded weights and Lipschitz activations are Lipschitz, with a constant that is finite and estimable.

Definition 5.13 (Robustness radius). robustnessRadius(f p, τ, L) = (f p - τ)/L, in MoF_04_LipschitzBasin.

Theorem 5.14 (Lipschitz basin ball). If f is L-Lipschitz with f p > τ, the ball of radius (f p - τ)/L around p lies inside the basin.

Proof. |f p' - f p| ≤ L · dist < f p - τ. ∎

lipschitz_basin_ball, with basin_ball_subset, perturbation_stability, and robustnessRadius_pos. The radius is the margin divided by how fast f can climb back down. This is a statement about the robustness of attacks: once well inside the unsafe region an entire neighborhood is unsafe, so small changes in phrasing do not rescue the model.

Theorem 5.15 (Deeper points have larger basins). If f p₁ ≤ f p₂, both above τ, their radii are ordered the same way.

Proof. (v - τ)/L increases in v. ∎

robustnessRadius_monotone. The more deviant the behavior, the more robust to perturbation, which attackers exploit by pushing deep rather than stopping at the first crossing.

Theorem 5.16 (Smoother models, larger basins per peak). A smaller Lipschitz constant gives a larger radius at fixed peak value.

Proof. (f p - τ)/L decreases in L. ∎

smoother_functions_larger_basins in MoF_Adv_04_ModelScale, with lipschitz_basin_component_width. Smoothness is usually considered desirable and is often enforced by regularization, but a smoother model has larger unsafe basins per peak. Smoothness does not remove the danger; it spreads it, while steepness concentrates it into thin spikes, harder to hit by chance and sharper when hit.

Is the Lipschitz assumption fair? A large L shrinks the guaranteed ball, which sounds like relief, but a large L is what a model needs to draw sharp narrow basins, and a large local growth rate is what defeats the defense. A large constant does not make a model safe; it makes the failures spiky, and spiky failures are just as easy to hit by gradient, since the gradient is largest where the surface is steepest.

Theorem 5.17 (Oscillation needs steepness). If f : [0,1] → ℝ is L-Lipschitz with f 0 = f 1 = 0 and f t = M > 0, then L ≥ 2M.

Proof. M ≤ L·t and M ≤ L·(1-t); add. ∎

higher_lipschitz_more_oscillation. Sharp transitions require a large L, and a large L is what the cost theory charges for.

Worked example: the linear ramp. For f(x) = ⟨w,x⟩ + b with ‖w‖ = L and f p = τ + m, the guaranteed ball of radius m/L is tight: moving along -w/‖w‖ decreases f at maximal rate, so the ball is inscribed in the basin, kissing the boundary at the foot of the perpendicular. Every later theorem about basin volume is a version of inscribing balls like this.

12.5. The coarea and cone bounds🔗

Definition 5.18 (The ε-band). coareaBand(f, τ, ε) = {τ - ε ≤ f ≤ τ}, in MoF_17_CoareaBound.

Theorem 5.19 (Ball inside the band). If f is L-Lipschitz and some c has f c = τ - ε/2, then B(c, ε/(4L)) lies in the band.

Proof. Across the ball the value moves by less than ε/4. ∎

lipschitz_ball_subset_band; the centre sits mid-band so the ball cannot escape either wall.

Theorem 5.20 (Coarea volume lower bound). μ(band) ≥ μ(B(c, ε/(4L))); in ℝ this is ε/(2L), and in ℝ^n it grows like (ε/(4L))^n.

Proof. Monotonicity under Theorem 5.19. ∎

epsilon_band_volume_lower_bound, with real and Euclidean specializations. The centre is free on a connected space by the IVT (exists_midpoint_for_band), making the argument unconditional (epsilon_band_volume_pos_unconditional). The band always has positive, computably bounded measure: the boundary is not a lonely level set but the spine of a slab.

Remark 5.21. A defender's classifier has an uncertainty band of width ε, and the true behaviors falling in it occupy volume at least ε/(2L). Sharpening shrinks it linearly, which is progress, but never to zero while ε > 0.

Definition 5.22 (Steep region). steepRegionR(f, τ, s, z) = {x | f x > τ + s·|x - z|}, in MoF_18_ConeBound, with steepRegion in MoF_11_EpsilonRobust and steepRegionRefined in MoF_20_RefinedPersistence.

Theorem 5.23 (Defense distortion bound). If f is L-Lipschitz, D is K-Lipschitz, and D z = z, then f(D x) ≥ f x - L(K+1)·dist(x,z).

Proof. dist(D x, x) ≤ (K+1)·dist(x,z), and f changes by at most L times that. ∎

defense_from_input_bound_R. The compound L(K+1) is the defense's maximum reach: how far below its input value it can pull the score. If f rises faster in some direction, the defense loses.

Theorem 5.24 (Cone measure bound). If f z = τ, D z = z, and f(z + t) ≥ τ + c·t on (0, δ₀) with c > L(K+1) =: s, then that interval lies in the steep region, the steep region has measure at least δ₀, and every steep point stays unsafe after defense.

Proof. f x ≥ τ + c·t > τ + s·t gives the inclusion and the measure; Theorem 5.23 then gives f(D x) > τ + s|x-z| - s|x-z| = τ. ∎

cone_measure_bound, assembling cone_segment_in_steep_region, steep_region_contains_Ioo, steep_region_measure_pos, and steep_region_measure_lower_bound. Chapter 1 gave one surviving query, the master theorem one surviving boundary point; this gives an entire cone of positive measure that remains unsafe after the defense has done its best.

Theorem 5.25 (Shallow boundaries can be defended). If f x ≤ f z + L·dist(x,z), the steep region is empty for every K ≥ 0.

Proof. f x ≤ τ + L·dist ≤ τ + L(K+1)·dist. ∎

shallow_boundary_no_persistence in MoF_19_OptimalDefense. The two theorems draw a sharp line: steep boundaries carry persistent positive-measure failure no defense removes, shallow ones do not, and whether a real model is steep or shallow at its boundary is the most important quantitative fact about its defensibility.

Worked example: a corner in the score. With f(x) = τ + G·x for x ≥ 0, so L = G, persistence needs K + 1 < 1, impossible. The corner is not steep relative to its own Lipschitz constant. Genuine persistence needs f to rise near z faster than elsewhere, which is the regime the gradient chain reaches through ‖∇f(z)‖.

12.6. Dimensional scaling🔗

Theorem 5.26 (Grid explosion). Discretizing d axes into N bins gives N^d cells, unbounded for N ≥ 2; covering needs at least N^d queries and exceeds any fixed budget.

Proof. The grid has cardinality N^d ≥ 2^d, and covering is a surjection onto it. ∎

grid_card, grid_exponential_growth, queries_lower_bound_surjective, no_fixed_budget_defense. Exhaustive defense is not expensive; it is impossible at any budget.

Theorem 5.27 (Coverage collapse). A patch of relative radius r < 1 covers fraction r^d → 0, and covering a fixed fraction needs (1/r)^d → ∞ patches.

Proof. Relative volume is the product of side fractions. ∎

coverage_fraction_vanishes, defense_patch_shrinks, exponential_base, bundled as DimensionalCurse. Each thing the defender builds covers a fraction shrinking exponentially with dimension. The attacker needs one point; the defender needs almost all.

Theorem 5.28 (Boundary structure). The boundary is closed, compact on compacta, empty exactly when f never equals τ, nonempty on a connected space when f straddles τ, and equal to f⁻¹({τ}).

Proof. Theorem 5.3 plus the IVT cases. ∎

boundary_is_closed, boundary_is_compact_on_compact, boundary_empty_of_no_crossing, boundary_nonempty_connected, boundary_is_preimage_singleton.

Theorem 5.29 (Regular points are isolated in one dimension). With nonzero derivative at a boundary point, some punctured neighborhood has f ≠ τ.

Proof sketch. A nonzero derivative makes f strictly monotone near z. ∎

regular_value_boundary, boundary_locally_finite_1d. Where regular, the boundary is thin and well-behaved; where the gradient degenerates it can thicken and fold, and whether real boundaries are regular or fractal is an open empirical question.

Theorem 5.30 (Complexity and crossings). A constant model has a trivial basin, a monotone model crosses at most once, and oscillation with many components requires L ≥ 2M to reach height M.

Proof. The monotone case squeezes f to τ between crossings; the rest is Theorem 5.17. ∎

constant_model_no_basin_empty, constant_model_no_basin_univ, low_complexity_few_crossings_1d, higher_lipschitz_more_oscillation. A bigger model is not automatically safer geometry; it is capable of a more complicated failure landscape.

Worked example: random points in the cube. In high dimension almost all volume is near the surface and distances concentrate. The attacker sampling at random lands in the peripheral bulk where an appreciable basin is found; the defender watches each patch cover an r^d sliver of that same bulk.

12.7. Gradient attacks🔗

Theorem 5.31 (An ascent direction exists). If f is differentiable at x with f' ≠ 0, some direction and step raise f.

Proof sketch. Pick v with f' v > 0 and restrict to the line. ∎

ascent_direction_exists, multivariate_ascent_direction in MoF_10_GradientAttack, on discrete_ascent_improvement and hasFDerivAt_line_restrict. This is the licence for gradient-based adversarial methods: away from critical points there is always a way to raise the score, and critical points are where the gradient vanishes (critical_point_iff_fderiv_eq_zero).

Theorem 5.32 (The gradient is steepest). Among unit directions ⟨g, v⟩ is maximized at g/‖g‖, giving directional derivative ‖g‖.

Proof. Cauchy-Schwarz. ∎

With fderiv_apply_eq_inner_gradient and real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq'. This is why attacks follow the gradient: it reaches the boundary in the fewest steps.

Theorem 5.33 (Near-optimal direction). If ‖f'‖ > c at z, some unit v has f' v > c.

Proof sketch. Normalize a vector of norm below 1 on which f' exceeds c. ∎

near_optimal_direction.

Theorem 5.34 (Derivative forces local growth). If f z = τ and f' v > c for a unit v, then f(z + tv) > τ + c·t for small t > 0.

Proof sketch. g(t) = f(z + tv) - τ - ct has g(0) = 0 and positive derivative. ∎

deriv_implies_local_growth, with deriv_implies_strict_local_growth.

Theorem 5.35 (Gradient chain to persistence). If f is differentiable at a boundary point with ‖f'‖ > ℓ(K+1), the steep region is nonempty and {f(D x) > τ} has positive measure.

Proof sketch. Theorem 5.33 gives a direction beating ℓ(K+1), Theorem 5.34 turns it into local growth placing a point in the steep region, and Theorem 5.24 upgrades that to a positive-measure surviving set. ∎

gradient_norm_implies_steep_nonempty, gradient_chain_persistent_unsafe, invoking persistent_unsafe_refined. Measure the gradient at the boundary; if it beats the defense's smoothing budget, following it reaches behaviors the defense cannot save, not one but a set of positive volume. The single number ‖∇f(z)‖ decides whether the model is persistently attackable. This is transversality_from_deriv in its sharpest form.

Remark 5.36. Chapter 1's attack was a construction with no notion of effort. The gradient attack is a process with a step count, (τ - f(start))/gain, which is a real budget. Both reach the same boundary; only the second has a price tag.

12.8. Transferability🔗

Say f and g are δ-close when |f x - g x| ≤ δ everywhere.

Theorem 5.37 (Transfer with margin). If f and g are δ-close and f p > τ + δ, then g p > τ.

Proof. g p ≥ f p - δ > τ. ∎

transfer_attack in MoF_06_Transferability, restated as transfer_margin_needed. The margin is the toll for crossing between models: an attack merely clearing τ on the source may fail on the target, one clearing τ + δ transfers. Attackers know this when they over-optimize, and over-optimization by δ is precisely what buys transfer.

Theorem 5.38 (Basin containment). {f > τ + δ} ⊆ {g > τ}, with equality of basins at δ = 0.

Proof. Theorem 5.37 pointwise. ∎

basin_containment, identical_models_identical_basins, zero_distance_free_transfer, with the two-sided pointwise_sandwich.

Theorem 5.39 (Transfer is computationally free). Given δ-closeness and a source success with margin δ, the target success follows with zero target evaluations.

Proof. No term in Theorem 5.37's proof evaluates g at a new point. ∎

transfer_is_free in MoF_Cost_07. An attacker who breaks one model gets every δ-close model free. Model families trained on similar data, or fine-tunes of a common base, are δ-close for small δ, so one attack sweeps the family, and closed deployment of a model whose base is public offers less protection than it appears.

A defense classifier is a function on the same space, so to the extent it agrees with what it guards it inherits its vulnerabilities, and to the extent it disagrees it misclassifies safe behavior. Closeness buys agreement at the price of shared failure; distance buys independence at the price of collateral refusals.

Theorem 5.40 (Empirical closeness underestimates). An empirical maximum disagreement is at most the true δ, and more samples raise it.

Proof. A maximum of quantities bounded by δ is bounded by δ. ∎

estimation_cost, more_samples_better_estimate. The estimation cost is paired evaluations, not an exponential quantity: transfer is cheap to plan and free to execute.

Worked example: a fine-tune and its base. If a light fine-tune changed the score by at most δ = 0.1, an attack with margin 0.15 transfers to the base and one with margin 0.05 need not. Safety fine-tuning with small δ leaves the base model's attacks almost entirely intact.

12.9. The cost theory🔗

The MoF_Cost series builds budgets in ten layers, and the punchline is one asymmetry: attack cost stays bounded while defense cost explodes with dimension.

Theorem 5.41 (Ball volume). An open ball of positive radius has positive volume, monotone in the radius; in ℝ it is 2r.

Proof. Nonempty opens have positive Lebesgue measure. ∎

ball_measure_pos, ball_measure_mono, ball_measure_scale in MoF_Cost_01_BallVolume.

Theorem 5.42 (Basin volume lower bound). The basin contains the robustness ball, so its measure is at least the ball's; for merely continuous f it is still positive.

Proof. Theorem 5.14 as a subset relation, plus Theorem 5.5. ∎

robustness_ball_subset_basin, basin_measure_ge_ball, basin_measure_ge_ball_pos, with basin_measurableSet. The attacker's target is a ball of volume at least (margin/L)^n times a dimensional constant.

Theorem 5.43 (Random search hitting time). With per-trial hit probability p, the miss probability (1-p)^n decreases to zero and the expected number of trials is 1/p.

Proof sketch. Powers of a number below one vanish; the geometric series sums to 1/p. ∎

miss_probability_vanishes, hit_probability_tends_to_one, geometric_sum_le_inverse, tsum_geometric_eq_inv in MoF_Cost_03_HittingTime. When p is a constant fraction this is cheap; the defender's only real hope is that p is exponentially small in high dimension, which is where gradient attacks earn their keep by replacing 1/p with a linear step count.

Theorem 5.44 (Estimation margin). If |f̂ - f| ≤ ε, then f̂ x > τ + ε implies f x > τ and f̂ x < τ - ε implies f x < τ; the undecidable band is {|f̂ - τ| ≤ ε}.

Proof. Rearranging the absolute-value inequality. ∎

estimation_error_bound_unsafe, estimation_error_bound_safe, estimation_uncertain_band, estimation_band_shrinks in MoF_Cost_04_Concentration. That band is exactly the coarea band: the band the classifier cannot resolve is the band the geometry says has positive volume.

Theorem 5.45 (Lipschitz interpolation). Holding the error below ε throughout [0,1]^d needs samples no farther than ε/L apart, hence on the order of (L/ε)^d.

Proof. The Lipschitz condition plus a covering count. ∎

lipschitz_estimation_error, estimation_improves_with_distance, total_estimation_budget in MoF_Cost_09_LipschitzEstimation, with sup_norm_triangle and n_samples_coverage. The defender's estimation problem inherits the curse directly, and concentration works against it: samples spread thin, so the interpolation bound is loose exactly where it matters.

Theorem 5.46 (Attack cost). An attack gaining δ per step on a score in [0,1] reaches τ from s₀ in at most ⌈(τ - s₀)/δ⌉ + 1 steps and takes at most ⌈1/δ⌉ useful steps.

Proof sketch. After n steps the score is at least s₀ + nδ, and it cannot exceed 1. ∎

attack_value_after_n_steps, steps_to_threshold, attack_cost_upper_bound, total_attack_cost in MoF_Cost_05_AttackCost, with attackSeq_convergent and finite_steps_bound. The budget is 1/δ, independent of dimension, because the attacker follows a one-dimensional trajectory and each step gains a fixed amount regardless of how many dimensions surround the path.

Theorem 5.47 (Defense cost). Covering with patches of relative radius r < 1 needs on the order of (1/r)^d patches; any budget has a critical dimension.

Proof. Fraction α needs α·(1/r)^d patches. ∎

patches_needed, defense_cost_exponential, critical_dimension in MoF_Cost_06_DefenseCost.

Theorem 5.48 (Transfer cost). Porting an attack across δ-close models costs zero target queries, and estimating δ grows with precision, not dimension.

Proof. Theorems 5.39 and 5.40. ∎

MoF_Cost_07_TransferCost. Transfer adds essentially nothing to the attack budget while multiplying its reach across a family.

Definition 5.49 (Cost ratio). costRatio(N, d, δ) = N^d · δ, in MoF_Cost_08_CostRatio, bundled as unifiedCostRatio on CostParameters in MoF_Cost_10_UnifiedTheory, with unifiedCostRatio_eq.

Theorem 5.50 (Cost asymmetry, master theorem). For fixed N ≥ 2 and δ > 0 the ratio is positive, increasing, and divergent in d, exceeding any R beyond a critical dimension. The attacker's budget is dimension-independent; the defender's is exponential.

Proof sketch. A positive constant times an exponential in d; the attack budget 1/δ contains no d. ∎

cost_ratio_tends_to_infinity, cost_ratio_exceeds_any_bound, attacker_advantage_quantified, MASTER_THEOREM_cost_asymmetry, with attack_budget_dimension_independent and defenseBudget_exponential. As a concrete anchor, two_dimension_ratio gives 6.25 already at d = 2, N = 25, δ = 0.01.

This is the chapter's quantitative summary. The boundary exists, is populated by a positive-measure region, is found at a dimension-independent cost, and is covered only at a dimension-exponential one. The ratio diverges and no budget closes the gap.

Theorem 5.51 (No K wins). Either G > L(K+1) and a persistent unsafe region of positive measure survives, or L(K+1) ≥ G and the failure band has width at least G·δ. For G > L the critical K* = G/L - 1 is where the modes trade off exactly and neither horn is escapable; for G ≤ L the boundary is shallow and defensible.

Proof sketch. A case split on one real comparison. Increasing K strictly increases L(K+1) (defense_band_monotone), flipping the first horn into the second with equality at K* (optimalK_critical), and both horns are realized for G > L (defense_dilemma_both_realizable). ∎

defense_cannot_win, optimal_K_exists, complete_defense_characterization in MoF_19_OptimalDefense. A gentle defense leaves persistent cones; an aggressive one smears the failure band wide, distorting behavior over a region growing linearly in K. At K* the defender has minimized total damage but not eliminated it.

Worked example: the cost ratio. With d = 20, N = 10, δ = 0.05, the attacker pays about twenty steps and the defender 10^20 cells. Double the dimension and the attacker still pays twenty steps while the defender pays 10^40. Nothing the defender does to N, r, or K touches the exponential in d.

The one honest pushback is the word "effective": the exponent is the dimension of the manifold the attack actually explores, and if that is low the ratio is manageable. The cost theory does not measure it for you; it tells you that this one number, not model size or defender cleverness, decides the contest.

12.10. Concentration of measure🔗

Theorem 5.52 (Markov bound on the basin). For integrable f ≥ 0, μ{f ≥ ε} ≤ (1/ε)∫f dμ.

Proof. The integrand is at least ε on {f ≥ ε}. ∎

markov_real_basin in MoF_Adv_10_MeasureBounds. A model whose average deviation is small cannot have a large high-deviation basin, which sounds like comfort but sets a floor, because the average is a property of the whole model and lowering it means changing the model everywhere at once.

The concentration phenomenon. On the sphere or under a Gaussian in ℝ^n, an L-Lipschitz f deviates from its median by more than t with probability at most about 2exp(-ct²/L²): it is nearly constant across almost all of a high-dimensional space. This is Lévy-Milman-Talagrand concentration, whose consequences are exactly the cost asymmetries the library proves.

Concentration and the curse are the same fact. With τ above the median the basin is the far tail, exponentially small in (τ - m)²/L² — good for the defender in that a random behavior is almost never unsafe, catastrophic in that Theorem 5.5 still guarantees the tail is nonempty, and the gradient chain skips the 1/p wait by climbing straight to it. Concentration hides the basin from random draws and does nothing to hide it from gradients.

Theorem 5.53 (Positive-measure failure band). On a connected Hausdorff metric space with a positive-on-opens measure, L-Lipschitz f, a K-Lipschitz defense fixing the safe region, and a transverse boundary point, the set {f(D x) > τ} has strictly positive measure.

Proof sketch. Transversality places a point in the steep region, distortion shows steep points stay unsafe, and the steep region is open and nonempty. ∎

epsilon_robust_impossibility, positive_measure_failure_band, persistent_unsafe_region in MoF_11_EpsilonRobust. This is the strongest form of the defense impossibility here, giving a surviving set of positive measure in full generality under honest Lipschitz hypotheses on both model and defense.

Remark 5.54 (The two faces). Toward the defender, concentration says samples spread thin and the nearest sample is far, so the interpolation bound is loose everywhere. Toward the attacker it says the space is one undifferentiated bulk where a Lipschitz score is nearly constant, so a gradient points reliably toward the rare tail. The defender sees a space too big to cover; the attacker sees one too smooth to hide the exit.

Worked example: the Gaussian annulus. Under a standard Gaussian, ‖x‖ concentrates around √n in a window of width about 1, so almost all mass sits in a thin annulus. Take f(x) = ‖x‖, 1-Lipschitz, and τ = √n + 3. The basin's mass is on the order of exp(-9c), independent of n, so random search costs a large fixed number.

12.11. Iterated and discrete attacks🔗

Theorem 5.55 (The attacker's running edge). The running maximum of scores is monotone nondecreasing. Under capacity parity, a defense with a fixed number of correction slots facing one more configuration must collapse two attacks to one output. Over T turns the defense reveals at least T classifications.

Proof sketch. A supremum over a growing set is nondecreasing (running_max_monotone); the rest is pigeonhole (one_more_attack_overwhelms) iterated to a permanent margin (attacker_permanent_edge), with each probe leaking a classification (defense_leaks_per_turn). ∎

In MoF_13_MultiTurn, with multi_turn_impossibility and boundary_points_accumulate. The attacker has a ratchet: each turn can only improve the best result, each probe extracts boundary information, and boundary points accumulate. A defense holding for one turn need not hold for a hundred, which is the formal shadow of long conversations eroding guardrails.

Theorem 5.56 (Discrete crossing and the discrete trilemma). On a finite chain with f 0 < τ and f(n+1) ≥ τ there is an adjacent straddling pair. A defense fixing every safe point fixes such a crossing. More abstractly, for any unsafe u, either D leaves u unsafe or D fails to be the identity where needed, and a verdict both complete and injective cannot exist on a space rich enough to encode its own decisions.

Proof sketch. Take the largest index with f i < τ (discrete_ivt); the rest is discrete_defense_boundary_fixed, discrete_trilemma, injectivity_forces_incompleteness, completeness_forces_noninjectivity. ∎

In MoF_12_Discrete. The last clause is where the geometry rejoins the diagonal: pigeonhole rather than connectedness, but the same conclusion. The continuum route reaches the boundary by connectedness, the discrete route by counting, the self-referential route by diagonalization. Three proofs, one boundary.

Remark 5.57. Chapter 1 built a query no boolean verdict answers by self-reference; discrete_trilemma builds an unsafe point no utility-preserving defense corrects, by order and counting. Both are instances of one pattern: a system asked to classify a domain it is embedded in must leave a witness uncovered. This chapter spent its length measuring that witness.

12.12. The two halves, joined🔗

The diagonal proves existence and nothing more, indifferent to quantity, cost, and dimension. That indifference is its strength and its limit.

This chapter proves the quantitative shape of the same failure: the boundary has positive-measure thickness, carries a persistent unsafe cone against any defense, is reachable at a dimension-independent cost, and is coverable only at a dimension-exponential one. Where the diagonal says a bad point exists, the geometry says a region of bad points exists, cheap to enter and expensive to seal, with the gap growing without bound.

A practitioner who absorbed only the diagonal might hope the bad point is rare, hard to find, or easy to patch; the geometry closes each hope. One who absorbed only the cost theory might think the problem is merely hard; the diagonal closes that, since the boundary is not hard to remove but impossible to remove.

12.13. Historical notes🔗

The IVT underlying the crossing results is Bolzano's, and reading the boundary as an unavoidable attack surface is the organizing idea of ManifoldProofs. The covering-number form of the curse is standard in nonparametric statistics. Concentration of measure is due in modern form to Lévy, Milman, and Talagrand, and its adversarial reading is the contribution of the cost layers.

13. Approximate Bridges to Real Models🔗

The impossibility theorems of Chapter 3 are exact. They assume confidence that is a perfect biconditional function of correctness, a probe that never misfires, a confidence field crossing the truth boundary cleanly. No deployed system meets any of these.

That reaction is wrong, and this chapter is the argument. The strict statement is the ε = 0 corner of a family of quantitative statements, each assuming only an error budget and each surviving it with a weakened but nonempty conclusion. The contradiction does not evaporate as the idealizations relax.

Everything is verified in two developments: the calibration bridges in HoF_12_Approximate, the metric degradation law in F_09_QuantitativeDegradation. Both import Mathlib, so the theorems are cited by verified name and proved here in prose; genuinely finite fragments carry the prefix c6_ and are elaborated as this document builds.

Why the effort is worth it: a skeptic can dismiss a theorem about a model that does not exist, but not one whose hypotheses are an error budget their own model satisfies. Once calibration is granted only within ε, coverage only outside a band, and universality only up to a distance, the hypotheses become measurable properties of a shipped system rather than idealizations, and the conclusion transfers to it. That is the difference between a result in a seminar and one in a deployment review.

13.1. What the exact theorems assume🔗

A model is M : Q → A × ℝ, with answer (M q).1 and confidence (M q).2. Correctness is a signed truth-distance field δ : Q × A → ℝ, negative when the answer is correct, positive when wrong, zero on the boundary; write δ(q) for δ(q, (M q).1). Fix a threshold c, running value 1/2.

Strict calibration is the biconditional conf(q) > c ↔ δ(q) < 0 and conf(q) < c ↔ δ(q) > 0, verified as StrictCalibrated. Faithfulness says conf(q) ≥ c → δ(q) < 0, verified as TrilemmaFaithful. Coverage says the truth-distance takes both signs, verified as TrilemmaCovering.

Under these, plus continuity of the confidence map and connectedness of Q, the strict trilemma derives False: coverage forces confidence above and below c, continuity forces a crossing at conf = c, and there calibration and faithfulness give incompatible signs for δ.

Two hypotheses a practitioner will defend are worth defending before weakening. Continuity is not exotic: a confidence computed from a softmax over logits smooth in a continuous embedding is continuous in that embedding, and the drift a deployment sees — paraphrase, added context, distribution shift — moves through embedding space rather than teleporting. Connectedness is subtler and is what Chapter 4 spends its effort on; the short version is that after embedding, the reachable region is path-connected often enough for the IVT to bite.

The sign convention drives every inequality. Negative truth-distance is good, and |δ(q)| is how far the answer sits from the boundary, so a large negative value is confidently correct and a value near zero is on the knife's edge. Confidence runs the same way relative to c. Calibration claims the two axes agree in sign, and this chapter is about how much they may disagree near the origin of both.

13.2. Two-sided ε-calibration🔗

Real calibration curves do not flip at a point. Close to δ = 0 the model is genuinely uncertain, confidence hovers near c, and small perturbations move it across the threshold with no reliable relation to correctness. The honest weakening demands nothing in that neighborhood.

Definition 6.1 (Two-sided ε-calibration). Fix ε ≥ 0. M is ε-calibrated at c if δ(q) < -ε → conf(q) > c + ε and δ(q) > ε → conf(q) < c - ε, for all q. The verified predicate is EpsCalibrated M δ c ε.

Proposition 6.2 (Contrapositives). ε-calibration is equivalent to conf(q) ≤ c + ε → δ(q) ≥ -ε together with conf(q) ≥ c - ε → δ(q) ≤ ε.

Proof. Each line is the contrapositive of one clause, and contraposition over a linear order is an equivalence. ∎

Remark 6.3. At ε = 0 the clauses become the two forward implications of strict calibration, the half the IVT argument uses. The verified strictCalibrated_to_epsCalibrated_zero_half shows StrictCalibrated implies EpsCalibrated M δ (1/2) 0, so nothing is lost by working in the weaker vocabulary from the start.

Example 6.4 (Reading an ε off a calibration table). Bin a model's answers by measured accuracy and reported confidence, normalized so c = 0.5. If every answer below truth-distance -0.1 reports confidence above 0.6, and every answer above 0.1 reports below 0.4, the model is ε-calibrated with ε = 0.1. Inside those bands the table may be ragged; the definition demands nothing there.

Definition 6.5 (ε-coverage). M is ε-covering if some q_t has δ(q_t) < -ε and some q_f has δ(q_f) > ε. The verified predicate is EpsCovering M δ ε.

The subscripts read "true" and "false": questions the model gets solidly right and solidly wrong, both far enough from the boundary that ε-calibration applies. At ε = 0 this is ordinary coverage.

Example 6.5b (Coverage bounds usable ε). If the easiest true question sits at -0.3 and the easiest false one at 0.3, ε-coverage holds for any ε < 0.3. But if the domain is hard and the most solidly-true question is only at -0.08, you cannot claim ε-coverage for ε ≥ 0.08, and the bridge runs only with a smaller slack than your calibration might support.

13.3. The approximate trilemma🔗

Theorem 6.6 (Approximate Hallucination Trilemma). Let Q be connected, the confidence continuous, and ε ≥ 0. If M is ε-covering, ε-calibrated at c, and threshold-inclusive faithful, then some q₀ has conf(q₀) = c and δ(q₀) ∈ [-ε, 0).

Proof. Coverage gives q_t with δ(q_t) < -ε and q_f with δ(q_f) > ε. Calibration turns these into conf(q_t) > c + ε and conf(q_f) < c - ε, so the continuous confidence is above and below c and the IVT lands q₀ with conf(q₀) = c. Calibration's contrapositive at q₀ gives δ(q₀) ≥ -ε; faithfulness, applicable since conf(q₀) = c ≥ c, gives δ(q₀) < 0. ∎

Remark 6.7 (Why the interval is half-open). The lower end is attained in principle; the upper end is not. The strict < 0 comes from faithfulness, which forbids confident correctness from touching the boundary; the weak ≥ -ε comes from calibration, which only bounds how far below the boundary a low-confidence question sits. The asymmetry is what lets ε → 0 recover a genuine contradiction rather than a degenerate point.

Example 6.8 (A concrete margin). With c = 0.5 and the ε = 0.1 model, Theorem 6.6 guarantees a question where the model reports confidence exactly 0.5 and is correct with truth-distance in [-0.1, 0) — right, but only just, while reporting a coin flip's confidence. Improving to ε = 0.03 tightens the margin without removing the question.

Example 6.8b (Tracing the intermediate value step). On [0,1] let conf(q) = 1 - q and δ(q) = q - 0.55, with c = 0.5, ε = 0.1. Coverage holds at q = 0 (δ = -0.55 < -0.1) and q = 1 (δ = 0.45 > 0.1). Confidence hits c at q = 0.5, where δ = -0.05, which lies in [-0.1, 0) exactly as the theorem predicts: correct by five hundredths while reporting a coin flip.

13.4. Recovering the exact contradiction🔗

Theorem 6.9 (Exact contradiction from the approximate bridge). Under Theorem 6.6's hypotheses at ε = 0, one derives False. Verified as exact_from_approx.

Proof. Theorem 6.6 returns δ(q₀) ∈ [0, 0), which is empty. ∎

Theorem 6.10 (Strict calibration through the bridge). Strict biconditional calibration, ordinary coverage, and threshold-inclusive faithfulness on a connected space with continuous confidence give False. Verified as exact_from_strictCalibrated_via_approx.

Proof. Convert to zero-slack approximate hypotheses by Remark 6.3 and apply Theorem 6.9. ∎

Remark 6.11. Theorem 6.10 needs continuity only of the confidence map, not of the answer or truth field, because the IVT step is applied to confidence alone. This economy is a direct benefit of factoring through the bridge, which exposes exactly which map must be continuous.

Remark 6.11b (The diagonal is still underneath). It can look as though the bridge traded the diagonal for the IVT and self-reference left the room. It did not. The forced q₀ is the liar_query witness a₀ in analytic clothes. There, a₀ is the index where the self-verdict must equal its own negation, impossible because negation has no fixed point. Here, q₀ is where confidence must equal the threshold, the one fixed point of the real complement. Same object, two controllers.

13.5. The tightening principle🔗

Theorem 6.12 (Tightening principle). If M is faithful, ε-covering, and both ε₁- and ε₂-calibrated with 0 ≤ ε₂ ≤ ε₁, the forced question from the ε₂ bridge has δ ∈ [-ε₂, 0) ⊆ [-ε₁, 0). Improving calibration cannot loosen the bound, and any strict improvement strictly tightens it.

theorem c6_tightening (ε₁ ε₂ : ℝ) (h : ε₂ ≤ ε₁) : Set.Ico (-ε₂) 0 ⊆ Set.Ico (-ε₁) 0 := ε₁:ℝε₂:ℝh:ε₂ ≤ ε₁⊢ Set.Ico (-ε₂) 0 ⊆ Set.Ico (-ε₁) 0 intro x ε₁:ℝε₂:ℝh:ε₂ ≤ ε₁x:ℝhx:x ∈ Set.Ico (-ε₂) 0⊢ x ∈ Set.Ico (-ε₁) 0 exact ⟨ε₁:ℝε₂:ℝh:ε₂ ≤ ε₁x:ℝhx:x ∈ Set.Ico (-ε₂) 0⊢ -ε₁ ≤ x All goals completed! 🐙, hx.2⟩ theorem c6_margin_bound (ε₂ x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Ico (-ε₂) 0) : |x| ≤ ε₂ := ε₂:ℝx:ℝhx:x ∈ Set.Ico (-ε₂) 0⊢ |x| ≤ ε₂ ε₂:ℝx:ℝhx:x ∈ Set.Ico (-ε₂) 0⊢ -x ≤ ε₂ All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. The interval inclusion is c6_tightening and the margin bound c6_margin_bound, both pure order arithmetic. ∎

Remark 6.13 (Calibration and faithfulness are not independent dials). A tempting mental model treats them as separate knobs each tunable to perfection. Faithfulness fixes the sign of δ(q₀) and calibration fixes its magnitude, and together they pin δ(q₀) into a shrinking interval the strict theorem shows must eventually be empty. You cannot hold faithfulness fixed and drive calibration to perfection.

Example 6.14 (Spending the budget). A program halving ε each quarter — 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125 — tracks the guaranteed margin down the same sequence. After a year the model is superbly calibrated and its forced fence-sitting question is correct by at most 0.0125 while reporting exactly threshold confidence. The program did not eliminate the question; it manufactured one on which the model is correct by an amount too small to matter.

Remark 6.14b (Where the naive optimization goes). A team optimizing calibration alone drives ε down until the shell [-ε, 0) is thinner than the resolution of the training signal, at which point further calibration cannot be achieved by more of the same. The bridge predicts the wall before the team hits it.

13.6. Localization to the transition band🔗

Proposition 6.15 (Localization). Under Theorem 6.6's hypotheses, every forced q₀ lies outside {conf > c + ε} and {conf < c - ε}, hence in the transition band {c - ε ≤ conf ≤ c + ε}.

theorem c6_localization (c ε : ℝ) (hε : 0 ≤ ε) : c ∈ Set.Icc (c - ε) (c + ε) ∧ ¬ (c > c + ε) ∧ ¬ (c < c - ε) := ⟨⟨c:ℝε:ℝhε:0 ≤ ε⊢ c - ε ≤ c All goals completed! 🐙, c:ℝε:ℝhε:0 ≤ ε⊢ c ≤ c + ε All goals completed! 🐙⟩, c:ℝε:ℝhε:0 ≤ ε⊢ ¬c > c + ε All goals completed! 🐙, c:ℝε:ℝhε:0 ≤ ε⊢ ¬c < c - ε All goals completed! 🐙⟩

Proof. conf(q₀) = c, and c6_localization places c in the band and outside both decisive regions. ∎

Localization is what makes the margin actionable. The forced question is not scattered anywhere in the space; it sits where the model reports near-threshold confidence, which is a region a deployment can monitor.

13.7. The discrete band constraint🔗

Theorem 6.16 (Discrete band constraint). On any sets, with no topology and no finiteness, if M is ε-calibrated at c and threshold-inclusive faithful, then any q with c ≤ conf(q) ≤ c + ε has δ(q) ∈ [-ε, 0). Verified as discrete_approx_bridge.

theorem c6_band (dq confq c eps : Int) -- ε-calibration, lower clause (hcal : dq < -eps → confq > c + eps) -- c-faithfulness (hfaith : confq ≥ c → dq < 0) -- upper half of the band (hge : confq ≥ c) -- not above the band (hle : confq ≤ c + eps) : -eps ≤ dq ∧ dq < 0 := dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤeps:ℤhcal:dq < -eps → confq > c + epshfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ c + eps⊢ -eps ≤ dq ∧ dq < 0 dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤeps:ℤhcal:dq < -eps → confq > c + epshfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ c + eps⊢ -eps ≤ dq dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤeps:ℤhcal:dq < -eps → confq > c + epshfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ c + epsh:dq < -eps⊢ -eps ≤ dqdq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤeps:ℤhcal:dq < -eps → confq > c + epshfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ c + epsh:-eps ≤ dq⊢ -eps ≤ dq dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤeps:ℤhcal:dq < -eps → confq > c + epshfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ c + epsh:dq < -eps⊢ -eps ≤ dq dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤeps:ℤhcal:dq < -eps → confq > c + epshfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ c + epsh:dq < -epsthis:confq > c + eps := hcal h⊢ -eps ≤ dq; All goals completed! 🐙 dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤeps:ℤhcal:dq < -eps → confq > c + epshfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ c + epsh:-eps ≤ dq⊢ -eps ≤ dq All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Faithfulness gives δ(q) < 0. For the lower bound, if δ(q) < -ε then calibration forces conf(q) > c + ε, contradicting the band. The integer transcription is c6_band, whose proof is two cases and omega. ∎

Corollary 6.17 (No boundary point in the upper band). No q with c ≤ conf(q) ≤ c + ε has δ(q) = 0. Verified as no_boundary_in_upper_band.

theorem c6_exact (dq confq c : Int) (hcal : dq < 0 → confq > c) (hfaith : confq ≥ c → dq < 0) (hge : confq ≥ c) (hle : confq ≤ c) : False := dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤhcal:dq < 0 → confq > chfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ c⊢ False dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤhcal:dq < 0 → confq > chfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ ch1:dq < 0 := hfaith hge⊢ False dq:ℤconfq:ℤc:ℤhcal:dq < 0 → confq > chfaith:confq ≥ c → dq < 0hge:confq ≥ chle:confq ≤ ch1:dq < 0 := hfaith hgeh2:confq > c := hcal h1⊢ False All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Theorem 6.16 gives δ(q) < 0. At ε = 0 the band collapses to conf(q) = c and the constraint becomes the contradiction c6_exact. ∎

The discrete bridge matters because it needs no connectedness and no continuity. It does not manufacture the band-crossing question; it constrains any question that happens to land there. Where the continuous bridge derives the forced question and then bounds it, the discrete one bounds whatever the deployment observes.

13.8. Two-slack separation🔗

Confidence and truth-distance live in different units, and a single ε conflates them.

Definition 6.18 (Two-slack separation). Fix a truth slack ε and a confidence margin γ. M is two-slack separating at c if δ(q) < -ε → conf(q) > c + γ and δ(q) > ε → conf(q) < c - γ. The verified predicate is TwoSlackSeparating, with EpsCalibrated the case γ = ε.

Theorem 6.19 (Two-slack coupling). On a connected space with continuous confidence, if M is ε-covering, two-slack separating with γ ≥ 0, and threshold-inclusive faithful, some q₀ has conf(q₀) = c and δ(q₀) ∈ [-ε, 0). Verified as two_slack_approx_coupling.

Proof. Identical in shape to Theorem 6.6, with γ doing on the confidence side what ε did. ∎

Example 6.19b (Two slacks with numbers). Report confidence on 0 to 100 with c = 50, and truth-distance on a 0 to 1 semantic scale. If clearly-true questions score above 70 and clearly-false ones below 30, the model is two-slack separating with ε = 0.1 and γ = 20. The two numbers live in different worlds, and keeping them separate is what lets each be measured in its own units.

Theorem 6.20 (The truth slack must be positive). Under two-slack separation with any γ ≥ 0, ε-coverage, and threshold-inclusive faithfulness on a connected space with continuous confidence, ε > 0. Verified as truth_slack_must_be_positive.

Proof. At ε = 0 Theorem 6.19 returns δ(q₀) ∈ [0, 0), empty. ∎

This is the budget statement. A system keeping a threshold-inclusive guarantee must carry a strictly positive margin of correctness on the confident side, and the infimum of feasible slack is a measurable width of its truth boundary.

Theorem 6.21 (Two-slack band bridge). On any sets, under two-slack separation and threshold-inclusive faithfulness, any q with c ≤ conf(q) ≤ c + γ has δ(q) ∈ [-ε, 0). Verified as two_slack_band_bridge, with no_boundary_in_upper_band_two_slack.

Proof. Theorem 6.16 with c + γ for c + ε. ∎

Remark 6.22 (Axioms). The two-slack results each print #print axioms. They rest on the classical and quotient axioms Mathlib's real analysis uses and nothing model-specific. The discrete bridges, being pure order arithmetic, are lightest; the continuous ones inherit the IVT's dependencies. The core-Lean c6_ fragments use none beyond computation.

13.9. The quantitative degradation law🔗

Definition 6.23 (ε-approximate universality). M is ε-approximately universal if for every target g some prompt a has dist (M a b) (g b) ≤ ε for all b. The verified predicate is ApproxUniversal M ε.

At ε = 0 in a metric space this is ordinary curried surjectivity. For ε > 0 it is the honest claim: the system can be steered near any behavior, not onto it.

Theorem 6.24 (Approximate Lawvere). If M is ε-approximately universal, every t : Y → Y has an approximate self-fixed-point: some a with dist (M a a) (t (M a a)) ≤ ε. Verified as approx_lawvere.

Proof. Apply ε-universality to the diagonal target g b = t (M b b) and instantiate at b = a. ∎

Theorem 6.25 (Quantitative degradation). Let M be ε-approximately universal, let dist (M a a) (introspect a) ≤ δ for all a, and let t be 1-Lipschitz. Then some a has dist (introspect a) (t (introspect a)) ≤ ε + 2δ. Verified as quantitative_trilemma.

theorem c6_triangle_bound (goal d1 d2 d3 eps del : Int) (htri : goal ≤ d1 + d2 + d3) (hd1 : d1 ≤ del) (hd2 : d2 ≤ eps) (hd3 : d3 ≤ del) : goal ≤ eps + 2 * del := goal:ℤd1:ℤd2:ℤd3:ℤeps:ℤdel:ℤhtri:goal ≤ d1 + d2 + d3hd1:d1 ≤ delhd2:d2 ≤ epshd3:d3 ≤ del⊢ goal ≤ eps + 2 * del All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Three legs: from introspect a to M a a costs δ, from there to t (M a a) costs ε by Theorem 6.24, and from there to t (introspect a) costs δ again since t is 1-Lipschitz. The arithmetic is c6_triangle_bound. ∎

Theorem 6.26 (Achievable region). If additionally dist (introspect a) (t (introspect a)) > γ for all a, then γ < ε + 2δ. The achievable triples lie in {γ ≤ ε + 2δ}. Verified as achievable_region_bound, with quantitative_impossibility when γ ≥ ε + 2δ.

Proof. Theorem 6.25 gives an a where the distance is at most ε + 2δ, and the hypothesis says it exceeds γ. ∎

Theorem 6.27 (Strict limit). At ε = δ = 0, any nontrivial γ > 0 gives False. Verified as strict_limit_recovers_trilemma.

theorem c6_strict_collapse (goal margin : Int) (hbound : goal ≤ 0 + 2 * 0) (hmargin : goal > margin) : margin < 0 := goal:ℤmargin:ℤhbound:goal ≤ 0 + 2 * 0hmargin:goal > margin⊢ margin < 0 All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Substituting into Theorem 6.26 gives γ < 0, the collapse c6_strict_collapse. ∎

Remark 6.27b (What a K-Lipschitz controller costs). If t is K-Lipschitz, the middle leg is bounded by Kδ rather than δ, so the budget becomes ε + (1 + K)δ, recovering ε + 2δ at K = 1. A controller amplifying differences has a larger achievable region, which is to say it is easier to satisfy and correspondingly says less.

Remark 6.28 (Two shapes of the same fact). The calibration bridge and the degradation law relax different idealizations and produce differently-shaped budgets, an interval and a half-space, but the mechanism is one: take the exact diagonal, insert a slack at each idealized equality, and carry the slacks through by linear arithmetic to a conclusion nonempty for positive slack and contradictory at zero.

13.10. From existence to measure🔗

Example 6.29 (A risk estimate with numbers). Take the ε = 0.05 model, so any forced question is correct by at most 0.05 and sits in the band conf ∈ [0.45, 0.55]. If Chapter 5's geometry reports that the band has basin volume 2% of the input space and the deployment's query distribution puts 0.5% of its mass there, then roughly one query in two hundred lands in the band, and there the model is correct by a margin no larger than 0.05 while reporting a coin flip.

Remark 6.30 (What the composite can and cannot claim). The estimate bounds a very specific quantity, the incidence and severity of forced threshold-confidence questions. It is not a claim about all model errors. Errors far from the band are ordinary mistakes the bridge says nothing about. What it captures is the irreducible residue: errors existing not because the model is undertrained but because faithfulness, calibration, coverage, and continuity cannot all hold.

Example 6.29b (The adversarial reading). Benignly, a random query lands in the band with the concentration probability. Adversarially, an attacker does not wait for random traffic but steers, and Chapter 5's hitting-time and gradient bounds say how cheaply an input can be nudged from a confidently-handled region into the band. The bridge's localization tells the attacker exactly where to aim, which is why the benign incidence figure is the wrong number for a security case.

Remark 6.31 (The whole bridge in one sentence). The exact impossibility is the zero-slack corner of a quantitative law; the law's conclusion is a nonempty margin rather than a contradiction; the margin tightens as the model improves rather than vanishing; it is localized to the transition band rather than spread everywhere; and Chapter 5's geometry turns the located margin into a rate.

13.11. The reading is where the work is🔗

Every theorem here has the same shape: a hypothesis that is an error budget, a conclusion that is a bound, and a limit at zero slack that recovers the exact statement. What the chapter does not do is tell you what ε, γ, or δ are for your system. Those are measurements, and the bridge is only as informative as they are honest.

13.12. Historical notes🔗

The strategy of relaxing an exact impossibility to a quantitative law with a recoverable limit is standard in approximation theory and in the robust-statistics tradition, and the specific bridges here are the companion libraries' HoF_12_Approximate and F_09_QuantitativeDegradation. The approximate Lawvere theorem is the metric shadow of Chapter 1's engine, and the ε + 2δ budget is a triangle inequality with the diagonal in the middle leg. Where prose and Lean differ, the Lean is authoritative.

14. Part III: Application and Evidence🔗

15. What It Means for AI Safety🔗

A theorem saying "you cannot have all three" is a menu, not a counsel of despair. This chapter spends the result: it reads the trilemma as a design constraint, works out what each corner costs, says when each is right, and marks the one quantity the theory refuses to fix. That quantity is where deployment risk lives.

The tone shifts. The rest of this thesis is mathematics checked by the kernel; this chapter is engineering, and its claims are judgments about costs, domains, and traffic. I mark explicitly which sentences are theorems and which are recommendations.

Three sentences carry the practical upshot. Every deployed system already lives at one of exactly three corners, and the theorem's value is that the list is complete, so the fourth option you may be chasing does not exist. Which corner is right is decided by your domain and by one number the theory does not give you, the density of real traffic near the boundary.

15.1. The constraint, stated as a triangle🔗

Two results from Chapter 3 drive the chapter, both one line of Lean: no_reflective_verdict, read twice.

The Hallucination Trilemma reads v p q as "the model is confident and correct about q." Faithfulness says a confident answer is correct, calibration that confidence tracks correctness, coverage that the model actually answers. Add reflectivity and the diagonal forces a query confidently correct exactly when it is not: liar_query in a safety costume.

The Defense Trilemma reads v p q as "the wrapper renders q safe," with utility preservation and completeness, and the arbitrary-text premise as the third leg. The forced witness is the injection "be unsafe exactly if you would be made safe."

Definition 7.1 (The design triangle). The design triangle has the three named conditions as vertices. A corner policy gives up exactly one vertex. The trilemma says the interior is empty.

Remark 7.2. The two readings share a proof term, checked by rfl in Chapter 3, so the menu below is written once and applies to both problems under the translation of Definition 7.1.

The corners are three ways of removing one leg of the diagonal, and the theorem's completeness is the statement that there is no fourth leg to remove.

15.2. Three relaxations, three cost models🔗

Each corner has a characteristic cost, failure mode, and class of domains. The cost models use symbols like ρ, ε, Cerr, Cref and combine them into expressions like ρ · ε. These are not theorems and are not precise.

15.2.1. Relaxation I: drop coverage, and abstain🔗

Keep faithfulness and calibration, and buy them by refusing where a confident answer would be a gamble. This is abstention with a reject option, and it is the corner most safety-critical deployments already run, sometimes without knowing it.

Why does it escape the diagonal? Because the diagonal needs the outcome type to have no fixed point under the flip. Abstention adds a third outcome the flip leaves alone, and once the flip has a fixed point Lawvere's theorem stops producing a contradiction and starts producing a consistent value.

inductive Outcome where | correct | wrong | abstain def c7_flip : Outcome → Outcome | .correct => .wrong | .wrong => .correct | .abstain => .abstain theorem c7_flip_fixed : ∃ y : Outcome, c7_flip y = y := ⟨.abstain, rfl⟩

Read this against lawvere. On a universal system with these outcomes, the diagonal behavior is named and evaluating there gives a fixed point of c7_flip. With the two-valued flip no such point exists and the system cannot be universal; with the abstaining flip the fixed point is abstain, and the self-referential query resolves to "I decline." The liar does not vanish; it becomes a query the system may refuse. In the continuum reading this is a cut: abstaining on an open region around the boundary can disconnect the true region from the false one, which is why refusal training is connectedness surgery.

Definition 7.3 (Abstention policy). An abstention policy returns a designated abstain outcome on a region R and answers on the complement. The abstention rate is the probability that deployment traffic lands in R.

Proposition 7.3a (Abstention preserves the surviving vertices). Outside R, an abstention policy leaves faithfulness and calibration exactly as they were, changing only coverage.

Proof. The answer map is unchanged outside R, so queries answered there receive the same answer and confidence, and faithfulness and calibration are conditions on answered queries. Coverage is the only vertex touched, since R can be placed over the strictly-wrong witnesses. ∎

Not formalized. The argument is bookkeeping over which hypotheses the policy touches, and the companion libraries model total answer maps only, so there is no declaration of partial answering for it to cite.

Cost model. You pay in refused queries: roughly a · u for abstention rate a and average value u of answering a query in R. Two features matter. R should hug the boundary, because that is where confident answers are least trustworthy, and the geometry of Chapter 5 tells you how small R can be for a target error rate through concentration near the boundary (MoF_Cost_04_Concentration).

Remark 7.4. Abstention preserves both surviving vertices exactly, which is why it is the safest corner to reason about. It does not blur the confidence signal and does not tolerate a class of errors; it removes queries from scope. The failure mode is a gap in coverage, and gaps are auditable in a way confident errors are not. If you can afford to refuse, refuse.

15.2.2. Relaxation II: relax faithfulness, and price a band🔗

Definition 7.5 (Confident-error band). A confident-error band of half-width ε is the set of queries with |dF| ≤ ε for the realized truth field. The policy answers confidently everywhere and accepts that answers inside the band may be wrong. The band mass is the probability that traffic lands in it.

Cost model. The confident-error rate is about ρ · ε, boundary density times band width, and the cost is that times Cerr.

Remark 7.6. The band is not a bug you failed to fix but a resource you spend on purpose. The danger is the temptation to pretend ε is zero and discover the band the hard way when traffic shifts and ρ rises. A team running this corner honestly writes down its ε, monitors its ρ, and treats both as shipped parameters.

Proposition 7.6a (The band has a positive floor). Under coverage and a threshold-inclusive guarantee on a connected domain, the truth slack compatible with separation cannot be zero. There is a strictly positive infimum of feasible slack.

Proof. This is truth_slack_must_be_positive of Chapter 6. ∎

Remark 7.6b (The band is where monitoring is cheap). Because the errors are confined to a neighborhood of a known surface, you can spend the monitoring budget on that surface rather than the whole input space. This is the hallucination reading of "monitor, don't eliminate."

15.2.3. Relaxation III: weaken calibration, and decouple🔗

Definition 7.7 (Decoupling). A model is decoupled at level κ if the mutual information between reported confidence and correctness is at most κ. Full decoupling is κ = 0: a confidence signal carrying no information about correctness.

Proposition 7.8 (Decoupling is invisible to accuracy). Top-1 accuracy depends on the answer map alone, so two models with identical answer maps and any two confidence fields have identical accuracy.

theorem c7_decoupling_invisible_to_accuracy {Q A C S : Type _} (acc : (Q → A) → S) (M₁ M₂ : Q → A × C) (h : ∀ q, (M₁ q).1 = (M₂ q).1) : acc (fun q => (M₁ q).1) = acc (fun q => (M₂ q).1) := Q:Type u_1A:Type u_2C:Type u_3S:Type u_4acc:(Q → A) → SM₁:Q → A × CM₂:Q → A × Ch:∀ (q : Q), (M₁ q).fst = (M₂ q).fst⊢ (acc fun q => (M₁ q).fst) = acc fun q => (M₂ q).fst Q:Type u_1A:Type u_2C:Type u_3S:Type u_4acc:(Q → A) → SM₁:Q → A × CM₂:Q → A × Ch:∀ (q : Q), (M₁ q).fst = (M₂ q).fst⊢ (fun q => (M₁ q).fst) = fun q => (M₂ q).fst Q:Type u_1A:Type u_2C:Type u_3S:Type u_4acc:(Q → A) → SM₁:Q → A × CM₂:Q → A × Ch:∀ (q : Q), (M₁ q).fst = (M₂ q).fstq:Q⊢ (M₁ q).fst = (M₂ q).fst All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. The accuracy functional sees only the first projection. ∎

This is why the corner is attractive to a team optimizing accuracy and dangerous to whatever consumes the confidence: the metric that would catch the drift is blind to it by construction.

Remark 7.9. The corners differ in where failure shows up. Abstention fails visibly in the coverage log as refusals. The band fails monitorably at a known surface as localized confident errors. Decoupling fails invisibly and downstream, as degraded decisions in systems that trusted the number. Prefer failures you can see.

Remark 7.9a (Decoupling cannot be detected by the producer alone). Whether weakening calibration is safe depends on the set of downstream consumers, which is not a property of the model. So the model's own team, looking only at the model, cannot determine whether it has entered the dangerous regime.

15.2.4. The corners side by side🔗

Remark 7.10a (There is no dominant corner). No corner dominates across all domains, which is why the trilemma is a menu. If one were always best the theorem would be a wall pointing at it. The right corner changes with the domain, and a shop that runs the same corner everywhere is running it in domains where it is wrong.

Proposition 7.10 (Blends satisfy the trilemma by partition). If the query space is partitioned into a region dropping coverage, one relaxing faithfulness, and one enforcing calibration, no single region carries all three conditions.

theorem c7_blend_no_region_has_all_three {Q : Type _} (A B C R₀ R₁ R₂ : Q → Prop) (hcover : ∀ q, R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ q) (h₀ : ∀ q, R₀ q → ¬ A q) (h₁ : ∀ q, R₁ q → ¬ B q) (h₂ : ∀ q, R₂ q → ¬ C q) : ∀ q, ¬ (A q ∧ B q ∧ C q) := Q:Type u_1A:Q → PropB:Q → PropC:Q → PropR₀:Q → PropR₁:Q → PropR₂:Q → Prophcover:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ qh₀:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q → ¬A qh₁:∀ (q : Q), R₁ q → ¬B qh₂:∀ (q : Q), R₂ q → ¬C q⊢ ∀ (q : Q), ¬(A q ∧ B q ∧ C q) intro q Q:Type u_1A:Q → PropB:Q → PropC:Q → PropR₀:Q → PropR₁:Q → PropR₂:Q → Prophcover:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ qh₀:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q → ¬A qh₁:∀ (q : Q), R₁ q → ¬B qh₂:∀ (q : Q), R₂ q → ¬C qq:Qh:A q ∧ B q ∧ C q⊢ False Q:Type u_1A:Q → PropB:Q → PropC:Q → PropR₀:Q → PropR₁:Q → PropR₂:Q → Prophcover:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ qh₀:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q → ¬A qh₁:∀ (q : Q), R₁ q → ¬B qh₂:∀ (q : Q), R₂ q → ¬C qq:Qh:A q ∧ B q ∧ C qhr:R₀ q⊢ FalseQ:Type u_1A:Q → PropB:Q → PropC:Q → PropR₀:Q → PropR₁:Q → PropR₂:Q → Prophcover:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ qh₀:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q → ¬A qh₁:∀ (q : Q), R₁ q → ¬B qh₂:∀ (q : Q), R₂ q → ¬C qq:Qh:A q ∧ B q ∧ C qhr:R₁ q⊢ FalseQ:Type u_1A:Q → PropB:Q → PropC:Q → PropR₀:Q → PropR₁:Q → PropR₂:Q → Prophcover:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ qh₀:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q → ¬A qh₁:∀ (q : Q), R₁ q → ¬B qh₂:∀ (q : Q), R₂ q → ¬C qq:Qh:A q ∧ B q ∧ C qhr:R₂ q⊢ False Q:Type u_1A:Q → PropB:Q → PropC:Q → PropR₀:Q → PropR₁:Q → PropR₂:Q → Prophcover:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ qh₀:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q → ¬A qh₁:∀ (q : Q), R₁ q → ¬B qh₂:∀ (q : Q), R₂ q → ¬C qq:Qh:A q ∧ B q ∧ C qhr:R₀ q⊢ False All goals completed! 🐙 Q:Type u_1A:Q → PropB:Q → PropC:Q → PropR₀:Q → PropR₁:Q → PropR₂:Q → Prophcover:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ qh₀:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q → ¬A qh₁:∀ (q : Q), R₁ q → ¬B qh₂:∀ (q : Q), R₂ q → ¬C qq:Qh:A q ∧ B q ∧ C qhr:R₁ q⊢ False All goals completed! 🐙 Q:Type u_1A:Q → PropB:Q → PropC:Q → PropR₀:Q → PropR₁:Q → PropR₂:Q → Prophcover:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q ∨ R₁ q ∨ R₂ qh₀:∀ (q : Q), R₀ q → ¬A qh₁:∀ (q : Q), R₁ q → ¬B qh₂:∀ (q : Q), R₂ q → ¬C qq:Qh:A q ∧ B q ∧ C qhr:R₂ q⊢ False All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Case analysis on which region the query lies in. ∎

Remark 7.10b (Region boundaries are themselves boundaries). Placing the reject region and the band introduces new decision surfaces, and those edges are decision boundaries with their own coupled points under the same theorem. This is not a regress that undoes the design: the edges are chosen by you, in the truth-field coordinate, so you can place them where behavior is benign rather than where the model's own boundary happens to fall.

15.3. The same menu for defense🔗

The three corners translate. The abstaining wrapper refuses a region of prompts, giving up completeness there. The priced residual surface accepts a bounded region of prompts the wrapper does not fully neutralize. The misreported safety score decouples the published score from actual safety, which is the defense analogue of decoupling and carries the same invisibility.

Remark 7.11 (Where the analogy strains). The strain is in the premise, not the menu.
