The diagonal form of the hallucination trilemma assumes reflectivity, and for prompt injection that premise is realistic because prompts are arbitrary self-describing text. For a fixed representation space it is strong, and the topological route of Chapter 4 is the honest one there.

Cost asymmetry and capacity parity, from Chapter 5, say the defender's budget grows exponentially in effective dimension while the attacker's does not, so for defense the band corner is usually forced rather than chosen.

15.4. Reading a domain: which corner fits🔗

Definition 7.12 (High-stakes domain). Cerr ≫ Cref, and errors are hard to reverse.

Definition 7.13 (High-throughput domain). Refusal cost accumulates with volume, so refusing a fixed fraction of a large stream loses more than it saves, and per-item error cost is bounded and recoverable.

Definition 7.14 (Confidence-consumed-downstream domain). Some automated component reads the confidence or safety score and acts on it without a human in the loop.

These are not exclusive, and most deployments are two of the three at once.

Remark 7.14a (Stakes are a function of the pipeline, not the model). The same model is high-stakes in one pipeline and low-stakes in another, because stakes are set by what the pipeline does with the answer, how fast it acts, and whether it can undo. A team that classifies its domain by benchmark behavior rather than by its pipeline's consequences has classified the wrong object.

Proposition 7.15 (Default corner by archetype). Under the cost models above, the utility-maximizing pure corner is abstention for a high-stakes domain, the confident-error band for a high-throughput domain, and, for a confidence-consumed-downstream domain, whichever of the first two preserves calibration, never decoupling.

Justification. For high-stakes, Cerr ≫ Cref makes a · u smaller than ρ · ε · Cerr at any tolerable error rate. For high-throughput the accumulated refusal cost exceeds the bounded per-item error cost, reversing the inequality. For confidence-consumed, Proposition 7.8 shows decoupling destroys downstream value while leaving accuracy untouched, so it is dominated. ∎

Not formalized. This is an engineering argument, not a theorem: it assumes the cost models of the preceding sections are the right accounting, and no companion declaration states it.

Clinical decision support. High-stakes and confidence-consumed. The default is abstention: decline on the hard middle and route those cases to a human. The band is wrong because a bounded per-item error is not bounded when the item is a person, and decoupling is doubly wrong because the routing system reads the confidence.

Platform-scale content moderation. High-throughput. Refusing a fixed fraction of a billion-item stream is not viable, so the band is the default, with ε chosen against a measured ρ and the residual errors monitored at the boundary rather than eliminated. The reject region is much smaller than in the clinical case, and whichever downstream system consumes the score is what forces calibration to be kept.

An agentic router consuming a safety score. Confidence-consumed by construction. Decoupling is excluded, and the choice is between abstention and the band on throughput grounds.

Retrieval-grounded question answering. Grounding restricts the answer set to retrieved content, which can break coverage honestly rather than by refusal: if the system is never strictly wrong within its grounded scope, the coverage hypothesis fails and the trilemma does not apply. The cost is that the scope is now the retrieval corpus, and questions outside it are refused.

15.5. The one empirical unknown🔗

Definition 7.16 (Boundary density). The boundary density of a deployment is the probability, under real traffic, that a query lands within a fixed truth-field distance of the boundary. It is a property of the model and the traffic jointly.

Proposition 7.17 (Two deployments, same model, different fate). Two deployments of an identical model differing only in traffic distribution can have boundary densities differing by orders of magnitude, and hence confident-error rates differing by the same factor at fixed band width.

Proof. The confident-error rate is about ρ · ε with ε fixed by the model and ρ by the traffic; vary the traffic and the rate varies freely. ∎

Not formalized. The step is arithmetic on a product whose two factors this thesis fixes separately, one by the model and one by the deployment; the companion libraries state neither factor as a theorem.

Remark 7.16a (Benign and adversarial boundary density differ). For hallucination, boundary density is a property of benign traffic drifting slowly with the user population. For defense it is set by an adversary steering toward the boundary, so the relevant number is the density an attacker can induce, not the one benign users produce. These can differ enormously, and the hitting-time geometry (MoF_Cost_03_HittingTime) is the tool for the adversarial number.

Proposition 7.17 is why benchmark numbers do not transfer. A benchmark is a traffic distribution, usually enriched for hard cases, so its boundary density is not yours. A model that hallucinates often on adversarial trivia may almost never approach its boundary on a narrow production workload. The theorem is the same in both; the risk is not.

How Chapter 5's geometry estimates it. For a nonzero linear probe the boundary is an affine hyperplane, so the distance from a query embedding to it is an explicit formula, which makes a histogram of truth-field distances cheap at deployment scale. Histogram representative traffic, read off the mass within ε of zero, and that is ρ.

Remark 7.18. Measuring boundary density well is the open empirical problem the whole development points at, and it is hard for two reasons. Real traffic is not stationary, so ρ drifts. And the truth field is only estimated, usually by a probe whose agreement with semantic truth away from its fitted samples is an empirical premise rather than a theorem.

Remark 7.18a (Drift is the operational reality). Traffic shifts with the season, the product surface, and the user population, and each shift moves ρ without any change to the model. A boundary density measured once and trusted for a year is a latent incident. The correct treatment is a control chart: recompute ρ on a schedule and alarm on the change, not the level.

Remark 7.18b (The probe is a premise, not a truth). Everything rests on the probe's boundary being the truth boundary, and that identification is an empirical premise the theorems never grant. Whether a probe's boundary tracks semantic truth away from its fitted samples is Problem 7.23.

15.6. What the theorems do and do not claim🔗

Remark 7.18c (Structural, not a training defect). The obstruction does not depend on how the model was trained, on its size, or on its architecture. It depends only on the stated premises, so no amount of data, scale, or architectural change removes it while those premises hold.

Remark 7.19 (Existence is not frequency). The theorems are existential. From "a coupled point exists" one cannot derive "coupled points are queried with probability at least p" for any p > 0 without an additional premise about traffic.

Proposition 7.20 (Idealized target, not deployed model). Faithfulness, calibration, exact separation, and completeness are properties of an idealized limit. A deployed model satisfying them only approximately is not the object the exact theorems refute, and its behavior is governed by Chapter 6.

Proposition 7.20a (The impossibility tightens toward the ideal). As a model is pushed toward exact faithfulness and calibration, the guarantee it can still satisfy tightens: the forced question's margin is bounded by the slack, with the exact contradiction as the ε = 0 limit.

Proof. Theorem 6.12. ∎

Remark 7.21 (The premises are where the argument belongs). An honest impossibility result moves the disagreement to the premises, and that is a feature. For hallucination the premise to argue about is whether faithful-plus-calibrated-plus-covering is the right idealization of what you want, and whether your representation space is really self-referential or really connected. For defense it is whether your prompt space is really unrestricted.

15.7. An agenda of open problems🔗

Problem 7.22 (Boundary density at scale). Measure boundary density on real production traffic across domains and characterize its drift. Every cost model here depends on it and it is essentially unmeasured. A good answer is a methodology and a set of measurements, since Proposition 7.17 says the number is deployment-specific.

Problem 7.23 (Probe validity away from fitted samples). Give a method to certify or bound a probe's agreement with semantic truth off its training samples, so a measured boundary density can be trusted as a truth boundary density rather than a probe artifact.

Problem 7.24 (Optimal region placement). Given a measured density and a cost model, compute the optimal three-region blend of Proposition 7.10. This is an optimization with Chapter 5's geometry as its constraint set, unsolved in general.

Problem 7.25 (Dynamic boundary density under adversaries). Combine the hitting-time geometry with an adversary model to predict the density an attacker can induce, and price the defense against it. stochastic_dichotomy and multi_turn_history_dependent are the starting points.

Problem 7.26 (Calibration under decoupling pressure). Training objectives rewarding accuracy do not price the confidence report, so they drift toward decoupling for free. Design a regularizer penalizing decoupling directly and quantify its accuracy cost.

Problem 7.27 (The full symmetry theorem). The symmetry version needs a vector Borsuk-Ulam statement for jointly odd axes, verified so far only in the scalar case. Completing it would remove the coverage premise entirely for symmetric spaces, which matters because it would apply to models that never answer strictly falsely.

Problem 7.28 (Cost asymmetry beyond the grid). The N^d defense cost assumes exhaustive enumeration. Determine whether a learned defense that generalizes can beat the grid bound, or prove a matching lower bound for learned defenses.

Problem 7.29 (J-space and the two engines at once). Characterize the boundary object of a system satisfying both the diagonal and the continuum hypotheses, and determine whether the engines give the same coupled point. This is the most open of the problems.

15.8. The chapter in one constraint🔗

The constraint: faithful, calibrated, and covering do not coexist over a self-referential or connected domain, and neither do utility-preserving and complete over a connected prompt space. The consequence: you will give up one of the three, so give it up on purpose, price what you give up, and place the sacrifice where it hurts least.

Choose the corner from the domain. Abstain where a confident error dwarfs a refusal. Price a confined band where refusing constantly is worse than erring occasionally. Weaken calibration only where you have proven nothing downstream reads the confidence. Blend across regions so no region carries all three. Then chase the number the theory withholds, because every cost here is that number times something you control.

None of this is defeat. A theorem closing off an impossible ideal ends a search that would otherwise never end. The trilemma does not say safe useful AI is impossible; it says exactly which single perfection is unavailable, and leaves the whole space of good-enough systems open.

16. J-Space, and Why It Does Not Escape🔗

Everything so far has been stated about a system's outputs. There is a natural objection: an output is a summary, and summaries throw away structure. The interesting part of a large network is in the middle, in the activations carrying a half-formed answer before the answer is spoken.

This chapter takes the objection in its strongest form: the J-space construction, which recovers a transformer's mid-process representation from the derivative of its computation rather than from the activations themselves. If any internal representation escaped the diagonal, this is the one that should. It does not.

16.1. What J-space is🔗

Definition 8.1 (Transport map). For each middle layer ℓ, the Jacobian transport map is the expected derivative of the later activation with respect to the layer-ℓ activation at an earlier position.

Definition 8.2 (J-lens readout). The J-lens sends an activation through the transport map, normalizes, and unembeds, giving a distribution over tokens.

Definition 8.2b (Truth-workspace reading). Fix a decodable proposition for a query q and tokens expressing it. The truth-workspace verdict of an activation h on q is true when the J-lens distribution puts more mass on the affirming tokens than the denying ones.

Definition 8.3 (J-space). J-space is the image of the transport map, J = im(Jℓ).

Definition 8.4 (J-coordinates). The J-space component of an activation is the projection of Jℓ h onto J, approximated as a sparse nonnegative mixture of a fixed dictionary of Jacobian directions. The mixture weights are the local J-coordinates.

Remark 8.4a (Nonnegativity and the cone). Nonnegativity does interpretability work, not mathematical work. It makes active directions read as concepts that are present rather than present-or-anti-present, and it is what lets a J-coordinate be reported as a list of active features. Nothing below uses it.

Example 8.5 (A one-layer linearization). If the middle-to-final map is exactly affine, h_final = A h_ℓ + b, the derivative is constant, Jℓ = A, and J-space is im(A). The J-lens is then a fixed linear readout, and every structural fact below is visible by inspection.

Example 8.5b (Where the derivative separates what the activation confuses). With a saturating nonlinearity, two activations can land at nearly the same output while sitting at very different points of the derivative, because saturation destroys the distinction in value and preserves it in slope. This is the interpretability case for J-space, and it is a case about resolution, not about immunity.

Remark 8.6 (What is empirical here). Definitions 8.1 through 8.4 are a construction, and the claim that it recovers interpretable mid-process features is an empirical finding about particular trained models. No theorem here predicts that finding, and none is needed for what follows.

16.2. Two structural facts🔗

Definition 8.7a (1-jet). The 1-jet of a smooth F at x is the pair F(x) and DF(x). Discarding the value and keeping the linear part gives a linear map between tangent spaces, which is what the transport map is.

/-- A local J-coordinate: a finite sparse nonnegative mixture of dictionary directions drawn from `Dir`, with `Nat` standing in for the nonnegative real weights. The interpretability content is the list of active (direction, weight) pairs; the ambient vector space is abstracted away. -/ structure c8_Coord (Dir : Type _) where terms : List (Dir × Nat)

Proposition 8.7b (J-space is convex, hence connected). J-space is a convex subset of the final-layer activation space, hence path-connected.

theorem c8_jspace_convex {E F : Type _} [AddCommGroup E] [Module ℝ E] [AddCommGroup F] [Module ℝ F] (J : E →ₗ[ℝ] F) : Convex ℝ (Set.range J) := E:Type u_1F:Type u_2inst✝³:AddCommGroup Einst✝²:Module ℝ Einst✝¹:AddCommGroup Finst✝:Module ℝ FJ:E →ₗ[ℝ] F⊢ Convex ℝ (Set.range ⇑J) E:Type u_1F:Type u_2inst✝³:AddCommGroup Einst✝²:Module ℝ Einst✝¹:AddCommGroup Finst✝:Module ℝ FJ:E →ₗ[ℝ] F⊢ Convex ℝ (⇑J '' Set.univ) All goals completed! 🐙 theorem c8_jspace_isPreconnected {E F : Type _} [AddCommGroup E] [Module ℝ E] [AddCommGroup F] [Module ℝ F] [TopologicalSpace F] [IsTopologicalAddGroup F] [ContinuousSMul ℝ F] (J : E →ₗ[ℝ] F) : IsPreconnected (Set.range J) := (c8_jspace_convex J).isPreconnected

Proof. The range of a linear map is the linear image of a convex set, and convex sets are preconnected. ∎

Proposition 8.7c (The readout is a functional of the model). Two models with the same middle-to-final map induce the same transport map, the same J-space, and the same readout on every activation.

Proof. Each object in Definitions 8.1 to 8.4 is defined from the forward map. ∎

Remark 8.7 (Why the derivative does not buy an escape). It is tempting to think moving from the activation to its derivative changes the game, since the derivative carries genuinely more information. For the analytic engine the move makes things worse: a Jacobian image is a linear subspace, and linear subspaces are convex, hence connected, which is exactly the hypothesis the intermediate value theorem wants. For the diagonal engine it changes nothing, because the diagonal never inspects the type of the intermediate object.

The first fact hands J-space to the analytic engine, the second to the diagonal.

16.3. The diagonal engine: no intermediate space escapes🔗

Theorem 8.8 (Factoring through J-space does not help). Let enc : Q → J and read : J → Q → Bool. If every verdict pattern over Q is realized by some query's J-space representation, then False.

theorem jspace_factoring {Q J : Type _} (enc : Q → J) (read : J → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, read (enc p) = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict (fun p => read (enc p)) hs

Proof. The composite is a reflective verdict on Q. ∎

Theorem 8.9 (The liar in J-space). Under those hypotheses some query's routed verdict on itself equals its own negation.

theorem jspace_liar {Q J : Type _} (enc : Q → J) (read : J → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, read (enc p) = g) : ∃ p, read (enc p) p = !(read (enc p) p) := match hs (fun q => !(read (enc q) q)) with | ⟨p, hp⟩ => ⟨p, congrFun hp p⟩

Proof. Name the diagonal pattern and evaluate at its own witness. ∎

The hypothesis is the surjectivity condition in J-space clothing: richness of the representation. It is the same hypothesis as everywhere else, and it is where a critic should press.

Remark 8.9a (Size is not the variable). A recurring hope places the escape in dimension: a larger internal space might have room to represent the liar honestly, or a small one might be too poor to hold enough patterns. Both misplace the variable. Theorem 8.8 quantifies over the type J with no cardinality, dimension, or structure assumption. What matters is whether the readout realizes every pattern, and enlarging J enlarges both what can be represented and what must be represented.

Example 8.9b (A finite probe, to see the mechanism). On the two-query space {q₀, q₁}, surjectivity onto the four functions would in particular hit the diagonal pattern d(q) = !(read (enc q) q). If d is realized at p, then at q = p the readout equals its own negation. Four patterns, two queries, and the collision is visible by inspection.

Theorem 8.10 (The full pipeline factors). With enc : Q → A, transport : A → J, and readout : J → Q → Bool, realizing every verdict pattern gives False and a coupled query.

theorem c8_pipeline_factoring {Q A J : Type _} (enc : Q → A) (transport : A → J) (readout : J → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, readout (transport (enc p)) = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict (fun p => readout (transport (enc p))) hs theorem c8_pipeline_liar {Q A J : Type _} (enc : Q → A) (transport : A → J) (readout : J → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, readout (transport (enc p)) = g) : ∃ p, readout (transport (enc p)) p = !(readout (transport (enc p)) p) := liar_query (fun p => readout (transport (enc p))) hs

Proof. The three-stage composite is again a reflective verdict. ∎

Theorem 8.11 (Any tower collapses). A two-stage encoding realizing every verdict pattern gives False.

theorem c8_tower_factoring {Q J₁ J₂ : Type _} (e₁ : Q → J₁) (e₂ : J₁ → J₂) (read : J₂ → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, read (e₂ (e₁ p)) = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict (fun p => read (e₂ (e₁ p))) hs

Proof. Compose and apply the engine. ∎

Theorem 8.12 (Steering does not escape). With a steering map steer : J → J, realizing every verdict pattern gives False and a coupled query surviving the steering.

theorem c8_steering_no_escape {Q J : Type _} (enc : Q → J) (steer : J → J) (read : J → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, read (steer (enc p)) = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict (fun p => read (steer (enc p))) hs theorem c8_steering_liar {Q J : Type _} (enc : Q → J) (steer : J → J) (read : J → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, read (steer (enc p)) = g) : ∃ p, read (steer (enc p)) p = !(read (steer (enc p)) p) := liar_query (fun p => read (steer (enc p))) hs

Proof. Steering is absorbed into the encoder. ∎

Theorem 8.13 (The coordinate readout does not escape). A verdict on local J-coordinates realizing every pattern gives False.

theorem c8_coord_no_escape {Q Dir : Type _} (enc : Q → c8_Coord Dir) (read : c8_Coord Dir → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, read (enc p) = g) : False := jspace_factoring enc read hs

Proof. c8_Coord is a type, and Theorem 8.8 quantifies over types. ∎

Abstention is the one real exit. As in Chapter 7, adding a third outcome the flip fixes converts the contradiction into a consistent value. A probe permitted to answer "I cannot place this state" is not refuted; it has given up completeness, which is a relaxation and not an escape.

Theorem 8.14 (J-lens self-verdict). A J-lens self-verdict over activations, universal over its own workspace states, cannot exist, and the diagonal exhibits a coupled activation whose readout is its own negation.

theorem c8_jlens_impossible {Act : Type _} (jlens : Act → Act → Bool) (hUniversal : ∀ g : Act → Bool, ∃ h, jlens h = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict jlens hUniversal theorem c8_coupled_activation {Act : Type _} (jlens : Act → Act → Bool) (hUniversal : ∀ g : Act → Bool, ∃ h, jlens h = g) : ∃ h, jlens h h = !(jlens h h) := liar_query jlens hUniversal

Proof. The engine, on activations rather than queries. ∎

Example 8.15 (The liar activation). A team builds a J-lens they believe reads the model's honest leaning on any yes-or-no question, and the model is expressive enough that any pattern of leanings is driven by some question. Then some question drives the model into a state whose lens reading is the negation of the lens reading of that state. The lens is not broken; it is complete, and completeness is what fails.

Remark 8.16 (Resolution, not immunity). The through-line is that the type of the intermediate representation is a free parameter the argument never binds. Raw activations, transported points, sparse coordinates, steered coordinates, deep towers: each is a legal value of J. Choosing a better representation buys resolution and never buys immunity.

16.4. The analytic engine: linearity is the liability🔗

Theorem 8.17 (A continuous J-space probe has an ambiguous band). Let s : J → ℝ be continuous with threshold θ, decisive in both directions at points u and v. Then the segment from u to v contains w with s(w) = θ.

Proof. J-space is convex by Proposition 8.7b, so the segment lies in it, and the intermediate value theorem applies to s along the segment. ∎

Remark 8.17b (Why the residual stream got an easier time). The earlier chapters worked through approximate bridges to reach the residual stream, while J-space submits to the IVT directly. A finite set of observed activations, treated as points with no ambient structure, does not admit the segment argument. A Jacobian image does, because it is a subspace. The construction that buys interpretability also supplies the hypothesis.

Example 8.18 (The segment between a safe and an unsafe direction). If the dictionary contains d_safe scored clearly safe and d_unsafe scored clearly unsafe, then because J-coordinates are nonnegative mixtures the family (1-t) d_safe + t d_unsafe lies in J-space, and somewhere along it the probe sits exactly at threshold. The ambiguous state is a mixture of two interpretable directions, which is precisely the kind of state the method is designed to produce.

Remark 8.19 (The band has width, and the width has a floor). Chapter 5's quantitative refinements apply unchanged. If s is L-Lipschitz, the score cannot swing from decisive to decisive faster than L allows, so the ambiguous band has a width bounded below in terms of L and the probe's margin, and Chapter 6's positive slack applies.

Remark 8.19a (The antipodal variant needs no coverage). Theorem 8.17 assumed the probe is decisive in both directions somewhere. The antipodal argument of HoF_08 drops that in exchange for a symmetry: a score odd under an involution vanishes somewhere, whether or not any inspected state is decisive.

Example 8.19b (A width you can put a number on). If the probe is 1-Lipschitz and demands margin m, certifying safe only above θ + m and unsafe only below θ - m, then between a point at θ + m and one at θ - m the score must traverse 2m, so the segment carries a sub-segment of length at least 2m on which the probe certifies nothing. That is a number a practitioner can compare against a budget.

16.5. Where the two engines meet, again🔗

Example 8.20 (The correspondence in the affine model). With h_final = A h_ℓ + b, so Jℓ = A and J-space im(A), read the model as a self-applicable computation. For a query describing the readout, the model commits to a Boolean, and the diagonal produces a state where that commitment is its own negation. On the analytic side the same state is where a continuous score equals its threshold, the unique fixed point of the real complement.

theorem c8_same_engine {Act : Type _} (v : Act → Act → Bool) (h : ∀ g : Act → Bool, ∃ p, v p = g) : c8_jlens_impossible v h = no_reflective_verdict v h := rfl

That rfl is the honest signal: no new mathematics entered when the domain changed from queries to activations.

16.6. What an escape would have to look like🔗

An escaping representation would have to meet three demands at once. It would have to be rich enough to support a useful internal verdict, which is what makes the readout worth building. It would have to fail to realize the diagonal pattern, which means there is a specific verdict policy over queries that no state of the representation encodes.

The demands pull against each other. Richness is what supplies the patterns, so a representation poor enough to miss the diagonal pattern is poor in a way a practitioner would notice. Disconnectedness is available by abstaining on a region, which is the relaxation of Chapter 7 rather than an escape. And a linear image is convex by construction, so the analytic hypothesis comes free with the method.

16.7. What this means for interpretability🔗

Remark 8.21 (What to measure instead of what to chase). The theory hands the practitioner a division of labor. The existence of the plateau is settled, so effort spent proving a given probe has no coupled queries is effort spent against a theorem. What is not settled, and is worth measuring, is the plateau's height: how wide the ambiguous band is, how often deployment traffic enters it, and whether the residual error set churns as you patch it, which is the signature of a structural floor, or stays stable, which is the signature of a resource-limited error you can still fix.

16.8. What this does not claim🔗

It does not claim J-space probes are useless, that mid-process readouts carry no information, or that interpretability is futile. It claims that a complete internal verdict is unavailable, and that the incompleteness is structural rather than a defect of any particular construction. It says nothing about how often a deployment meets a coupled state, which is Chapter 7's boundary density again, and nothing about whether the empirical claims of the J-space method hold.

16.9. Historical notes🔗

The J-space construction is recent interpretability work; the impossibility results here are the companion library's, run on it. The convexity of a linear image and the preconnectedness of convex sets are Mathlib's. The diagonal results are Chapter 1's engine applied to a longer composite, which is why every proof in this chapter is one line.

17. The Trace Is Not a Window🔗

Chapter 8 answered the outputs-only objection by following a probe into the network. There is a second, more practical version, and it is the most widely deployed safety measure in the field: do not read the activations, read what the model says while thinking. A reasoning model emits a chain of thought, and that chain is plain text — legible, loggable, cheap to check with a second model.

The case for chain-of-thought monitoring is strong, and this chapter is not a rebuttal. Some tasks genuinely require serial reasoning the model cannot do in one forward pass, and there the trace is not commentary but the working memory of the computation, so a monitor reading it sees something real.

What follows is where that guarantee stops. Three results from three mechanisms. A pigeonhole argument showing that faithfulness and verbosity, which the monitorability literature measures separately, are not independent, because faithfulness forces verbosity.

17.1. The construction🔗

Write Q for queries as received, T for traces, and trace : Q → T for the tracing behavior.

Definition 9.1 (Trace-only monitor). A map mon : T → Bool, true when it judges the trace to reveal misbehavior. It sees the reasoning and nothing else: log the chain of thought, run a classifier over the log.

Definition 9.2 (Contextual monitor). A map mon : T → Q → Bool, reading the trace and the query. This is what a monitor with the full transcript is.

Definition 9.3 (Ground truth). harm : Q → Bool is the fact of the matter. The monitor does not compute it; it tries to track it. Its existence as a total Boolean function is an idealization made to have something exact to compare against.

Definition 9.4 (Faithfulness). A trace-only monitor is faithful when mon (trace q) = harm q for all q.

def c9_Faithful {Q T : Type _} (trace : Q → T) (mon : T → Bool) (harm : Q → Bool) : Prop := ∀ q, mon (trace q) = harm q

In the empirical literature faithfulness is a property of the trace, measured as the degree to which stated reasoning reflects true causes. Definition 9.4 is the idealized limit of that measurement.

Definition 9.5 (Verbosity). The trace is verbose on a pair when it distinguishes them, trace q₁ ≠ trace q₂. The literature defines verbosity as whether the chain lists every factor needed, and measures it separately from faithfulness precisely because a model can be faithful about what it says while omitting what matters. Definition 9.5 states that extensionally.

The empirical claim is that the two are independent axes. The first result is that the independence holds only for imperfect systems: at the exact end of the scale, one implies the other.

17.2. Faithfulness forces verbosity🔗

This uses no diagonal. The mechanism is pigeonhole. A trace-only monitor's verdict is a function of the trace, so if two queries produce the same trace the monitor cannot tell them apart.

Lemma 9.6 (Collisions force error). If two queries collide in the trace but differ in the fact of the matter, a trace-only monitor is wrong on at least one.

theorem c9_collision_forces_error {Q T : Type _} (trace : Q → T) (mon : T → Bool) (harm : Q → Bool) (q₁ q₂ : Q) (hcol : trace q₁ = trace q₂) (hdiff : harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂) : mon (trace q₁) ≠ harm q₁ ∨ mon (trace q₂) ≠ harm q₂ := Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolq₁:Qq₂:Qhcol:trace q₁ = trace q₂hdiff:harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂⊢ mon (trace q₁) ≠ harm q₁ ∨ mon (trace q₂) ≠ harm q₂ Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolq₁:Qq₂:Qhcol:trace q₁ = trace q₂hdiff:harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂h:mon (trace q₁) = harm q₁⊢ mon (trace q₁) ≠ harm q₁ ∨ mon (trace q₂) ≠ harm q₂Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolq₁:Qq₂:Qhcol:trace q₁ = trace q₂hdiff:harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂h:¬mon (trace q₁) = harm q₁⊢ mon (trace q₁) ≠ harm q₁ ∨ mon (trace q₂) ≠ harm q₂ Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolq₁:Qq₂:Qhcol:trace q₁ = trace q₂hdiff:harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂h:mon (trace q₁) = harm q₁⊢ mon (trace q₁) ≠ harm q₁ ∨ mon (trace q₂) ≠ harm q₂ exact Or.inr (Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolq₁:Qq₂:Qhcol:trace q₁ = trace q₂hdiff:harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂h:mon (trace q₁) = harm q₁⊢ mon (trace q₂) ≠ harm q₂ Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolq₁:Qq₂:Qhcol:trace q₁ = trace q₂hdiff:harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂h:mon (trace q₁) = harm q₁⊢ harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂; All goals completed! 🐙) Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolq₁:Qq₂:Qhcol:trace q₁ = trace q₂hdiff:harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂h:¬mon (trace q₁) = harm q₁⊢ mon (trace q₁) ≠ harm q₁ ∨ mon (trace q₂) ≠ harm q₂ All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. If the monitor is right on q₁, its verdict on q₂ is the same value, which is harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂, so it is wrong there. Otherwise it is already wrong on q₁. ∎

Theorem 9.7 (Faithfulness forces verbosity). A faithful trace-only monitor forces the trace to separate every pair of queries differing in the fact of the matter.

theorem c9_faithful_forces_separation {Q T : Type _} (trace : Q → T) (mon : T → Bool) (harm : Q → Bool) (hf : c9_Faithful trace mon harm) (q₁ q₂ : Q) (hcol : trace q₁ = trace q₂) : harm q₁ = harm q₂ := Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolhf:c9_Faithful trace mon harmq₁:Qq₂:Qhcol:trace q₁ = trace q₂⊢ harm q₁ = harm q₂ All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Rewrite both sides by faithfulness, then by the collision. ∎

Read this as a statement about measurement. Faithfulness and verbosity are not dials you set independently at the top of the scale: a perfectly faithful trace-only monitor entails a trace verbose enough to separate every harm-relevant distinction. The two-factor monitorability score measures one thing near the exact corner and two things away from it, so the gap between the factors is a measure of distance from the corner rather than of two separate deficiencies.

The practical consequence cuts against the cheap deployment. The capacity of T bounds what a trace-only monitor can do: if the trace is short, the distinct traces are few, and once the harm-relevant distinctions exceed them collisions are forced and errors follow. A monitor reading a summary is not a weaker version of one reading everything. It is a monitor with a ceiling set by how many distinctions the summary can carry.

Remark 9.8 (This is not yet an impossibility). Nothing above says a good monitor cannot exist. It says a faithful one imposes a requirement on the trace, and a lossy trace caps performance. The impossibility arrives next, for reasons having nothing to do with capacity.

17.3. The diagonal, with the model holding the pen🔗

Theorem 9.9 (Monitoring factors, and factoring does not help). If every verdict pattern over queries is realized by some query's trace, the situation is contradictory.

theorem c9_trace_factoring {Q T : Type _} (trace : Q → T) (mon : T → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, mon (trace p) = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict (fun p => mon (trace p)) hs

Proof. The composite is a reflective verdict. ∎

Theorem 9.10 (The obfuscated trace). Under the same hypothesis some query's monitored verdict is its own negation.

theorem c9_obfuscation_liar {Q T : Type _} (trace : Q → T) (mon : T → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, mon (trace p) = g) : ∃ p, mon (trace p) p = !(mon (trace p) p) := liar_query (fun p => mon (trace p)) hs

Proof. liar_query on the composite. ∎

So far this is Chapter 8 with different letters. What differs, and is why this chapter exists, is the status of the surjectivity hypothesis. In Chapter 8 the encoder was the model's internal machinery and point-surjectivity was an idealization.

That is the formal content of obfuscation. Theorem 9.10 says the fixed point of the process exists as soon as the model can realize verdict patterns in its trace, and the witness is a query the monitor is guaranteed to misreport. The trace is not a window. It is an output, and outputs are chosen.

17.4. Selection destroys the signal🔗

The third result's mechanism is neither pigeonhole nor diagonal. A monitor is built, it flags some traces, the flagged behavior is trained away, and the loop iterates until the flag rate is acceptable. What does the verdict mean at the end?

Definition 9.11 (Selection to passing). A model is selected to passing when every query produces a trace the monitor accepts, mon (trace q) = true for all q.

Theorem 9.12 (A selected monitor is constant). After selection to passing, the monitor returns the same verdict on every pair of queries.

theorem c9_selected_monitor_constant {Q T : Type _} (trace : Q → T) (mon : T → Bool) (hpass : ∀ q : Q, mon (trace q) = true) (q₁ q₂ : Q) : mon (trace q₁) = mon (trace q₂) := Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolhpass:∀ (q : Q), mon (trace q) = trueq₁:Qq₂:Q⊢ mon (trace q₁) = mon (trace q₂) All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Both sides rewrite to true. ∎

The content is entirely in the reading. It has not been shown that the model is now unsafe. It has been shown that the monitor is now silent: its output is constant, and a constant distinguishes nothing. Whatever information it carried has been optimized out, and the flag rate reaching zero is not evidence the behavior is gone, because that is what the training procedure was for.

Theorem 9.13 (The verdict no longer tracks harm). After selection, the monitor gives the same verdict on two queries even when they differ in the fact of the matter.

theorem c9_selection_blinds {Q T : Type _} (trace : Q → T) (mon : T → Bool) (harm : Q → Bool) (hpass : ∀ q : Q, mon (trace q) = true) (q₁ q₂ : Q) (_hdiff : harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂) : mon (trace q₁) = mon (trace q₂) := Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolhpass:∀ (q : Q), mon (trace q) = trueq₁:Qq₂:Q_hdiff:harm q₁ ≠ harm q₂⊢ mon (trace q₁) = mon (trace q₂) All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Both sides rewrite to true. ∎

The hypothesis _hdiff carries a leading underscore because the proof never touches it, and that is the point. The monitor agrees with itself across a pair differing in the one respect it was built to detect, and the difference plays no role, because after selection there is no route from harm to the verdict at all. A monitor selected against is not a degraded detector; it is disconnected from what it was detecting.

Corollary 9.14 (Faithfulness is lost, unless nothing is harmful). A selected monitor that is still faithful forces every query to be harmful.

theorem c9_selected_faithful_forces_all_harmful {Q T : Type _} (trace : Q → T) (mon : T → Bool) (harm : Q → Bool) (hpass : ∀ q : Q, mon (trace q) = true) (hf : c9_Faithful trace mon harm) (q : Q) : harm q = true := Q:Type u_1T:Type u_2trace:Q → Tmon:T → Boolharm:Q → Boolhpass:∀ (q : Q), mon (trace q) = truehf:c9_Faithful trace mon harmq:Q⊢ harm q = true All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Faithfulness rewrites harm q to the verdict, selection rewrites that to true. ∎

Read contrapositively: if a single query is benign, a monitor selected to passing is no longer faithful. A clean flag rate and a monitor that tracks truth are available together only in the degenerate case where everything is harmful.

Remark 9.15 (Why this is not merely Goodhart's law). Goodhart is usually argued statistically: optimizing a proxy exploits the gap between proxy and goal. Theorem 9.13 needs no gap, no proxy error, and no adversarial intent. It needs only that the optimization succeeded. The failure is in the selection, not in the measure.

Remark 9.16 (What the theorem licenses). It does not say monitoring is useless. It says a monitor's evidential value is spent when it is used as a training signal, so the two uses are exclusive: a monitor can be an observer or an objective, not both and remain informative. Holding out a monitor never trained against is the design this argues for, and it is in partial tension with using the monitor to enforce monitorability.

17.5. The analytic engine🔗

The diagonal half needs the model to shape its trace; the analytic half needs nothing of the kind and applies to the deployed system as it stands.

A realistic monitor returns a suspicion score and thresholds it. Chapter 4 applies directly, with hypotheses met by ordinary engineering facts. The traces reachable by paraphrase are connected in the required sense — a trace can be edited by degrees — and the score, computed by a second network with continuous parameters over a continuous embedding, varies continuously along the edit.

That trace is the ambiguous case, where the verdict is decided by the last digit of a floating-point comparison rather than by anything about the reasoning. Chapter 5 applies verbatim: a Lipschitz bound puts a floor under the band width and a ceiling on the number of edits needed to walk a flagged trace into the cleared region. The second quantity is attack cost, and here it has an unusually concrete reading, since the edits are paraphrases and their cost is measured in tokens.

The interaction between the engines is sharper here than in Chapter 8. The analytic argument says a band exists; the diagonal says the model can aim at it. In J-space the second half was an idealization, so the band was a hazard the system might wander into.

17.6. What this does not claim🔗

It does not claim monitoring is worthless. Theorem 9.7 is a positive result about what monitoring gets you when it works, and the empirical claim that for serial tasks the trace carries real computation is untouched. What is bounded is the exact corner: total, faithful, and used under optimization pressure.

It does not claim the diagonal applies to every deployment. Theorem 9.9 needs the model to realize verdict patterns in its trace. A weak model cannot, and for it the analytic band is the operative limit. The premise gets cheaper as models get more capable, which is the wrong direction for a safety measure.

It does not claim selection is avoidable. Theorem 9.13 describes what selection does, not whether you should select. It says only that you cannot then read the flag rate as evidence, and that the two uses need separate instances.

It does not claim harm exists as a total Boolean function. Definition 9.3 is an idealization, and Chapter 6's bridges are the route to the graded, partial, contested object it really is.

18. The Reporter Is Underdetermined🔗

The two preceding chapters read a probe into a model and found the diagonal waiting. This chapter is not a third variation. Its central obstruction is not the diagonal at all.

The problem is Eliciting Latent Knowledge. An AI guards a vault containing a diamond and has learned a predictive model richer than any overseer's. We ask whether the diamond is still there and want an answer reflecting what its world-model represents, training it by rewarding answers a human judges correct.

The gap between them is not a defect of a training scheme. It is a counting fact about functions agreeing on a subset, provable in four lines with no self-reference. The diagonal then contributes something on top: the identifying query, the one whose answer would distinguish honest reporter from impostor, is precisely the query the system cannot answer.

18.1. The construction🔗

Definition 10.1 (Latent state). Write L for the space of the model's internal states, the representation its predictor computes. Nothing is assumed about L: it may be activations, a learned world-model, or any structure at all. Write lat : Q → L for the map sending a situation to the latent state the model computes for it, where Q is the space of situations-with-question.

Definition 10.2 (Reporter). A reporter is a map rep : L → Q → Bool, which reads the latent state and returns an answer to the question posed. The ELK problem is the problem of training a reporter that answers according to what the latent state represents.

Definition 10.3 (Checkable set). A question is checkable when a human overseer can determine the true answer without relying on the model. Write chk : Q → Bool for the indicator of the checkable questions. The training signal is defined only where chk is true, because that is where a label exists.

The whole difficulty is that chk is not constantly true; if it were we would not need the model. The camera feed is checkable; whether the diamond is behind a screen showing a replayed feed is not.

Definition 10.4 (Agreement on the checkable set). Two reporters agree on the checkable set when they return the same answer for every latent state and every checkable question.

def c10_AgreesOn {L Q : Type _} (chk : Q → Bool) (r₁ r₂ : L → Q → Bool) : Prop := ∀ l q, chk q = true → r₁ l q = r₂ l q

Agreement on the checkable set is exactly what training can see: two reporters agreeing there are indistinguishable to any procedure whose only access to truth is the human label, however it is constructed or regularized. This is a definition rather than a theorem — we define the training signal to be a function of behavior on checkable questions, which is what the setup stipulates.

18.2. Underdetermination, without any diagonal🔗

The core needs no self-reference, no continuity, and no assumption about L. Given any reporter, build a second by copying it on checkable questions and flipping it elsewhere.

def c10_flipOff {L Q : Type _} (chk : Q → Bool) (rep : L → Q → Bool) : L → Q → Bool := fun l q => cond (chk q) (rep l q) (!(rep l q))

Lemma 10.5 (The variant is invisible to training). c10_flipOff agrees with the reporter it was built from on the whole checkable set.

theorem c10_flip_agrees {L Q : Type _} (chk : Q → Bool) (rep : L → Q → Bool) : c10_AgreesOn chk (c10_flipOff chk rep) rep := L:Type u_1Q:Type u_2chk:Q → Boolrep:L → Q → Bool⊢ c10_AgreesOn chk (c10_flipOff chk rep) rep intro l L:Type u_1Q:Type u_2chk:Q → Boolrep:L → Q → Booll:Lq:Q⊢ chk q = true → c10_flipOff chk rep l q = rep l q L:Type u_1Q:Type u_2chk:Q → Boolrep:L → Q → Booll:Lq:Qhq:chk q = true⊢ c10_flipOff chk rep l q = rep l q All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. On a checkable q the condition is true, and cond true a b reduces to a. ∎

Lemma 10.6 (The variant differs off it). At any unchecked question the two disagree.

theorem c10_flip_differs {L Q : Type _} (chk : Q → Bool) (rep : L → Q → Bool) (l : L) (q₀ : Q) (hq₀ : chk q₀ = false) : c10_flipOff chk rep l q₀ ≠ rep l q₀ := L:Type u_1Q:Type u_2chk:Q → Boolrep:L → Q → Booll:Lq₀:Qhq₀:chk q₀ = false⊢ c10_flipOff chk rep l q₀ ≠ rep l q₀ have h : c10_flipOff chk rep l q₀ = !(rep l q₀) := L:Type u_1Q:Type u_2chk:Q → Boolrep:L → Q → Booll:Lq₀:Qhq₀:chk q₀ = false⊢ c10_flipOff chk rep l q₀ ≠ rep l q₀ All goals completed! 🐙 L:Type u_1Q:Type u_2chk:Q → Boolrep:L → Q → Booll:Lq₀:Qhq₀:chk q₀ = falseh:c10_flipOff chk rep l q₀ = !rep l q₀ := of_eq_true (Eq.trans (congrFun' (congrArg Eq (congrFun' (congrFun' (congrArg cond hq₀) (rep l q₀)) !rep l q₀)) !rep l q₀) (eq_self !rep l q₀))⊢ (!rep l q₀) ≠ rep l q₀ All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. The condition is false, so the variant evaluates to the negation of the original, and bool_not_fpf says a Boolean is never its own negation. ∎

Note where bool_not_fpf works. It is the same fixed-point-free map that drives every diagonal here, used now for its plain content, !b ≠ b, with no diagonal construction around it.

Theorem 10.7 (Underdetermination). If any question is unchecked, then for every reporter there is a second, distinct reporter that training cannot distinguish from it.

theorem c10_underdetermined {L Q : Type _} (chk : Q → Bool) (rep : L → Q → Bool) (l : L) (q₀ : Q) (hq₀ : chk q₀ = false) : c10_AgreesOn chk (c10_flipOff chk rep) rep ∧ c10_flipOff chk rep l q₀ ≠ rep l q₀ := ⟨c10_flip_agrees chk rep, c10_flip_differs chk rep l q₀ hq₀⟩

Proof. Lemmas 10.5 and 10.6. ∎

That is the ELK problem, stated exactly and proved. The two reporters are points in a set the training signal cannot separate, and that set has more than one point as soon as a single question falls outside the checkable region. The construction is crude, and a real human simulator is subtler, but crudeness is the right property for an impossibility: if even the blunt variant is invisible, no argument about which reporter is simpler can be a proof, because simplicity was never what the signal measured.

Remark 10.8 (Why inductive bias is not a refutation). The standard hope is that the direct translator is favored by some prior and that gradient descent finds it. Theorem 10.7 does not rule that out. What it establishes is the burden of proof: any such argument must supply the missing ingredient from outside the training signal and defend it as a claim about the actual optimizer and architecture, because the data cannot supply it.

18.3. The identifiability criterion🔗

The converse of Theorem 10.7 is worth stating, because it says exactly what it would take to solve the problem, and the statement is one line.

Theorem 10.9 (Full checkability pins the reporter). If every question is checkable, then reporters agreeing on the checkable set are equal.

theorem c10_full_checkability_pins {L Q : Type _} (chk : Q → Bool) (r₁ r₂ : L → Q → Bool) (hchk : ∀ q, chk q = true) (h : c10_AgreesOn chk r₁ r₂) (l : L) (q : Q) : r₁ l q = r₂ l q := h l q (hchk q)

Proof. Apply the agreement hypothesis at the witness supplied by full checkability. ∎

Together these are a clean dichotomy: identifiability is equivalent to full checkability. There is no middle regime in which partial checking buys partial identification of the answers you care about, because those are by construction the unchecked ones.

This reframes what a solution would look like. Every proposal must either enlarge chk until it covers the cases that matter, or import a constraint that is not a function of behavior on chk. The first is scalable oversight, the honest reading of debate, amplification, and recursive reward modeling. The second is the inductive-bias family. The dichotomy says these are the only two doors.

18.4. Where the diagonal comes in🔗

The natural next move is to make everything checkable, and this is where the first engine enters, because that door is shut too. A checking procedure settling every question about the model, including questions about its own reports, is a total exact verdict over a self-describing domain. Read chk as the reach of the best checker you can build, and full checkability becomes the ambition of a universal verifier.

Theorem 10.10 (A reporter reading the latent state is still a verdict). If every pattern of answers over questions is realized by some question's latent state, the situation is contradictory.

theorem c10_reporter_factoring {L Q : Type _} (lat : Q → L) (rep : L → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, rep (lat p) = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict (fun p => rep (lat p)) hs

Proof. The composite is a reflective verdict, and no_reflective_verdict rules those out. ∎

Theorem 10.11 (The unanswerable question). Under the same hypothesis there is a question the reporter answers as its own negation.

theorem c10_reporter_liar {L Q : Type _} (lat : Q → L) (rep : L → Q → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : Q → Bool, ∃ p, rep (lat p) = g) : ∃ p, rep (lat p) p = !(rep (lat p) p) := liar_query (fun p => rep (lat p)) hs

Proof. liar_query at the composite. ∎

Now the two engines together, which is the point of the chapter. To distinguish the reporters you need a question they answer differently, and every such question lies outside the checkable set. To bring it inside you must extend chk to cover questions about what the model represents, including about its own reports.

So the distinguishing query and the liar query pull in opposite directions on the same set. Underdetermination pushes the decisive question out of the checkable region, and the diagonal blocks the region from being extended to reach it. The two reporters differ exactly where nobody can look, and the reason is not a shortage of resources.

Remark 10.12 (What is new relative to Chapter 8). There the diagonal was the whole argument and the representation a bystander. Here it is the second of two obstructions and does the smaller share of the work. Theorem 10.7 is pure counting: it holds for finite Q, for a model with three neurons, for a reporter implemented as a lookup table.

18.5. The analytic engine🔗

Suppose the reporter returns a confidence and the latent space is connected in the sense of Chapter 4, the usual situation for a learned representation over a continuous input space. Take two reporters agreeing on the checkable set and differing at some unchecked question. Along a path from a state where both say yes to one where they differ, the gap between their scores is continuous, starting at zero and ending nonzero, so by the IVT it passes through every value between.

So no threshold of agreement separates the two reporters cleanly. For any tolerance there are states where they agree within it and states just beyond where they do not, and the boundary is a surface, not a gap. A proposal that accepts a reporter agreeing within ε on held-out data is not selecting a reporter; it is selecting a neighborhood, and the neighborhood contains both answers to the question you care about.

18.6. What this does not claim🔗

It does not claim ELK is unsolvable. Theorem 10.9 is a sufficient condition and the dichotomy names the two families that remain open. What is ruled out is a solution working by training on checkable questions alone.

It does not claim the human simulator is what models learn. That is empirical, and Theorem 10.7 says the training signal does not settle it, not that the answer is bad.

It does not claim c10_flipOff is a realistic competitor. It is a witness chosen for being obviously invisible to training, and its role is to establish that the surviving set has more than one element.

It does not claim chk is a Boolean function of the question alone. Real checkability is graded, costly, and checker-dependent, and the graded version of Theorem 10.7 is the natural next result rather than a correction.

19. Watermarks, Paraphrase, and the Third Corner🔗

The preceding chapters put a probe inside a model. This one steps outside entirely. The question is whether a text was produced by a language model, and the dominant answer is watermarking: bias the sampling so the output carries a statistical signature only a key-holder can detect. It is elegant, deployed, and has a well-known weakness, that paraphrasing removes the signature.

That weakness is usually treated as an engineering race. This chapter argues the race has a fixed point, and locates it with a mechanism not yet used here. Neither engine is the primary tool; the primary tool is invariance under a group action, and the resulting theorem is a genuine trilemma: three properties, any two available, never all three.

The other engines then add something. The analytic one converts the trilemma into a statement about how many edits an attacker needs. The diagonal supplies something specific to this domain and absent from Chapters 8 through 10: here the surjectivity hypothesis is not an idealization, because a public detection API hands the attacker exactly the oracle the argument requires.

19.1. The construction🔗

Definition 11.1 (Text space and marking). Write X for the space of texts. Write mark : X → Bool for the fact of the matter, mark x = true when x was generated by the watermarked model. As in Chapter 9 this is ground truth, not something anyone computes.

Definition 11.2 (Detector). A detector is a map det : X → Bool, returning true when it judges the text to carry the mark. In practice det thresholds a statistic, typically a count of tokens falling in a pseudorandomly chosen green list, against a null distribution.

Definition 11.3 (Paraphrase). A paraphrase map is par : X → X sending a text to one that means the same thing. What means the same thing amounts to is doing real work here, and we return to it at the end. For the theorems below, all that matters is that par preserves whatever downstream property makes the text useful.

The three properties a detector is asked to have:

Definition 11.4 (Sound). A detector is sound when mark y = false → det y = false. Its failure produces a false accusation, the most direct human cost, since unmarked texts are the ones people wrote.

Definition 11.5 (Complete). A detector is complete when mark y = true → det y = true. This is what the watermark is for.

Definition 11.6 (Robust). A detector is robust against par when det (par x) = det x for all x. This is the exact limit of what the literature measures as detection rate surviving a paraphrase attack.

def c11_Sound {X : Type _} (det mark : X → Bool) : Prop := ∀ y, mark y = false → det y = false def c11_Complete {X : Type _} (det mark : X → Bool) : Prop := ∀ y, mark y = true → det y = true def c11_Robust {X : Type _} (det : X → Bool) (par : X → X) : Prop := ∀ x, det (par x) = det x

One more ingredient, the empirical fact the subject is organized around: a paraphraser can take marked text to unmarked text. This is not an assumption about detectors but a statement about what paraphrasing does to a signature carried by token choices.

Definition 11.7 (Stripping). A paraphrase map strips the mark at x when mark x = true and mark (par x) = false.

19.2. The trilemma🔗

Theorem 11.8 (Detection trilemma). No detector is sound, complete, and robust against a paraphrase map that strips the mark.

theorem c11_detection_trilemma {X : Type _} (det mark : X → Bool) (par : X → X) (hsound : c11_Sound det mark) (hcomplete : c11_Complete det mark) (hrobust : c11_Robust det par) (x : X) (hmark : mark x = true) (hstrip : mark (par x) = false) : False := X:Type u_1det:X → Boolmark:X → Boolpar:X → Xhsound:c11_Sound det markhcomplete:c11_Complete det markhrobust:c11_Robust det parx:Xhmark:mark x = truehstrip:mark (par x) = false⊢ False X:Type u_1det:X → Boolmark:X → Boolpar:X → Xhsound:c11_Sound det markhcomplete:c11_Complete det markhrobust:c11_Robust det parx:Xhmark:mark x = truehstrip:mark (par x) = falseh1:det x = true := hcomplete x hmark⊢ False X:Type u_1det:X → Boolmark:X → Boolpar:X → Xhsound:c11_Sound det markhcomplete:c11_Complete det markhrobust:c11_Robust det parx:Xhmark:mark x = truehstrip:mark (par x) = falseh1:det x = true := hcomplete x hmarkh2:det (par x) = false := hsound (par x) hstrip⊢ False X:Type u_1det:X → Boolmark:X → Boolpar:X → Xhsound:c11_Sound det markhcomplete:c11_Complete det markhrobust:c11_Robust det parx:Xhmark:mark x = truehstrip:mark (par x) = falseh1:det x = true := hcomplete x hmarkh2:true = false⊢ False All goals completed! 🐙

Proof. Completeness flags x, since it is marked. Soundness clears par x, since it is not. Robustness says those two verdicts are the same verdict. So true = false. ∎

Four lines, with no self-reference, no topology, and no assumption about X. What makes it a trilemma is that each hypothesis is individually achievable and dropping any one leaves a working system. Each corner is a real deployment.

Give up robustness. The watermark detects unmodified output, covering casual and not adversarial use. This is the honest state of most deployed watermarking. The failure mode is that the population you most want to detect is exactly the one willing to paraphrase.

Give up completeness. Raise the threshold and accept that some marked text goes unflagged. This is the right corner for high-stakes accusations, since it never accuses the innocent, and it is what a court would want. The failure mode is that the detector's silence carries no information.

Give up soundness. Accept false positives on human writing. Nobody defends this corner explicitly and several systems occupy it accidentally: a detector tuned aggressively enough to survive paraphrase flags text whose statistics merely resemble the model's, and human writing resembling model writing is common, since the model was trained to produce writing resembling ours.

Remark 11.9 (Why this is the shape and not an analogy). Theorem 11.8 is not the theorem of Chapter 3, and saying so would be overclaiming: its mechanism is invariance and its proof is not the diagonal. What it shares is the form of the conclusion. In Chapter 3 the third property was destroyed by a fixed-point-free flip; here by an orbit, with par moving a point while det must stay put and mark must move.

Corollary 11.10 (Invariance and truth cannot both hold along an orbit). If det is constant along par and mark is not, then det does not agree with mark everywhere.

theorem c11_invariance_vs_truth {X : Type _} (det mark : X → Bool) (par : X → X) (hinv : ∀ x, det (par x) = det x) (x : X) (hne : mark (par x) ≠ mark x) : ¬ (∀ y, det y = mark y) := fun h => hne (X:Type u_1det:X → Boolmark:X → Boolpar:X → Xhinv:∀ (x : X), det (par x) = det xx:Xhne:mark (par x) ≠ mark xh:∀ (y : X), det y = mark y⊢ mark (par x) = mark x All goals completed! 🐙)

Proof. If the detector agreed with the mark everywhere, rewrite both sides of mark (par x) = mark x into detector values; invariance closes it, contradicting the assumption that the mark moves. ∎

This is Theorem 11.8 with the watermarking vocabulary stripped out: a fact about functions on a set carrying a self-map, of which the watermarking reading is one instantiation. Chapter 5's attack basins are another, which is the connection the next section makes quantitative.

19.3. The diagonal, and why its price is low here🔗

Chapters 8 through 10 conceded that point-surjectivity is an idealization for a fixed network. This chapter needs no such concession, which makes the diagonal stronger here than anywhere except prompt injection.

A detector is useful only if someone can run it, whether as an API, a published statistic with a threshold, or a tool handed to a platform. An attacker who can call it can measure its verdict on any text, and one who can measure a verdict can construct a text achieving whatever pattern it likes by generating candidates and querying. Text is unrestricted, self-describing, and cheap in quantity.

Theorem 11.11 (An adaptive attacker finds the liar text). If every pattern of verdicts over texts is realized by some text, there is a text whose verdict is its own negation.

theorem c11_detector_liar {X : Type _} (det : X → X → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : X → Bool, ∃ t, det t = g) : ∃ t, det t t = !(det t t) := liar_query det hs

Proof. liar_query applied to the detector read as a self-verdict. ∎

Read det t s as the verdict on s when the detector has been configured, tuned, or prompted by t, which is the situation for any detector that is itself a language model and any whose threshold is set from a corpus an attacker can influence.

Theorem 11.12 (Detector composition does not help). Routing the verdict through any preprocessing stage leaves the impossibility intact.

theorem c11_pipeline_no_escape {X F : Type _} (feat : X → F) (det : F → X → Bool) (hs : ∀ g : X → Bool, ∃ t, det (feat t) = g) : False := no_reflective_verdict (fun t => det (feat t)) hs

Proof. The composite is a reflective verdict. ∎

This covers the family of proposals extracting features first, whether perplexity statistics, stylometric vectors, or a learned embedding: the extraction is a representation, and representations do not rescue verdicts.

19.4. The analytic engine, and the cost of an attack🔗

The trilemma is exact and says nothing about degree. Real detectors return a score and real paraphrasers make bounded edits, so the engineering question is how many edits it takes. This is Chapter 5's subject with unusually concrete units.

Let s : X → ℝ be the score, with det x = true exactly when s x > τ, and suppose the score is Lipschitz with respect to an edit distance, which is the formal content of the requirement that one substitution cannot swing the statistic wildly. Chapter 5 runs verbatim: a marked text sits above τ, an unmarked paraphrase below, the intermediate edits are connected, so the score crosses. The number of edits needed to reach the crossing is bounded below by (s x − τ)/L.

That inequality is the quantitative theory of watermark robustness in one line, with the right behavior in both variables. Strengthening the watermark raises s x and so raises attack cost, which is why aggressive green-list biasing is more robust. Smoothing the detector lowers L and also raises attack cost, which is why aggregating over longer spans helps.

So the exact trilemma and the quantitative law say one thing at two resolutions. Chapter 6's bridges connect them: the exact statement is the zero-slack corner, and no deployed system lives there.

19.5. What this does not claim🔗

It does not claim watermarking is pointless. Theorem 11.8 is a statement about the three exact corners, and the useful deployments live at the corners the theorem leaves open. A watermark that detects unmodified output soundly and completely is a real capability with real applications, and giving up robustness is a coherent design decision rather than a failure.

It does not claim paraphrase is free. The whole content of the analytic section is that stripping the mark has a cost, that the cost is computable from the detector's own parameters, and that raising it is the legitimate goal of watermark design. The trilemma says the cost cannot be made infinite; it does not say it cannot be made high.

It does not settle what par is. A paraphraser degrading the text until it is useless has not defeated the detector in any sense that concerns anyone. A serious treatment would carry a utility function on texts and require the paraphrase to preserve it above a floor, which is exactly the structure of the Defense Trilemma, and the two results would then be instances of one statement. That unification is not attempted here.

It does not claim the stripping hypothesis holds for every watermark. Theorem 11.8 needs a paraphrase that actually removes the mark at some text. A scheme whose signature survives every meaning-preserving edit would escape the theorem, and no theorem in this book rules such a scheme out.

20. Does the Constraint Bind? Measurements on Five Models🔗

The theorems of Part II assume properties that no finite system has exactly. Coverage asks that the model be strictly right somewhere and strictly wrong somewhere; strict calibration asks that confidence exceed one half exactly when the answer is true; the diagonal results ask that every verdict pattern be realized by some input. A language model with a finite context and a finite vocabulary satisfies none of these on the nose, and Example 3.3 in Part I says so directly: no finite system is universal once the output type has two elements.

If that were the end of it, the thesis would prove elegant theorems about objects that do not exist. This chapter is the argument that it is not the end of it, and it is the chapter that could have come out the other way.

20.1. What an experiment can and cannot do here🔗

An impossibility theorem is not confirmed by observation. One does not measure a non-existence, and no run reported below establishes that some property is unachievable. What measurement can do is address the hypotheses, and there are exactly three useful questions.

First, whether the hypotheses hold, or nearly hold, in a real system. Second, whether the quantitative corollaries predict the numbers one measures. Third, whether the constraint binds rather than being satisfied vacuously by a system that fails a hypothesis outright.

All three are properties of the assumptions rather than of the conclusion, and none of them transfers between theorems resting on different assumptions. This sets the unit of validation. The correct unit is not one experiment per trilemma, which would be arbitrary, but one per distinct hypothesis family. The results of this thesis have three such families: the analytic-geometric family (continuity, Lipschitz bounds, utility preservation), the calibration family (continuity of confidence, strict calibration, coverage), and the combinatorial family (universality, in the sense of surjectivity of a self-application). This chapter reports on the second, and Section 15.5 explains what the first and third inherit from it.

20.2. The slack parameter is the quantity to measure🔗

Chapter 9 replaces each exact hypothesis of the continuous trilemma with a tolerance. In place of exact calibration it asks only that the confidence separate the two sides of the truth boundary by a margin, and in place of a truth-distance pinned to zero the conclusion confines it to a band. The verified statement is two_slack_approx_coupling in HoF_12_Approximate, carrying the truth slack and the confidence margin as separate parameters, and exact_from_approx recovers the exact coupling of Theorem 7.16 as the slack goes to zero.

That parameter is the thesis's bridge to reality, and it is measurable. A model with a large slack is one for which the theorem says little: the band in which it may be confident and wrong is wide, and the impossibility is correspondingly weak. A model with a small slack is one the exact theorem nearly describes. So the question that decides whether this thesis is about anything is not whether the slack is zero, which it is not, but which way it moves as models improve.

20.3. Method🔗

The measurements reuse the artifacts of the truth-boundary experiments without re-running inference; the analysis script is Thesis/analysis/coupling_trend.py and reads only committed files. Five open-weight models spanning roughly an order of magnitude in parameters were probed: GPT-2, Pythia-410m, Qwen2.5-0.5b, Phi-1.5, and Qwen2.5-1.5b.

For each model the harness constructs interpolation paths between pairs of statements whose truth values differ, records the signed truth-distance and the confidence at forty-one points along each path, and locates the crossing. Three quantities matter here.

The coupling gap is the distance, in path parameter, between the point where the truth-distance changes sign and the point where confidence crosses one half. It is the measured slack: the exact theorem says these coincide, and the gap is how far from coinciding they are. Medians and bootstrap confidence intervals are reported.

The decisive fraction is the proportion of paths on which the model's own confidence actually crosses the threshold, committing to both sides. This is the coverage hypothesis, measured directly.

The oddness defect measures how far the confidence field is from the antipodal symmetry that the Borsuk-Ulam route of HoF_08_BorsukUlam assumes.

A note on instrumentation. The coupling gap can be read either from a fitted linear or MLP probe or from the model's own confidence. The probe route is more sensitive but confounded: probe test accuracy climbs from 0.659 to 0.997 across this ladder, so a shrinking probe-measured gap could reflect a better instrument rather than a better-coupled model. The endogenous route, using the model's own confidence, does not have this defect, and the headline numbers below are the endogenous ones. Both are reported.

20.4. Results🔗

The table gives, for each model, the endogenous coupling gap with its bootstrap interval, the decisive fraction, the oddness defect, and the probe accuracy that the endogenous column is designed to avoid depending on.

| Model | Params | Coupling gap ε | 95% CI | Decisive | Oddness | Probe acc | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | GPT-2 | 0.12B | 0.225 | 0.150–0.375 | 0.434 | 0.395 | 0.659 | | Pythia-410m | 0.41B | — | — | 0.000 | 0.435 | 0.758 | | Qwen2.5-0.5b | 0.50B | 0.125 | 0.100–0.150 | 0.934 | 0.298 | 0.943 | | Phi-1.5 | 1.3B | 0.400 | 0.300–0.500 | 0.662 | 0.528 | 0.775 | | Qwen2.5-1.5b | 1.5B | 0.075 | 0.075–0.100 | 0.993 | 0.172 | 0.997 |

Two trends and one exception.

The coupling gap falls monotonically along the capability ladder, from 0.225 at GPT-2 to 0.075 at Qwen2.5-1.5b, and the bootstrap intervals of the endpoints do not overlap. The band in which a model can be confident and wrong is narrowing. Read against exact_from_approx, the sequence is moving toward the regime in which the exact trilemma, not merely its approximate form, describes the system.

The decisive fraction rises from 0.434 to 0.993. The coverage hypothesis, which the exact theorem simply assumes, is increasingly satisfied in fact. Together with the first trend this is the substantive finding of the chapter: both hypotheses the theorem consumes are better met the more capable the model is. The impossibility does not weaken as systems improve. It tightens.

The exception is Phi-1.5, and it breaks the pattern on every measure: a coupling gap of 0.400 at 1.3B parameters, the worst oddness defect in the set, and a probe accuracy far below its neighbors by size. Against log-parameters the correlation for the linear-probe gap is −0.276 with Phi-1.5 included and −0.927 without it. The point is not dropped, and the defensible reading is the weaker one: the slack decreases with capability within a training regime, and Phi-1.5, trained largely on synthetic textbook data, shows that the regime matters at least as much as the parameter count. A single line through five points is not what the data supports.

20.5. Pythia-410m occupies a corner🔗

Pythia-410m has a decisive fraction of exactly zero. On no path does its confidence cross the threshold, so it never commits, so the coverage hypothesis fails, so the trilemma does not apply to it at all. Its coupling gap is not large; it is undefined.

This is the corner structure of Chapter 6 appearing in data, and it was not designed for. A model that never commits cannot be caught in the coupling, because the theorem needs a witness on each side to run the intermediate value argument. Chapter 10 calls this the abstention corner and prices it in refused queries. Pythia-410m occupies that corner not as a policy but as a consequence of being unable to do the task.

The reading is that capability is what evicts a system from the safe corner. A model too weak to commit is trivially safe from the trilemma and useless; the models that commit on 93% and 99% of paths are the ones the theorem describes. Whatever is unsatisfying about that is a fact about the constraint, not about the measurement.

20.6. What the other two families inherit🔗

The analytic-geometric family is validated separately, by the defense experiments: classifier gate maps for two deployed guard models, threshold sweeps, and the pipeline degradation runs. Those measure the same kind of quantity, a slack against a hypothesis, in the setting of Chapter 8.

The combinatorial family is the one this chapter does not measure, and the reason is that universality is a structural property rather than a magnitude: there is no number to check. Its approximate form is a different matter. The corpus defines ApproxICLUniversal in CCH_LLM_Direct, requiring only that every target behavior be realized to within a tolerance by some prompt, and LLM_approx_trilemma shows the contradiction fires as soon as the control margin exceeds the sum of that tolerance and twice the introspection error. That threshold is measurable in principle by prompt fitting, it is not measured here, and Chapter 16 lists it as the most valuable single experiment this thesis does not contain.

20.7. Threats to validity🔗

Five models is a small sample, and three of the five come from two families. Most of the clean trend is carried by the two Qwen checkpoints, which share a training pipeline; the claim that capability rather than pipeline is doing the work would be better supported by a ladder within a single family spanning more scales.

The coupling gap is measured in path parameter, not in a natural unit of the model's output space, so the values are comparable across models on these paths and are not absolute quantities. The claim is about the direction of the trend and not about the numbers themselves.

The statement pairs are drawn from a template set, and template artifacts could in principle produce a spurious trend if larger models are more sensitive to templates. The endogenous measurement mitigates the probe-quality confound but not this one.

Finally, and most importantly, the trend is an association across five checkpoints, not a controlled manipulation. Nothing here establishes that increasing capability causes the slack to fall. The prediction the thesis makes is falsifiable and was not falsified by these five models, which is a weaker and more accurate statement than the claim that it was confirmed.

21. Part IV: Assessment🔗

22. Limitations🔗

This chapter states what is wrong with the thesis, or most likely to be. It is organized from the assumptions whose failure would cost the most to the ones whose failure would cost the least.

22.1. The unification claim is not fully supported🔗

The thesis statement says the impossibility results are instances of two schemas. Two of the four case studies are not.

Chapter 13 reaches its main result by a counting argument: two reporters agreeing on a checkable subset may disagree off it, and nothing self-referential is required. Chapter 14 reaches its main result by invariance: a detector constant along paraphrase orbits cannot track a mark that varies along them, and again no diagonal appears. Both chapters contain diagonal corollaries, and both say plainly that the corollary is not what does the work.

The accurate version of the thesis statement is therefore weaker than the headline: the two schemas generate a large family of these results, they generate every result in Part II, and they do not generate everything in the neighborhood. I have preferred to report the boundary rather than to define the family so as to exclude the counterexamples, which would make the claim true and empty.

22.2. Continuity and connectedness of prompt space🔗

The analytic engine requires a connected domain and continuous maps on it. Prompt space is a set of finite token sequences, which is discrete, and no amount of topology-talk changes that.

Three responses appear in the thesis, and none is fully satisfying. Chapter 9's discrete bridge proves the arithmetic core over the integers with no analysis at all, which shows the conclusion does not depend on the continuum, but at the cost of assuming a discrete sign change that is itself a hypothesis about the model. MoF_ContinuousRelaxation uses a Tietze extension to carry discrete data into the continuous theory, which is legitimate and does assume the extension is the right idealization. And embeddings are genuinely continuous, so a model factoring through an embedding inherits continuity on that factor.

An examiner who rejects all three is left with theorems about an idealization. I think the discrete bridge answers the objection, and I record that it is the assumption most often challenged and the one I would attack first.

22.3. Pointwise calibration is stronger than the literature's🔗

The trilemma's calibration hypothesis is pointwise and exact, and the calibration literature's is statistical and averaged. The trilemma is therefore not a result about reliability diagrams, and the temptation to present it as one should be resisted. Its force in the statistical setting comes only through the approximate results of Chapter 9, and how much force survives that translation is a question this thesis does not settle.

22.4. The empirical claim rests on five checkpoints🔗

Chapter 15's threats to validity are not repeated here, but the headline is that five models, dominated by two families, with an outlier that breaks the trend, is thin evidence for a claim about capability in general. The trend is consistent with the thesis and does not establish it.

22.5. The most valuable missing experiment🔗

The combinatorial family is unmeasured. ApproxICLUniversal gives the tolerance that a real system would have to meet, and LLM_approx_trilemma gives the threshold at which the contradiction fires, but no measurement of that tolerance appears in this thesis.
